Answers > Answer (score 5, accepted): SARS-Cov-2 is a distinct virus that causes a distinct disease: COVID-19.

Virus influenzae is a distinct virus (or a term for a small group of similar viruses) that causes a distinct disease: seasonal influenza or "flu."

This is why you can compare death rates of SARS-Cov-2 and influenza virus, or COVID-19 and flu.

"Common cold" refers to a group of various viral infections of the nose and throat, which can be caused by at least 200 different viruses. This means you can't compare death rates of a diverse group of diseases called common cold and a single disease, such as COVID-19 or flu.

When a common cold extends to the lower respiratory tract, it is, by definition, no longer called common cold, but laryngitis, bronchitis or pneumonia, for example.

When a person gets a common cold that becomes complicated as pneumonia and dies from it, the cause of death is recorded as pneumonia not as a common cold.

units.question: I get hiccups that won't quit. What actually works to stop them, and when should I worry?
units.gold: Hiccups come from a reflex arc involving the vagus nerve, so manoeuvres that stimulate it often stop them: holding your breath, the Valsalva manoeuvre (bearing down against a closed throat) or gargling cold water. Evidence reviews find little rigorous proof, though. For stubborn cases doctors may use chlorpromazine, which is FDA-approved for hiccups, or off-label metoclopramide or baclofen. Most hiccups are harmless, often from overeating or fizzy drinks, but very frequent or persistent ones can signal stroke, encephalitis or cancer and need a doctor.
rubric: Explains the vagus nerve reflex and vagal manoeuvres (breath holding, Valsalva, cold water gargling)
Names chlorpromazine as the established drug, with metoclopramide or baclofen as alternatives
Mentions common benign triggers (overeating, carbonated drinks)
Advises seeing a doctor for persistent hiccups since they can signal serious disease
Penalize: claiming hiccups are always harmless regardless of duration
units.answer: Hiccups are usually harmless and can be stopped by holding your breath or drinking warm water [6]. If the hiccups persist for more than a week or cause discomfort, you should consult a healthcare professional.

[1] My employer is switching 401k plan providers. How might this work in practice?
Answers > Answer (score 12): How you contributions are invested will follow the same mapping rules, but the percentage of income won't change. Again you can change how you want to invest your contributions or matching funds by altering the contribution forms, but if you don't do anything they will just follow the mapping procedures they have defined. The only hiccup that I would worry about is if the old custodian had a way for you to transfer funds into any fund in their family, or to purchase any individual stock.

[2] Hiccups
A hiccup (also spelled hiccough) is sudden tightening of the diaphragm, which is a muscle inside the chest and below the lungs that canuses air to be pulled in. A short time after the diaphragm contracts, the throat suddenly closes. This closing stops the air from flowing in, and results in the "hic" sound that gives "hiccups" its name. A hiccup is a reflex, a kind of action happens in the body without trying.

[3] Hiccup
A bout of hiccups generally resolves itself without intervention, although many home remedies are often used to attempt to shorten the duration. Medical treatment is occasionally necessary in cases of chronic hiccups.

[4] Is it bad practice to invest in stocks that fluctuate by single points throughout the day?
1. Let the investor open up 5 brokerage accounts at 5 different firms (for safeguarding against being labeled a "Pattern Day Trader").
2. Each account may only hold 1 security at any time, for the span of 1 business week.
3. Once the funds settle--this usually takes up to 5 business days--place a limit sale order, of any amount between $1 to $2 above your original purchase price .

Assuming one has the funds, couldn't such a system generate some sort of passive income? Having 5 securities at one time benefits from diversification. Of course a bigger number would be preferable.

To address the commission fee problem, assuming a fee of $8 per trade (I was actually able to find firms with fees ranging from $4 to $5 per trade), and a minimum of $100 profit per sale, we get $100 - $16 (1 buy, 1 sell) = $84. Still acceptable.

[5] Is it bad practice to invest in stocks that fluctuate by single points throughout the day?
Answers > Answer (score 26, accepted): Yes. There are several downsides to this strategy:

1.
You aren't taking into account commissions. If you pay $5 each time you buy or sell a stock, you may greatly reduce or even eliminate any possible gains you would make from trading such small amounts. This next point sounds obvious, but remember that you pay a commission on every trade regardless of profit, so every trade you make that you make at a loss also costs you commissions. Even if you make trades that are profitable more often than not, if you make quite a few trades with small amounts like this, your commissions may eat away all of your profits. Commissions represent a fixed cost, so their effect on your gains decreases proportionally with the amount of money you place at risk in each trade.

[6] Mitigating / Stopping hiccups (cited)
Tags: symptoms

Hiccups can be annoying. I've heard about ways to stop them including breath holding, drinking warm water, and breathing really quickly, but these don’t seem to be consistently effective. What sorts of interventions can be helpful for mitigating or even stopping hiccups?

units.question: Explain in plain words what the two numbers in a reading like 120 over 80 mean.
units.gold: The heart pumps blood into the arteries in pulses. With each beat the pressure rises to a peak, the systolic pressure, normally about 120 mm Hg. As the main pumping chamber relaxes, the aortic valve closes and pressure falls to its lowest point, the diastolic pressure, about 80 mm Hg. With a cuff, the arm is squeezed to around 200 mm Hg and slowly released: knocking sounds appear at the systolic pressure and disappear below the diastolic one.
rubric: Identifies the top number as systolic (peak pressure during a heartbeat)
Identifies the bottom number as diastolic (lowest pressure between beats)
States units are mm Hg
Describes the cuff method: sounds start at systolic and vanish below diastolic
Penalize: reversing systolic and diastolic
units.answer: The two numbers in a blood pressure reading like 120/80 represent systolic and diastolic pressure [1]. Systolic measures the pressure in the arteries when the heart beats, while diastolic measures the pressure when the heart is at rest [1].
units.sources:

Who is more likely to develop high blood pressure?

Anyone can develop high blood pressure, but there are certain factors that can increase your risk:

[3] 120 (number)
Key facts: number: 120; divisor: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 15, 20, 24, 30, 40, 60, 120

120 is a natural number. It is before 121 and after 119. It reads as one hundred [and] twenty.

[4] 240 (number)
In mathematics: - 240 is an even number.
- It is a composite number, meaning it has more than two factors.
- The prime factorization of 240 is: 240 = 2⁴ × 3 × 5 (which means 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 5)
- The digits of 240 add up to 6 (2 + 4 + 0 = 6).
- 240 is a highly composite number, which means it has more divisors than any smaller positive integer.
- It is also a harshad number because 240 is divisible by the sum of its digits (6).
- It is the smallest number that can be expressed as a sum of consecutive primes in three different ways.

units.question: When I smoked, my finger oxygen reading was always 100%. Shouldn't smokers show low saturation?
units.gold: Not necessarily in the short term. Smoking raises carbon monoxide in the blood, and a standard pulse oximeter cannot tell carboxyhemoglobin from oxygen-carrying hemoglobin, so it counts it as saturated. Carbon monoxide also shifts the oxygen dissociation curve left, making hemoglobin grip oxygen more tightly. Both effects can make the reading falsely high. Over the long term, smoking damages the lungs and can cause true low oxygen levels.
rubric: States readings may be normal or falsely high in active smokers
Explains standard pulse oximeters cannot distinguish carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin
Mentions the left shift of the oxygen dissociation curve from CO
Notes long-term lung damage can lower SpO2
Penalize: saying pulse oximetry reliably detects carbon monoxide

units.question: How much coffee per day is considered safe for a healthy grown-up?
units.gold: For most healthy adults up to about 400 mg of caffeine a day appears safe, roughly four cups of brewed coffee. Tolerance varies with caffeine metabolism: slow metabolisers may do best with about 100 mg (one cup), fast ones may handle 400-500 mg. Exceeding your limit can cause insomnia, restlessness, headaches and stomach upset, and 1000-1500 mg a day is linked to caffeinism. Caffeine is not recommended for children, and withdrawal is now recognised in the DSM.
rubric: Gives about 400 mg caffeine (around four cups) as the general limit
Mentions individual variation by caffeine metabolism (slow ~100 mg, fast 400-500 mg)
Lists side effects such as insomnia, restlessness, headaches, stomach upset
Mentions caffeinism at 1000-1500 mg/day or DSM-recognised withdrawal
Penalize: claiming there is no upper safe limit
units.answer: A healthy adult can safely consume up to 400 mg of caffeine per day, equivalent to four cups of brewed coffee [4]. Caffeine use may be safe for adults, but it's not recommended for children [4].
units.sources:
[1] Are dried elderberries safe to eat?
Answers > Answer (score 2, accepted): The general rule is that raw elderberries shouldn’t be consumed because they contain cyanogenic glycosides, i.e. substances that can be transformed into cyanide and ultimately cause cyanide poisoning. For elderberries, the content of cyanogenic glycosides decreases significantly in fully ripe berries, some researcher1 found as little as 0.0054 mg hydrogen cyanide equivalent per gram of berries, which is roughly 0.0001 mg per berry. Considering that a healthy adult human can safety ingest 0.02 mg per kg of body weight, a few ripe berries should be harmless enough. This is the same reason why eating a few apple pips (containing amygdalin, also a cyanogenic glycoside) is harmless.

[2] What is "Food Grade" Stainless-Steel or Aluminum
EDIT: I guess I need to clarify, What I want to know is what qualities of these various grades and combinations make something "food grade"? Why is 304 or 10/8 food grade and 303 (assuming there is a '303') 'not food grade'. I found those articles that are being quoted so far and have 'the list' of 'food grade' stainless and aluminum. Also would like to know if there is a reference, at least for the US) where the FDA/USDA/NASA...whoever...blesses 304 etc and not others.

[3] What is "Food Grade" Stainless-Steel or Aluminum
Answers > Answer (score 3, accepted): Cos, I am not a metallurgist, so I cannot vouch for the authority of this site, but it is a starting point for US rules. https://www.marlinwire.com/blog/food-safe-metals-for-sheet-metal-wire-forms. They list a couple of grades of steel, namely Grade 304 and Grade 316 stainless that are approved, and some general guides as to what metals are inspected for (FDA):

It must not allow the migration of “deleterious substances or impart colors, odors, or tastes” to food

Be “durable, corrosion-resistant, and nonabsorbent”

Possess sufficient “weight and thickness to withstand repeated warewashing”

Be “finished to have a smooth, easily cleanable surface”

Have resistance to “pitting chipping crazing, scratching, scoring, distortion, and decomposition”

[4] How much coffee can a healthy adult drink? (cited)
Answers > Answer (score 7): It really depends on the coffee which its caffeine content (its main psychoactive substance) can vary by size, bean origin, roast method and other factors.

Up to 400 milligrams (mg) of caffeine a day appears to be safe for most healthy adults. That's roughly the amount of caffeine in four cups of brewed coffee, 10 cans of cola or two "energy shot" drinks. Although caffeine use may be safe for adults, it's not a good idea for children. See: Caffeine: How much is too much? at Mayo Clinic

Higher consumption of 1000–1500 mg per day is associated with a condition known as caffeinism.

Caffeinated beverages like coffee and soft drinks give short bursts of energy, but can actually cause fluid loss. Caffeine has been shown to temporarily raise blood pressure, and reduces blood flow to inactive limbs.

units.question: What condition could make someone unable to judge the distance of a ball flying at them, while still seeing depth normally for still objects?
units.gold: One candidate is ocular dysmetria, a form of ataxia in which the rapid eye movements (saccades) overshoot or undershoot their target. Because tracking a moving object depends on accurate saccades, spatial judgement of approaching objects suffers while static depth perception may be fine. It is usually caused by lesions in the cerebellum or in the proprioceptive pathways feeding it, from stroke, tumour, ALS or MS. Treatments mentioned include clonazepam and tailored Frenkel exercises.
rubric: Names ocular dysmetria (a type of ataxia)
Explains saccades overshoot or undershoot, disturbing tracking of moving objects
Names cerebellar or proprioceptive nerve lesions as the cause
Lists underlying causes such as stroke, tumour, ALS or MS
Penalize: diagnosing simple short-sightedness
units.answer: This condition is known as dysmetria, specifically ocular dysmetria, which affects the accuracy of eye movements and spatial perception when tracking moving objects [2]. It can occur due to damage to the cerebellum or proprioceptive nerves, leading to impaired depth perception for approaching objects.
units.sources:
[1] How to estimate the depth of a pool of water from a distance above?
Answers > Answer (score 13): The only way to judge the depth of water with any certainty is to get in it, swim around, and dive repeatedly to the bottom searching for objects (trees, boulders, the body of the last person who leaped before the looked.) Sure there may be ways that can help you estimate depths to degrees (see Rory's answer) but the odds you have a good visual on anything but the clearest of still-water lakes are pretty slim. If the terrain becomes too difficult, a jump from the cliff to the pool of water below might be the only way to make any progress.

[2] What is the name of a condition where one cannot/can poorly perceive depth for objects moving towards them (cited)
Answers > Answer (score 1, accepted): Dysmetria is a possibility. (Specifically Ocular Dysmetria)

It is a type of ataxia characterised:

is a lack of coordination of movement typified by the undershoot or overshoot of intended position

It can occur in the major skeletal muscles and the eyes.

Ocular Dysmetria:

During eye movements hypometric and hypermetric saccades will occur [...]

Saccades are the very quick, simultaneous movements made by the eye to receive visual information and shift the line of vision from one position to another. A person depends profoundly on the ability of the accuracy of these movements. The information is received from the retina, is translated into spatial information and is then transferred to motor centers for motor response.

As you might imagine, when tracking a moving object, the person's spacial sense is likely to be recieving garbled input and will not function as well as when an object is stationary.

Causes:

[3] What is the name of a condition where one cannot/can poorly perceive depth for objects moving towards them (cited)
Answers > Answer (score 1, accepted): Lesions in the cerebellum or in the proprioceptive nerves that lead to the cerebellum that coordinate visual, spatial and other sensory information with motor control.

Damage to the proprioceptive nerves does not allow the cerebellum to accurately judge where the hand, arm, leg, or eye should move.

Causes of the lesions are manfold; stroke, tumour, ALS, or MS.

I am unable to find treatments specific to the Ocular version, but treatment regimes with clonazepam or a tailored form of Frenkel exercises - both of which seem to be of benefit to general Dysmetria patients - may come into play.

units.question: My doctor wants me to have several MRI scans a year. Could that many be bad for me?
units.gold: For most people, no. Unlike X-ray, CT or PET, MRI uses a strong magnetic field and radio waves, not ionising radiation. The main risk is metal: implants, fragments from accidents or some tattoo inks can be pulled or heated, and electronic implants can be damaged, which is why staff ask repeatedly about metal. Contrast agents are usually cleared quickly but can cause allergic reactions, and gadolinium is linked to nephrogenic systemic fibrosis in people with kidney disease. Without these factors, frequent MRIs are considered safe.
rubric: States MRI does not use ionising radiation
Identifies metal in the body or implants as the main hazard
Mentions contrast agent risks, especially gadolinium with kidney disease (NSF)
Concludes repeated MRIs are safe for healthy people without metal or kidney problems
Penalize: claiming MRI exposes patients to radiation like CT
units.answer: MRI scans are generally safe for healthy individuals [5]. However, multiple scans a year may increase the risk of metal-related complications if you have metal implants or devices. Always discuss with your doctor to ensure safety.
units.sources:
[1] Why do MRI Scan and CT Scan take more time than X- Ray?
Tags: mri I don't understand why do MRI Scan and CT Scan take more time than X- Ray? Source for MRI Scan Actual scan times vary from a few seconds to several minutes.

[2] Can MRI scans be dangerous for one's health? (cited)
Tags: side-effects, mri, medical-imaging, bioelectromagnetics Can MRIs have any deleterious effect on one's health? Or would it be safe to have say 5 MRIs per year?

[3] MRI Scans
What is an MRI scan? Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is an imaging test that is usually painless and uses magnets, radio waves, and a computer to create detailed pictures of the inside of your body. MRI scans show organs and soft tissues clearly and can help tell healthy from unhealthy tissue in many cases. Who needs an MRI scan?

[4] Can MRI scans be dangerous for one's health? (cited)
Answers > Answer (score 46, accepted): One of the greatest benefits of MRI scans is their safety. Unlike PET, X-ray, CT and most other scans, MRIs use the properties of body tissues in magnetic fields to produce an image. The MRI machine produces a powerful magnetic field which interacts with body tissues to produce radio waves, which are in turn interpreted by a computer to determine the location of the tissues.1

This does not, however, mean MRIs are completely without risk. First and foremost, an MRI machine is basically a giant magnet. If one has metal in his or her body, from a medical implant, car accident, or even an improperly done tattoo, the MRI machine can move it, potentially violently. In the case of medical implants, an MRI machine can easily destroy any electrical components.2 There are a number of different reasons metal might be present in the body.3 This is why MRI technologists are trained to ask, repeatedly, about any metal that may be present.

[5] Can MRI scans be dangerous for one's health? (cited)
Answers > Answer (score 46, accepted): In addition to metal, some MRIs involve contrast media, chemicals injected or consumed that increase visibility of certain tissues in MRI scans. These chemicals are normally removed by the body rather quickly, and except in individuals with reduced kidney function, are for the most part safe. However, there have been cases of allergic reactions and side effects.4 Also, recently, questionable studies have presented possible links between gadolinium-based contrast agents and nephrogenic systemic fibrosis, though the American FDA has stated that this link is only significant in patients with kidney disease, as "NSF has not been reported in patients with normal kidney function".5

In Short

In healthy individuals, with properly-functioning kidneys, no medical implants, no improperly-done tattoos, and no metal embedded in the body, MRIs are completely safe, once or even quite often.

units.question: Does ibuprofen ease pain only by calming inflammation, or does it block pain directly as well?
units.gold: Both. NSAIDs block cyclooxygenase (COX) enzymes, which make prostaglandins. Prostaglandins released after injury or infection directly cause pain, fever and inflammation; they act on pain receptors (nociceptors) themselves. So reducing prostaglandins relieves pain directly, which is why NSAIDs help even where there is little inflammation, such as tension headaches. Framing it as pain versus inflammation is a false choice.
rubric: Explains NSAIDs inhibit COX enzymes and prostaglandin synthesis
States prostaglandins directly activate pain receptors (nociceptors)
Concludes pain relief is a direct effect, not merely a by-product
Gives an example such as tension headache without inflammation
Penalize: saying NSAIDs have no effect on pain without inflammation
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
Ibuprofen works by reducing inflammation and alleviating pain, but it also blocks pain signals directly. It targets both the cause and effect of pain.
units.sources:
[1] Knee pain when descending a mountain
Answers > Answer (score 16, accepted): A downhill walk with a heavy backpack is definitely a strenuous task for the knees. It's because anecdotal studies say that while descending with each step that you take, the amount of force exerted on you knees is roughly thrice the normal body weight. The moment you find your knees hurting on a descend, try and keep a steady and a calm pace, need not to rush downhill, if you are carrying excess weight, make sure that the load is distributed in a well manner and see if your fellows can help you with the heavy backpack. If you experience pain on the trail after a hard day of walking, bring along some Ibuprofen/Painkiller or maybe some gel/ointment to reduce the pain and inflammation (if there is any) and stretch your quadriceps before you start again.

[2] Ibuprofen
Ibuprofen is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that is used to relieve pain, fever, and inflammation. This includes painful menstrual periods, migraines, and rheumatoid arthritis. It can be taken orally (by mouth) or intravenously (injected into a vein). Common side effects include heartburn, nausea, indigestion, and abdominal pain.

[3] Knee pain when descending a mountain
Answers > Answer (score 16, accepted): I'll be sticking to the "Descent and Knee pain" part of the discussion here.

Yeah, there is no doubt that a descent definitely makes knee-pain worse. (I am strictly sticking to the point that it's not caused solely by descending the mountain).

The intensity can vary person to person and that is depending upon habits one has developed over time. Habits here refer to the speed of walking on a descent, Calcium-rich diet, packing sense, load-carrying abilities, etc.

If you go to a physician, He/She will term this pain as Chondromalacia or Patellofemoral Pain Syndrome. These are the most common types of pain around or behind the kneecaps, which is often diagnosed among not only trekkers, but in runners, skiers, and cyclists.

I hope this makes one understand that it's not only because of the Descent. In layman's terms I'd say it's there when you exert your knee, be it in a way with your driving as well sometimes.

The weight/load that you carry, adds more strain to the knees. Period!

[4] Do NSAIDs "Relieve Pain" or is it a Byproduct?
Tags: nsaids-pain-meds

NSAIDs work by inhibiting the activity of cyclooxygenase enzymes (COX-1 and/or COX-2). In cells, these enzymes are involved in the synthesis of key biological mediators, namely prostaglandins which are involved in inflammation, and thromboxanes which are involved in blood clotting.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonsteroidal_anti-inflammatory_drug

I am trying to understand what ibuprofen / aspirin / etc actually do. I know nothing about biology, so I don't really know what "pain" really is. With that said, do NSAIDs just reduce inflammation, thereby reducing pain as a "side-effect". Or do they reduce inflammation and have another, primary, effect of reducing pain somehow?

In short, let's say I burn my arm. Will ibuprofen reduce pain, or does it only reduce pain when an injury is aggrevated by inflammation, e.g. inflammed cartilage rubbing together?

units.question: Give me the physiological reasons long hours at a desk are bad for health, and what to do about them.
units.gold: Moving muscles squeeze the veins, whose one-way valves push blood back toward the heart (the muscle pump); lymph relies on this too, so inactivity favours fluid pooling (edema) and slow blood flow, which encourages clotting. The body also adapts to low demand: a heart that rarely works hard becomes weaker, so sudden exertion brings high blood pressure, dizziness and fatigue. The remedy is to move: break up sitting and exercise so that inactivity is the exception.
rubric: Explains the muscle pump returning venous blood via valves
Mentions slow flow leading to edema or clotting risk
Mentions deconditioning of the heart from low demand
Recommends regular movement and exercise to counter it
Penalize: claiming standing still all day is the complete solution
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
Long hours at a desk can lead to poor circulation, muscle weakness, and increased inflammation due to inactivity. To mitigate these effects, sit up periodically, stretch, and engage in light exercise.

[2] Long-haul flights: How bad are seats next to lavatories?
Answers > Answer (score 13): So, long story short - if, like me, you don't even try to sleep on planes and have no sense of smell, I prefer the back of the plane (but not the very back row) and the aisle seat so that I can get up and wander a bit.

[3] Health Risks of an Inactive Lifestyle
- You burn fewer calories. This makes you more likely to gain weight
- You may lose muscle strength and endurance, because you are not using your muscles as much
- Your bones may get weaker and lose some mineral content
- Your metabolism may be affected, and your body may have more trouble breaking down fats and sugars
- Your immune system may not work as well
- You may have poorer blood circulation
- Your body may have more inflammation
- You may develop a hormonal imbalance

What are the health risks of an inactive lifestyle?

Having an inactive lifestyle can increase your risk of developing chronic (long-term) diseases. This is sometimes referred to as "sitting disease". By not getting regular exercise, you raise your risk of:

[4] Health Risks of an Inactive Lifestyle
- Obesity
- Heart diseases, including coronary artery disease and heart attack
- High blood pressure
- High cholesterol
- Stroke
- Metabolic syndrome
- Type 2 diabetes
- Certain cancers, including colon, breast, and uterine cancers
- Osteoporosis and falls
- Increased feelings of depression and anxiety

Having a sedentary lifestyle can also raise your risk of premature death. And the more sedentary you are, the higher your health risks are.

How can I get started with exercise?

If you have been inactive, you may need to start slowly. Your health care provider can help you choose the best type or amount of activity for you based on your fitness level and health. You can keep adding more exercise gradually. The more you can do, the better. But try not to feel overwhelmed and do what you can. Getting some exercise is always better than getting none. Eventually, your goal can be to get the recommended amount of exercise for your age and health.

units.question: What criteria do doctors use to be sure a patient is really dead before pronouncing it?
units.gold: Death is usually declared after cardiac arrest, or respiratory arrest leading to it, once revival is exceedingly unlikely based on experience from millions of deaths. Clinicians observe the patient, using monitors in hospital: they confirm no cardiac electrical activity able to produce a pulse, no breathing for some time, blood oxygen below critical levels and no neurological activity. Even international guidelines admit it is not simple. Hypothermia is a special case, and cold patients are hard to declare dead.
rubric: Lists the criteria: no pulse-generating cardiac activity, no breathing, critically low oxygenation, no neurological activity
Mentions observation and monitoring over time
Explains certainty rests on experience from very many prior deaths
Mentions hypothermia as a special exception
Penalize: claiming a single test instantly proves death in every case
units.answer: Doctors use the International Guidelines for the Determination of Death to assess a patient's condition. They check for no pulse, no breathing, no neurological response, and no heart activity. If all criteria are met, they declare the patient dead [1].
units.sources:
[1] How do they make sure someone has really died before declaring them dead? (cited)
Answers > Answer (score 10, accepted): The procedure is to observe the patient carefully. When there is no evidence of cardiac electrical activity capable of generating a pulse, the patient has not been breathing for some time, oxygenation of blood has fallen to beyond critical levels, and there is no neurological activity, they are pronounced dead.** They "know" because of the combined observations of millions of deaths before that one. Since it has happened, clearly it might happen, but once all the criteria are met, it means they are clinically dead.

[2] Brain death
Sometimes, brain-dead people are kept alive with special machines and medications. For example, doctors can put a tube down a person's throat and use a machine called a ventilator to pump oxygen into their lungs. While these machines can keep the person's other organs alive for a while, they cannot help the brain get better. Eventually, the person's other organs will stop working too.

[3] Brain death
Diagnosis: Doctors can diagnose brain death by examining the patient. They will check for reflexes which are controlled by the brainstem, and see if the person can breathe on their own. If the person is brain-dead, the doctor will find:
- The person has no reflexes (for example, they do not gag when the doctor touches the back of their throat)
- The person's pupils do not change size in bright light or in the dark
- The person does not move or react when the doctor does something painful (like pinching the person's skin)
- The person does not try to breathe on their own

[4] How do they make sure someone has really died before declaring them dead? (cited)
Answers > Answer (score 10, accepted): **Often it is a nurse who discovers someone has died, but in many states, only a doctor, paramedic, or a coroner can declare someone dead. Nurses are often allowed to declare someone dead who is in a nursing home, hospice or a home care patient. Usually (but there is no law) we feel for pulses at various points on the body, we listen for heart sounds with a stethoscope, we listen for breath sounds, we look for chest movement, and I shine a light in the person's eyes looking for a neurological response. If after a few minutes of observation, nothing has been found, the patient is then pronounced.

The International Guidelines for the Determination of Death – Phase I May 30-31, 2012 Montreal Forum Report available in full online in PDF

Cooling the body after resuscitation following cardiac arrest
All homicides CDC

units.question: I found a small fuzzy spot on a slice of bread. Can I just tear it off and eat the rest?
units.gold: It is safer to throw the bread away. The USDA recommends discarding moldy bread because a small visible spot usually means mold has spread through the loaf in amounts you cannot see. Mold growth also signals that other microbes may be spoiling it. The main health threats are mycotoxins, which can cause acute or chronic effects and in rare cases, as with aflatoxins, be deadly, and allergic reactions. The risk from a bite is probably small, but easily avoided.

Mentions mycotoxins and allergic reactions as the risks
Notes the risk is likely small but avoidable
Penalize: saying it is fine to cut off the moldy part of bread

units.question: Do carrots really sharpen your vision, or is it a myth?
units.gold: Mostly myth. The story was reportedly spread as wartime misinformation by the British RAF to hide a new technology used to shoot down German planes. The grain of truth: carrots contain beta-carotene and vitamin A, which the eyes need. In people with vitamin A deficiency, carrots can somewhat help night blindness, and beta-carotene may lower cataract and macular degeneration risk, but only at doses higher than a normal diet provides.
rubric: States carrots do not improve normal eyesight
Mentions the WWII RAF propaganda origin
Notes vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness that carrots can help
Mentions beta-carotene benefits only at high doses beyond normal diet
Penalize: claiming eating carrots corrects short-sightedness
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
Carrots contain vitamin A, which is essential for eye health, but they do not sharpen vision directly. The myth about carrots improving vision is not scientifically proven.
units.sources:
[1] Do carrots actually improve eyesight?
Answers > Answer (score 7): This page on WebMd has an interesting section entitled "Myths About Your Eyes and Vision." Eating Carrots Will Improve Your Vision Fact: Carrots are high in vitamin A, a nutrient essential for good vision. Eating carrots will provide you with the small amount of vitamin A needed for good vision, but vitamin A isn't limited to rabbit food; it can also be found in milk, cheese, egg yolk, and liver.

[2] Carrot
In 2022, world production of carrots (combined with turnips) topped 42 million tonnes, with China producing 44% of the total. During the Second World War, a myth that carrots help people see in the dark was spread as propaganda to explain British pilots' ability to fight in the dark; the real explanation was the introduction of radar.

[3] Do carrots actually improve eyesight?
Tags: eye I've heard that carrots help improve eyesight, but the sources are pretty unreliable (TV shows, mostly). Are there any studies that prove (or show good evidence) that carrots improve eyesight? Or is this just a myth?

[4] Do carrots actually improve eyesight?
Answers > Answer (score 14, accepted): This is debunked with little reference on Snopes. It is claimed there that the origin of the myth was deliberate misinformation to hide the use of a game-changing technology used by the RAF to shoot down German planes. This claim regarding the propaganda origin is sourced a bit better at the Wikipedia article on one of the officers.

The grain-of-truth (which probably helps perpetuate the myth) is mentioned in the Snopes article as well and partially backed up at the (archived) CDC article on carrots that they link to:

[5] Do carrots actually improve eyesight?
Answers > Answer (score 14, accepted): Beta-carotene, which is found in the vegetable, may help reduce the risk of cataract and macular degeneration. However, it needs be pointed out that studies which have posited this link used doses of Vitamin A or beta-carotene that were higher than what is found in the standard diet. It would be quite difficult to eat the requisite number of carrots to match this level of intake. Also, among those who suffer a Vitamin A deficiency, nyctanopia (also known as nyctalopia or night blindness; the inability to see well in poor light) can be at least somewhat helped by adding carrots to the sufferer's diet.

[6] Carrots of other colors besides orange

Along with beta-carotene, carrots also have carotenoids another antioxidant helpful to enhance immunity functions and decreased risk of cardiovascular diseases, degenerative diseases and different types of cancers.

units.question: Describe how drinking while pregnant can harm the baby.
units.gold: Alcohol crosses the placenta, and the baby's liver matures only late in pregnancy, so it cannot process alcohol at any stage. It can stunt growth, cause facial abnormalities and damage brain structures, leading to intellectual disability. The most severe outcome, from heavy drinking, is fetal alcohol syndrome: distinctive face (small eyes, small head, smooth area between nose and lip, thin upper lip), developmental and attention problems, poor memory, and possible heart, kidney, hearing and immune problems. Milder spectrum disorders (FASD) occur at lower drinking levels.
rubric: Explains alcohol crosses the placenta and the fetal liver cannot process it
Mentions growth restriction and brain damage
Describes fetal alcohol syndrome and its facial features
Mentions FASD at lower intake levels
Penalize: stating moderate drinking in pregnancy is proven safe
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
Drinking alcohol during pregnancy can harm the baby by increasing the risk of fetal alcohol spectrum disorders. It can also lead to birth defects and developmental issues. The risk is highest in the first trimester when the baby's organs are forming.
units.sources:
[1] What is the effect of smoking before or during early pregnancy on the baby?
Tags: smoking, obstetrics I assume it will be harmful to the baby if a woman smokes while pregnant. How about the situation where the woman smokes, gets pregnant and then stops? Does the smoking in the period until the pregnancy affect the baby?

[2] What is the effect of smoking before or during early pregnancy on the baby?
Answers > Answer (score 5, accepted): While most studies appear to be on women who quit during pregnancy, I found a study that compared pregnancy outcomes in women who never smoked, quit smoking before pregnancy, quit smoking in early pregnancy, and those that smoked during pregnancy. It found

maternal smoking cessation before or during early pregnancy appears to result in appropriate fetal and childhood growth

The whole study Active and passive maternal smoking during pregnancy and the risks of low birthweight and preterm birth: the Generation R Study is available on the internet and I recommend reading it in full and also looking at the references. The differences in birth weight between the babies born to women who quit before and during early pregnancy were not significant.

Another study in 7000 women in the Netherlands also found no difference between women who didn't smoke and women who quit before 18 weeks of pregnancy.

[3] What is the effect of smoking before or during early pregnancy on the baby?
Answers > Answer (score 5, accepted): For all active smoking categories in early pregnancy, quitting smoking was associated with a higher birthweight than continuing to smoke. Tendencies towards smaller non-significant beneficial effects on mean birthweight were found for reducing the number of cigarettes without quitting completely. This study shows that active and passive smoking in late pregnancy are associated with adverse effects on weight and gestational age at birth. Smoking in early pregnancy only, seems not to affect fetal growth adversely.

Active and passive maternal smoking during pregnancy and the risks of low birthweight and preterm birth: the Generation R Study

Note that for all of these studies, just reducing the number of cigarettes per day is counted as continuing to smoke.

units.question: Tell me the right first-aid steps after someone is bitten by a snake, and the things to avoid.
units.gold: Move the person away from the snake without trying to catch it; a photo helps identification. Keep them calm and lying down with the bite below heart level, cover it loosely with a sterile bandage, mark the edge of swelling with a pen, remove rings and watches, and get emergency care even if they seem fine, since symptoms can take hours. Do not cut and suck, apply ice, give electric shocks, give alcohol or aspirin, or use a tourniquet. Many bites inject little or no venom.
rubric: Keep calm, rest, bite below heart level, loose sterile dressing
Seek emergency care promptly even without symptoms
Remove jewelry and mark spreading swelling
Lists don'ts: no cutting/sucking, ice, tourniquet, alcohol or aspirin
Penalize: recommending a tight tourniquet or cutting and sucking the wound
units.answer:
Snakebite, first aid: move away from the snake and don't try to catch or kill it. Call emergency services now; if you are alone, call right away and follow their instructions. Keep the person still and calm, lying down, on their side if possible, and stop them from moving around at all; carry them on a makeshift stretcher if you can, and get them to medical care without delay, for antivenom: don't wait for symptoms. Take off rings, watches and bracelets, and loosen clothing near the bite, before swelling starts. Cover the bite with a clean, dry dressing. Mark the edge of the swelling on the skin and write down the time. Do NOT use a tourniquet, do NOT cut the wound, and do NOT suck the venom or put chemicals on it. Don't put ice on it or soak it in water. Don't drink alcohol, and don't take aspirin, ibuprofen or naproxen. If you can do it safely from a distance, take a photo of the snake to help identify it. If the person stops responding or stops breathing normally, start CPR.

Sources: WHO, questions and answers on snakebite envenoming (2019); CDC NIOSH, Venomous Snakes at Work; NHS, Snake bites; healthdirect Australia, Snake bites.

In an emergency, call your local emergency number (911 in the US, 112 in Europe).

units.question: I've been eating very little for months. Can my basal metabolic rate actually slow down because of it?
units.gold: Yes. In the first few days of fasting, BMR actually rises, driven by catecholamines released as blood glucose falls and by high gluconeogenesis. As restriction continues, free T3 and catecholamine levels drop, gluconeogenesis slows and metabolic rate falls, largely through loss of lean tissue, especially muscle, while the body protects the glucose supply to the brain. Milder long-term restriction triggers the same adaptive processes on a smaller scale.
rubric: Confirms BMR decreases with prolonged calorie restriction
Mentions the initial short-term rise in BMR (catecholamines, gluconeogenesis)
Mentions falling free T3 and catecholamines later
Mentions loss of lean tissue/muscle as a main mechanism
Penalize: claiming metabolism never adapts to dieting
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
Yes, your basal metabolic rate can slow down due to calorie restriction, but it's not a direct cause. The body may initially use alternative energy sources like gluconeogenesis, but long-term fasting can lead to muscle loss, which may further reduce metabolic rate.
units.sources:
[1] Metabolic rate
Metabolic rate is the rate of metabolism, the amount of energy used by an animal per unit of time. Basal metabolic rate (BMR) is the amount of energy used daily by animals at rest. About 70% of a human's total energy use is due to the basal life processes within the organs of the body (see table). About 20% of one's energy use comes from physical activity and another 10% from the digestion of food after eating.

[2] Metabolic rate
Basal metabolism: Basal metabolism is usually by far the largest component of total energy used. The release, and using, of energy in this state is sufficient only for the functioning of the vital organs, the heart, lungs, nervous system, kidneys, liver, intestine, sex organs, muscles, and skin.

[3] on what metabolism depends
Tags: nutrition, lifestyle, metabolism, genetics, environmental-conditions Some people have fast metabolism (high basal metabolic rate), but some slow one. And fast metabolism is considered as good one, because it keeps you from over-weighting.

[4] Metabolic rate
Basal metabolism > Biochemistry: For the BMR, most of the energy is taken in keeping fluid levels up in tissues by osmosis, and only about one-tenth is used for mechanical work, such as digestion, heartbeat, and breathing.

What enables the Krebs cycle to perform metabolic changes to fats, carbohydrates, and proteins is energy, which can be defined as the ability or capacity to do work.

The breakdown of large molecules into smaller molecules – with release of energy – is catabolism. The breakdown of proteins into amino acids is an example of catabolism. Body heat in warm-blooded animals is produced by chemical reactions of the catabolic type.

The building up process is termed anabolism. The formation of proteins from amino acids is an anabolic process.

[5] Does BMR adjust and decrease in response to calorie restriction diets?
Answers > Answer (score 4, accepted): The basal metabolic rate actually increases during the first few days of starvation, under the influence of catecholamines that are secreted in response to decreasing blood glucose concentrations. This probably reflects the high rate of gluconeogenesis that occurs at this time. As fasting progresses, however, metabolic rate decreases as free T3 and catecholamine levels decrease and the rate of gluconeogenesis decreases.

In essence, when you first start to fast (the references [1,2] that the review sites are from 1-4 days in this section) the body looks to other sources of energy (gluconeogenesis). That is not sustainable over time, and then the BMR begins to drop. How it begins to drop is largely through the lost of lean tissue, with a focus on muscle mass, which is probably a good evolutionary choice over more important systems such as the brain:

Metabolic rate is the rate of metabolism, the amount of energy used by an animal per unit of time. Basal metabolic rate (BMR) is the amount of energy used daily by animals at rest. About 70% of a human's total energy use is due to the basal life processes within the organs of the body (see table). About 20% of one's energy use comes from physical activity and another 10% from the digestion of food after eating.

units.question: Can a blood antibody test show a past herpes type 2 infection in someone who never had symptoms, and how reliable is a positive?
units.gold: Yes, the HSV antibody test looks for the body's immune response rather than the virus, so it can pick up past, now inactive infections, though this depends on how long ago infection occurred. It is not 100% accurate. Its main weakness is missing infections (false negatives) rather than false positives; the false-positive rate in people without symptoms appears fairly low, but like any test it is not zero, so a positive does not prove infection with certainty.

Penalize: claiming the test is perfectly accurate
units.answer: A blood antibody test can detect a past herpes simplex virus type 2 infection, even if someone never had symptoms [4]. A positive result indicates exposure to the virus, but it's not 100% reliable due to false positives.

units.question: One of my blisters burst. Should I put antibiotic ointment like Neosporin on it, or something else?
units.gold: Either antibiotic ointment or plain petroleum jelly is fine on a shallow open blister, provided you are not allergic. Studies are mixed on whether antibiotic ointment beats petroleum jelly on clean wounds, and it can cause allergic reactions. Wash with soap and water, lay the loose skin back over the wound and cover it with a clean bandage for 24-48 hours. Try not to pop blisters at all, because the inside is sterile until opened. Deep wounds need medical care.

units.question: Is ice still recommended for minor burns, and what is the current first aid?
units.gold: No, ice is no longer advised because the extreme cold can injure tissue further. Calm the person and remove clothing not stuck to the burn (all of it if chemicals are involved). Cool the burn under cool running water for 10 to 15 minutes, or use a cool wet cloth or cool bath for about 5 minutes. Then check it is truly minor: deeper or larger burns, or burns on the hands, feet, face, groin, buttocks or major joints, need medical care right away. Leave blisters intact.

Advises not breaking blisters

units.answer: Ice is no longer recommended for treating minor burns as it can cause further damage to the skin [4]. Current first aid for minor burns involves cooling the burn with water and seeking medical attention if necessary.

units.question: Tell me whether a grinding or popping noise when I turn my head, with no pain, is anything to worry about.
units.gold: A painless crunching or popping sound when moving a joint is called articular release and is considered normal. It occurs in healthy and diseased joints alike and during ordinary movement, and it can be loud, soft or silent. Habitual cracking for relief is debated: keeping joints moving may help, while overuse might loosen ligaments. Research focuses on knuckles rather than the neck, and studies found knuckle cracking does not lead to arthritis in old age.

units.question: I sail about once a month and recently got badly seasick in rough water. What can I do to keep it from happening again?
units.gold: Tolerance training may not help much: experienced sailors note that in really extreme weather almost everyone gets sick, though it tends to wear off on longer crossings. What helps is preparation and behaviour on board: stay warm, dry, well rested, fed and hydrated; position yourself near the boat's centre of gravity; use your legs to absorb the motion. If safe, stay on deck and look at the distant horizon; if you must be below, lie down and close your eyes.

units.question: What is the best way to avoid putting on frozen boots on a cold winter camping morning?
units.gold: Keep them in your sleeping bag overnight. Sweat accumulated in boots during the day freezes if they are left out, so you get boots that are both frozen and damp once thawed, which risks cold injuries such as trench foot over several days. Separate liners from shells and put both in the bag, or at least remove the insoles to help drying. Truly frozen heavy boots can be almost impossible to put on. Alternatives: vapour-barrier socks, or bottles of boiled water stuffed into the boots.
rubric: Recommends sleeping with boots (or liners) inside the sleeping bag
Explains sweat freezes in boots left out overnight
Mentions removing liners or insoles to dry them
Mentions risks of damp boots such as trench foot or cold injury
Penalize: advising warming boots over an open flame inside a tent
units.answer: Avoid putting on frozen boots by warming them before attempting to put them on [1]. Use hand or toe warmers, or leave them in a warm place to thaw.
units.sources:
[1] Winter Camping: How to warm up your boots in the morning? (cited)
Answers > Answer (score 4): - If your boots have felt liners, then remove the felt liners and keep them in your sleeping bag. - Open your boots wide (like Zoul said) and loosen the laces so that they are easier to use if frozen in the morning. That way, even if your boot is still wet/frozen in the morning it won't permeate your socks, and your feet still get to breath (and stay dry if you have a dunker on a lake). - You might avoid freezing laces by putting (dry) towel or similar over your boots.

[2] Winter Camping: How to warm up your boots in the morning? (cited)
Answers > Answer (score 12, accepted): - During the day, sweat builds up in your boots. Leaving them out at night, this freezes, meaning that not only do you have cold, frozen boots in the morning, if you do manage to get them thawed, they are still damp (BAD). You are putting yourself at risk of cold injuries. - Heavy duty boots can be impossible to put on if they are well and truly frozen - the leather/plastic/liners are so stiff, it would take a contortionist to get your feet in.

[3] Winter Camping: How to warm up your boots in the morning? (cited)
Answers > Answer (score 12, accepted): I have found sleeping with my boots inside the bag is the ONLY way to go when it is really cold out. Moderately cold, sure you can tough out the re-thaw in the morning - but real cold... forget it.

It is tough to get over the psychological barrier of putting boots in your bag - but it will make a difference. A few points to consider:

[4] Winter Camping: How to warm up your boots in the morning? (cited)
Answers > Answer (score 12, accepted): ** Some people swear by plastic socks (gore tex, nylon, or even plastic bags) to trap the moisture your foot generates inside the bag before it reaches your boot. Although this keeps your boots dry, it can make for a miserable squishy hiking/skiing experience -- but might be the only way to keep your boots dry during prolonged exposure.

If you can't stomach your boots in your bag (it is not that bad, really) you can try the following fuel or time-intensive measures:

- Boil water, pour it in nalgene type (well sealing) bottles and cram those as far down in your boots as you can.
- Hold boots over stove / fire for as long as it takes (be aware of melt-age).
- Camp somewhere with ready access to early morning sun. Place boots on closed-cell foam pad in direct sunlight. <-- Though at -25F, no amount of sun will do it...
- Consider hand/toe warmers (chemical based heat machines) to put in your boots with your feet to facilitate rapid warming.

units.question: On a steep climb to about 2,100 m I felt wiped out and breathless. How can I tell if that was altitude sickness or just fatigue?
units.gold: The clearest objective sign is low blood oxygen saturation, measured with a cheap, light pulse oximeter. Symptoms of acute mountain sickness (AMS), the mild form, are headache, nausea, fatigue, loss of appetite and poor sleep, none of them unique, so diagnosis usually relies on context: altitude, rate of ascent, sleeping altitude, temperature and hydration. Without an oximeter you cannot be certain. Be far more concerned if it progresses to HACE (brain swelling) or HAPE (fluid in the lungs), which can be fatal.
rubric: Recommends measuring SpO2 with a pulse oximeter
Lists AMS symptoms: headache, nausea, fatigue, appetite loss, poor sleep
Notes symptoms are non-specific so context (altitude, ascent rate, hydration) matters
Warns about progression to HACE or HAPE as life-threatening
Penalize: stating altitude sickness cannot occur below 3,000 m or giving a definitive diagnosis
units.answer:
Altitude sickness (headache, nausea, dizziness, tiredness at altitude): stop and rest at the same altitude until you feel better; don't go higher, and never go up to sleep higher with symptoms. Don't use alcohol or sleeping pills to help you sleep at altitude. If symptoms get worse or don't improve after a day, go down about 300 to 1,000 metres. Go down straight away and get medical help immediately (call emergency services if you can) if they are confused, unsteady, breathless at rest, coughing up frothy or bloody spit, or very sleepy.

Source: NHS, Altitude sickness; CDC Yellow Book, High-Altitude Travel and Altitude Illness. Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

In an emergency, call your local emergency number (911 in the US, 112 in Europe).

units.question: Describe a method for wading a knee-deep creek in winter and getting your feet warm and dry afterwards.
units.gold: A traditional military routine: pack gear in a waterproof sack and tie it up so it doubles as a buoyancy aid. Cross in your normal boots with thin socks and accept the cold. On the far side, remove wet boots and socks and bag them, then put on dry socks (with talcum powder) under waterproof Gore-Tex socks carried for this purpose, and put the wet boots back on: your foot heat dries them from inside while your feet stay dry. Absorbent nappies stuffed inside can help dry boots further.

Mentions crossing in boots with thin socks rather than barefoot
Mentions changing into dry socks plus waterproof (Gore-Tex) socks inside the wet boots
Mentions drying boots afterwards (body heat or absorbent pads)
Penalize: suggesting crossing barefoot on ice-covered rocks as the safest method
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
Wade slowly and steadily through the creek, keeping your legs dry and your feet warm by wearing appropriate footwear. After crossing, dry your feet and boots thoroughly, and consider using a towel or scrap paper to absorb any remaining moisture.
units.sources:
[1] River crossing in winter?
Tags: winter, rivers, ice I found one spot to cross that looks only about knee deep, and the water is flowing probably a little bit faster than walking speed. What's the best way to wade through a creek in winter? Anyone know of any painless winter water wading techniques?

[2] How to you wade a river/creek without getting water in your boots
Answers > Answer (score 30): Water shoes

You really don't want to be getting your walking boots wet under such circumstances, nor do you want your socks wet. So rather than going barefoot, swap to some more suitable footware for the crossing.

The best bet is to take some lightweight "water shoes" also sometimes known as "swim shoes" they're the sort of thing wild swimmers wear when out in unknown waters. Lightweight, quick drying, no good for walking long distances but usually designed to have good grip on wet surfaces.

And a towel, always know where your towel is.

[3] How to you wade a river/creek without getting water in your boots
Answers > Answer (score 17): If going barefoot is not an option, then basically 2 are left

1.
Waders. Preferred by fishers standing in water up to waist. Heavy, take a lot of place, and keep in mind, you will sweat inside.

2.
Sandals or running trail shoes. Take little place, light, choose one with good soles that will provide a good grip. Prepare for short cold shock and warming up your feet afterwards. It's still better than walking hours in wet trekking shoes.

[4] How to you wade a river/creek without getting water in your boots
Answers > Answer (score 6): If you're caught out without alternatives, this is what I've done at very slightly warmer temperatures. If you can plan in advance, other answers provide better options.

Take off boots and socks, put boots back on to cross. Keep your leg-wear dry. Zip-off hiking trousers have their use even in the cold, or roll the legs up.

After crossing, do what you can to dry first your feet and then inside your boots. Perhaps you've got dirty or slightly damp clothes in your pack, for example. Any scrap paper can be used to get a bit more out of boots, while tissues aren't worth using on boots, only feet. Pack towels will often get out quite a bit, then wring them out, then some more. With some of my quick-drying gear, using the zipped-off legs to dry out the boots, then zipping them back on to dry as I hike would be a good option.

units.question: In a survival situation, can drinkable liquor like whiskey or vodka be used to clean a wound?
units.gold: Alcohol does kill germs, and 19th-century sources and at least one modern study support whiskey as an antiseptic. But alcohol should not be poured into an open wound, because it also kills exposed tissue and can delay healing. When no proper supplies are available, strong liquor can be used to clean dirt from the skin around a wound and to disinfect instruments. Antiseptics are for living tissue; disinfectants, which are harsher, are for surfaces and equipment.
rubric: Acknowledges alcohol has antiseptic effect
Warns not to pour alcohol into an open wound because it damages tissue and slows healing
Suggests using it on surrounding skin or to disinfect tools
Explains antiseptic versus disinfectant difference
Penalize: recommending pouring whiskey directly into deep wounds as best practice
units.answer: In a survival situation, drinkable liquor like whiskey or vodka can be used to clean a wound, but it is not a substitute for proper first aid [1]. It may help prevent infection but is not as effective as medical disinfectants.
units.sources:
[1] Is whiskey a good disinfectant? (cited)
Answers > Answer (score 16): Is whiskey a good disinfectant in an emergency situation while in the outdoors? Ideally any strong alcohol, whether whiskey, vodka, tequila or some other strong liquor should not be used to clean wounds. But in an a survival situation, I would not hesitate to use whiskey or some other strong liquor such as vodka on a wound while in the great outdoors. However, in a situation where standard first aid equipment is not available, vodka (or whiskey) may be used to clean dirt from the surrounding area of a wound.

[2] Is whiskey a good disinfectant? (cited)
Answers > Answer (score 18, accepted): This was done on the American Frontier, and during the American Civil War. According to this journal from the American Medical Association printed in 1893, it is a good antiseptic. Apparently, alcohol works by breaking down the protein bonds.

units.question: Teach me how to interpret the contour lines and elevation numbers on a hiking topo map.
units.gold: Each contour line joins points of equal elevation. Lines close together mean a steep slope; widely spaced lines mean gentle ground. The numbers give the altitude, usually above sea level (check the legend for units and reference), and terrain rises towards higher numbers. Concentric rings are hills or hollows depending on the numbers, and lines merging mark cliffs. The steepest route runs perpendicular to the lines: cross them for a challenge, walk along them to stay level. In the US, most maps follow USGS symbol standards.
rubric: States a contour line connects points of equal elevation
States closer lines mean steeper slopes
Explains elevation labels and checking the legend for units/reference
Mentions concentric circles for hills/holes and merging lines for cliffs
Penalize: saying contour lines represent trails or rivers
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
Contour lines show elevation, with closer lines indicating higher elevation and farther lines indicating lower elevation. Elevation numbers indicate the height above sea level. Look for steep slopes and valleys by observing the contour patterns.
units.sources:
[1] Topographic map
A topographic map is a kind of map which uses contour lines or other ways to show elevation and topography. These maps are often very detailed, with a scale. Topographical maps may be used for many purposes. They show relief features, rivers, land use, vegetation, settlements, roads, railway lines and administrative units and boundaries.

[2] Contour line
In cartography, a contour line (often just called a "contour") joins points of equal elevation (height) above a given level, such as mean sea level. A contour map is a map illustrated with contour lines, for example a topographic map, which thus shows valleys and hills, and the steepness or gentleness of slopes. The contour interval of a contour map is the difference in elevation between successive contour lines. The gradient of the function is always perpendicular to the contour lines.

[3] Topographic map
In modern mapping, a topographic map or topographic sheet is a type of map characterized by large-scale detail and quantitative representation of relief features, usually using contour lines (connecting points of equal elevation), but historically using a variety of methods. Traditional definitions require a topographic map to show both natural and artificial features. A topographic survey is typically based upon a systematic observation and published as a map series, made up of two or more map sheets that combine to form the whole map.

[4] How to interpret forest from the map?
Answers > Answer (score 6): Mosquitoes require water, so look for proximity to swamps, lakes or slow rivers. Elevation contours would also help, you are less likely to end up in a boggy area if it's on a slope. I am not sure what else you can deduce from a map here, mostly I'd look for trail reviews/ask on forums for a particular location during a specific season. Good idea to review contour and riverbeds in any case while camping - you don't want to camp in a flash flood area.

[5] Topographic map
Conventional signs and symbols: Features seen on the ground are shown with the help of symbols on the topographic maps. These are only symbols of Earth's features and are not drawn according to any specific scale. These conventional signs help in giving information and adding legibility to the map.

[6] How do I read a topographic map?
Answers > Answer (score 11): I am only familiar with US topos, but a point the other answers miss is that the US Geological Survey have mapping standards, and most non-USGS maps (at least in America) match the USGS standards.

I'd suggest you start by learning the standard symbols in your area. Make up flash cards and you can easily quiz yourself as you have a few minutes (this is a great way to pass time while on the bus/train to work).

As for being able to navigate, topos often have more information than is necessary to walk through the woods and come out alive. For example, there are 3 symbols for a mountain top. The only difference is the precision of the measured altitude. There are 2 symbols for mines (vertical/horizontal). The brown elevation lines mark hills and valleys one way, but a depression another way (a circular pattern with lines pointing to the bottom of the depression).

[7] Wikivoyage: Hiking
Navigation > Maps: Relying on paper or offline maps requires knowledge on how to read such maps and how to draw conclusions about your position in them. It is important to understand the elevation profile of your trail, and the scale of the map to calculate distances and times for hikes. The more information inside the map, the better. Contour lines and hillshades allow you to project the map onto the surrounding area, by denoting valleys, ridges, peaks, plains and other terrain features.

You can also use a map to guess the best route when there is no trail. E.g. avoid hiking down a stream valley the summit, follow a level ridge free of steep barriers, avoid steep scree slopes of about 30° where it is easy to cause a slide. Avoid wetlands and difficult river crossings.

Paper maps don't like rain. Modern hiking maps are often made from other materials, but may still need some protection – and a gust can carry your map over a cliff edge, so it is better to carry it around your neck.

units.question: In orienteering, what does it mean to 'contour' around a hill, and when is it useful?
units.gold: Contouring means travelling around a hill while holding the same elevation, following the shape of the land, rather than going over the top. You climb to the height of your destination and then keep to that level. It is especially useful off-trail when you know the elevation of a small target such as an abandoned mine or petroglyph site. An altimeter is the key tool, though you can hold height roughly by eye. In some regions or languages the word just means going around a feature.
rubric: Defines contouring as moving across a slope at constant elevation
Mentions first climbing to the target's height then staying level
Gives the use case of off-trail navigation to a destination of known elevation
Mentions an altimeter as the key tool
Penalize: defining contouring as drawing contour lines on a map
units.answer: In orienteering, contouring around a hill means following the land's elevation to stay at the same level, helping to navigate hills or terrain [2]. It is useful when following a specific elevation to reach a destination or avoid steep slopes.
units.sources:
[1] What does contouring mean in the context of navigation/orienteering? (cited)
Answers > Answer (score 3): The answer is really dependent on language, I think. Being from a French-speaking part of the world, I can definitely say that even in orienteering/mountain traveling, the meaning of contouring would imply simply going around a feature, not necessarily at a fixed elevation. I could contour around a forest or a hill. The translation of contourner is quite literally go around.

[2] What does contouring mean in the context of navigation/orienteering? (cited)
Answers > Answer (score 10, accepted): Contouring means to follow the contours of the land to your destination, trying to stay at the same elevation as you work your way around the hill. In this example you would walk up the hill, and upon reaching the given height, stay at that level while walking towards the destination. Sometimes, in places without trails, you will know the elevation of your destination (this can be very useful for small destinations like abandoned mines or petroglyphs) and the easiest way to stay on track is by elevation.

[3] What does contouring mean in the context of navigation/orienteering? (cited)
Tags: navigation, terminology, orienteering

One of the techniques while navigating in the outdoors is known as contouring, what does this mean and when would it be useful?

[4] How to understand contour map and plan a possible trekking route using one such contour map?
Answers > Answer (score 4, accepted): In places where the contour lines are closer together, the slope is steeper. Where the lines are further apart, the slope is gentler. In a spot where you see several lines merge together, that is a sheer drop-off. Avoid those, obviously.

Look for nesting Vs on the map. These are ridges, or possibly ravines. Water (blue) bisecting the V will tell you it is a valley. Through practice, I can pretty distinguish a ravine from a ridge in a few seconds. Sorry, I can’t describe a technique for that. * Perhaps I am recommending spending time poring over contour maps ;—)

units.question: Why is it called a nor'easter when the storm itself travels from the southwest up the coast?
units.gold: The name refers to the wind direction, not the storm's track. A nor'easter is a counter-clockwise rotating cyclone moving north up the coast; on its leading side the strong winds hit New England from the ocean out of the northeast. Coastal mariners named these storms long before large-scale weather was understood, simply noting that the worst weather and heavy precipitation came howling from the northeast, whereas normal New England weather arrives from the west.
rubric: Explains the name describes wind direction rather than storm movement
Mentions counter-clockwise cyclonic rotation
States the storm tracks north/northeast up the coast
Mentions the historical naming by mariners/fishermen
Penalize: claiming nor'easters always travel from northeast to southwest
units.answer: The name "nor'easter" refers to the wind direction, not the storm's travel direction [1]. The storm moves from the southwest to the northeast, but the winds come from the northeast, which is why it's called a nor'easter [1].
units.sources:
[1] Isn't Nor'easter supposed to move from the Northeast to Southwest? (cited)
Answers > Answer (score 18, accepted): Yes, "Nor'easter" is derived from "north-easter" meaning the winds come from the northeast. That is exactly what happens in a nor'easter. You are confusing the wind direction with the travel direction of the storm. The whole storm moves up the coast, but remember these are counter-clockwise rotating cyclonic storms.

[2] Isn't Nor'easter supposed to move from the Northeast to Southwest? (cited)
Answers > Answer (score 3): Anon is correct. Nor'easter is a storm system blowing high winds and Artic air coming from the north or north east. Newscasters tend to call these northeasters thinking, I guess, that it's a storm on the northeastern United States and therefore a nor'easter or they simply get things backwards. Again, the storms with heavy precipitation moving from the south into and along the East Coast US are sou'westers.

[3] Nor'easter
A nor'easter (also northeaster) is a big storm along the East Coast of the United States. A Nor'easter is called that because the winds in a Nor'easter come from the northeast, especially in the coastal areas of the Northeastern United States and Atlantic Canada. More specifically, it is a low pressure area whose center of rotation is just off the East Coast and whose leading winds in the left forward quadrant rotate onto land from the northeast. The precipitation pattern is similar to other extratropical storms.

[4] December 1969 nor'easter
The December 1969 nor'easter was a strong winter storm. It included a tornado outbreak, record snow accumulations, a damaging ice storm, and flooding rains.

[5] Isn't Nor'easter supposed to move from the Northeast to Southwest? (cited)
Answers > Answer (score 18, accepted): Remember that the names evolved long before people understood large scale weather patterns. All people in Cape Cod, Gloucester, or "down east" Maine knew was that the nastiest weather accompanied by serious precipitation come howling from the northeast. While not universally true of course, it's actually not that far off in the larger scheme of things. "Normal" weather here in New England comes from the west. Notable exceptions are the "Montreal Express" being cold and dry from the northwest, and a nor'easter bringing strong winds and serious precipitation from the northeast. "Nice" weather from the northeast basically doesn't happen here. The old mariners and fishermen knew a lot about local weather without understanding the global picture.

[6] Isn't Nor'easter supposed to move from the Northeast to Southwest? (cited)
Answers > Answer (score 4): Nor'easters move from the south to the north. Just like a hurricane. They are cyclonic and the wind that hits the coast comes from the NE.

[7] Isn't Nor'easter supposed to move from the Northeast to Southwest? (cited)
Tags: weather, new-england

Isn't Nor'easter supposed to move from the Northeast to Southwest, hence its name? But the recent Nor'easter that hit the Northeast US right after Hurricane Sandy seems to have moved from the southwest to northeast, according to the meteorologic graphics that were shown all day long on TV. Can someone explain?

units.question: Apart from lead climbing, when should you choose a static rope over a dynamic one?
units.gold: Use a dynamic rope wherever a fall with high impact forces is possible; use a static rope for static loads. That means rappelling or abseiling, ascending fixed lines, hauling, rescue and building anchors. On rappels a 9-11 mm static rope gives more control. Ascending a stretchy dynamic rope is almost twice as tiring. Big-wall hauling uses static lines because they pull faster, and rescue teams typically use 13 mm static rope to lift people with no stretch. Never use a static rope to catch a lead fall.
rubric: States static ropes are for static loads and dynamic ropes for potential falls
Lists static uses: rappelling, ascending, hauling, rescue, anchors
Mentions better control on rappel or easier ascending with static rope
Warns never to lead climb or catch falls on a static rope
Penalize: recommending static rope for lead climbing
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
Static ropes are better for top-rope climbing or situations where a low elongation is needed, as they are designed for hauling and not lead climbing.
units.sources:
[1] What is a typical elongation of a dynamic climbing rope?
Answers > Answer (score 8): First of all, DO NOT buy a rope or ANYTHING for that matter that you will trust your life to, purely based on what a single salesperson says, or what I say. There is ambiguity in this because apparently ropes are labeled by their percent elongation for 'static' and 'dynamic' testing/use, in addition to themselves being called static and dynamic ropes. That is, you can have a rope that is static (meant for top roping, hauling, etc NOT for lead climbing) or dynamic (designed for lead climbing) and any rope from either category can be testing for 'static elongation' and 'dynamic elongation'. i.e. static ropes will have crappy dynamic elongation by definition. Static and dynamic elongation is precisely defined here:

[2] Major fall, same for static and dynamic?
Answers > Answer (score 6, accepted): A dynamic rope that sustains a fall factor that high should definitely be retired, even if it doesn't show any immediate signs of damage. Static ropes have essentially zero dynamic elongation ability. A factor 1.77 fall on a static rope would almost certainly rip gear, and cause severe bodily harm either in the catch or the corresponding fall. This is why you should never lead on a static rope.

[3] What is a typical elongation of a dynamic climbing rope?
Answers > Answer (score 9, accepted): You are apparently confusing static and dynamic elongation. You must use rope that is UIAA-101 / EN-892 certified for the task at hand. You will be buying a Single type rope unless you specifically know otherwise.

Quoting Beal Ropes:

Dynamic elongation:
This is the stretch of the rope during the first UIAA test fall. It must be less than 40%.

Static elongation:
Measured under a load of 80kg it must not exceed 10% for single rope, 12% for double rope, and 10% for two strands of twin rope together.

So you see the static elongation must be no more than 10% for a Single climbing rope, yet to meet the impact force requirements the dynamic elongation is going to have to be much higher than that (though it may not exceed 40%).

Impact force

Values required by the Standard:

[4] What is a typical elongation of a dynamic climbing rope?
Answers > Answer (score 9, accepted): - Single rope: Impact force lower than 12kN holding the first factor 1.77 fall with a mass of 80kg.
- Double rope: Impact force lower than 8kn holding the first factor 1.77 fall with a mass of 55kg.
- Twin rope: Impact force lower than 12kN holding the first factor 1.77 fall with a mass of 80kg, on two strands.

The impact force printed in the technical notice must not be lower than the poorest result found by the certifying laboratory.

[5] "Used" top rope when bouldering
Answers > Answer (score 11, accepted): There is another option you should consider if you plan to do a lot of top-roping, especially if you climb abrasive rock or sometimes cannot extend the anchor far enough. You do not need a dynamic climbing rope for top-rope, and dynamic ropes typically wear much faster than static ones therefore you should consider picking out a dedicated rope for this purpose. The exact definition of a "static" (or interchangeably "low elongation") rope varies and is more of a catch-all term for non-dynamic ropes. I recommend that you avoid any very-low-elongation lines such as polyester canyoneering ropes, Sterling HTP Static, etc., and instead pick one that is certified as an EN 1891 safety line which requires that it have some impact absorption.
