A factor 1.77 fall on a static rope would almost certainly rip gear, and cause severe bodily harm either in the catch or the corresponding fall. This is why you should never lead on a static rope.

[5] What is a typical elongation of a dynamic climbing rope?
Answers > Answer (score 8): First of all, DO NOT buy a rope or ANYTHING for that matter that you will trust your life to, purely based on what a single salesperson says, or what I say. There is ambiguity in this because apparently ropes are labeled by their percent elongation for 'static' and 'dynamic' testing/use, in addition to themselves being called static and dynamic ropes. That is, you can have a rope that is static (meant for top roping, hauling, etc NOT for lead climbing) or dynamic (designed for lead climbing) and any rope from either category can be testing for 'static elongation' and 'dynamic elongation'. i.e. static ropes will have crappy dynamic elongation by definition. units.question: We often camp where wild pigs roam. If a group of them charges, what should I do?
units.gold: Wild boars rarely attack; often a lead animal bluffs aggressively just long enough for the group to escape. Staying quiet and observing usually provokes nothing. If threatened, try to distract them by throwing a jacket or backpack, climb or retreat if possible, and make yourselves look bigger to scare them off. The main danger is the tusks piercing the thigh and its large artery, which can cause fatal bleeding, so protect your legs. Boars fed by people lose their fear and are harder to intimidate.

Warns the main injury risk is tusks piercing the thigh/femoral artery

Penalize: recommending approaching or cornering boars

units.question: Tell me how to use up the last bit of gas in my camp stove canisters and how to throw them away properly.
units.gold: To use the remaining gas, run the stove with the canister inverted: liquid fuel is fed by gravity instead of relying on vapour pressure, so you can burn more of it, though the setup is heavier. Alternatively, adapters let you refill canisters from others or from larger cans, with real safety caveats. To dispose of a canister, vent all remaining gas, then puncture the sidewall (Jetboil makes a tool for this) and put it in the appropriate metal recycling bin.

units.question: Is there real evidence that hiking poles help your knees and legs?
units.gold: Yes, with a trade-off. A 2007 study found poles reduce joint strain when descending with a load. A 2010 study of walkers climbing and descending Snowdon found less muscle damage and soreness with poles, about a 25% reduction in leg muscle strain. However, a 2008 study found poles increase oxygen use and calorie burn, so they make hiking slightly less efficient even though it does not feel harder. In short: less damaging to the body, but more exertion.

Cites reduced muscle damage/soreness (about 25% in the Snowdon study)
Notes poles increase energy expenditure/oxygen consumption
Summarises: less damage to the body, more exertion
Penalize: claiming poles are proven to make hiking less tiring overall

units.sources:
[1] Are trekking poles proven to be helpful?
Answers > Answer (score 36, accepted): Here are some scientific papers, with my brief summaries.

Saunders MJ ; Hipp GR ; Wenos DL ; Deaton ML, "Trekking poles increase physiological responses to hiking without increased perceived exertion," J Strength Cond Res 2008 Sep; 22(5): 1468-74

Using trekking poles caused them to burn calories faster, as measured by VO2max. In other words, they make you less efficient, which is the opposite of what a lot of people seem to believe.

Bohne M ; Abendroth-Smith J, "Effects of hiking downhill using trekking poles while carrying external loads," Med Sci Sports Exerc 2007 Jan; 39(1): 177-83

Using trekking poles reduces strain on joints when going downhill.

Glyn Howatson et al., "Trekking Poles Reduce Exercise-Induced Muscle Injury during Mountain Walking," Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, published ahead of print, 13 May 2010, doi: 10.1249/MSS.0b013e3181e4b649

Subjects reported less muscle soreness after climbing Mt Snowdon if they used trekking poles.

units.question: I'm backpacking in Yosemite. Which animals are an actual risk, and can I bring bear spray?
units.gold: There are no wolves or boars in Yosemite; coyotes are harmless. Rattlesnakes live at lower elevations, so watch the trail. Mountain lions exist but are rarely seen; hiking with one or two other adults reduces risk. Neither snakes nor lions live above the timberline at about 10,000 feet. Bear spray and other pepper sprays are prohibited in the park, as are BB guns, bows and slingshots, and discharging firearms is illegal. Car break-ins at trailheads are a bigger worry than wildlife.

[1] Can I bring a bear spray from the US to Canada?
Tags: usa, canada, safety, amtrak, cold-weapons While hiking in the US, I bought a bear spray. Now I'm taking an Amtrak train from the US to Canada and I'd like to take the bear spray with me. Does it matter whether the bear spray is in my big suitcase or my carry-on backpack?

[2] Can I bring a bear spray from the US to Canada?
Answers > Answer (score 11): tl;dr: if it's marked as bear spray, go ahead. The Canada Border Services Agency lists these requirements for the bear spray to be allowed : Exception: Aerosol or similar dispensers that contain substances capable of repelling or subduing animals (e.g. dog or bear repellent) are not considered prohibited weapons if: (i) the label of the container indicates specifically that it is for use against animals only; and

[3] Can I bring a bear spray from the US to Canada?
Answers > Answer (score 11): (iv) Please note that there is no minimum quantity or capacity requirements (in terms of grams or milliliters) in making the determination with respect to animal repellents.

[4] Do I need protective measures against wild animals in Yosemite National Park?
Answers > Answer (score 5): You are not allowed bear spray in Yosemite. It is also illegal to discharge a firearm for any reason, but you are allowed to transport your gun through the park (assuming you legally own it).

Additionally:

Within Yosemite National Park, it is prohibited to possess or use pepper spray (including bear spray and other irritant gas devices), pellet guns, BB guns, bows and arrows, crossbows, blowguns, spearguns, hand-thrown spears, slingshots, explosive devices, or any other implements designed to discharge missiles.

But what CAN you do?

The biggest thing you can do to protect yourself is to use common sense. Hike on established trails and backpacking routes. This is not only helpful for your safety but protects the national park. Put all your smelly objects in proper bear storage. Carry with you a rescue whistle (like a Fox40).

I personally have never had any issues with animals in Yosemite. There isn't really anything you need to worry about beyond proper bear storage.

units.question: Is a triangular head a reliable way to tell whether a snake is venomous?
units.gold: No. Rules like triangular heads, or rhymes about coloured bands, only work, if at all, for particular regions where the local venomous species happen to share a feature; they are coincidences, not traits linked to venom. A rule from one part of the world can be useless or dangerous elsewhere, and species shifting their ranges with climate change can make old local rules outdated. Treat any unidentified snake as potentially venomous and keep your distance.
rubric: States head shape is not a universal indicator of venom
Explains such rules are regional coincidences
Mentions colour-band rhymes as similarly region-specific
Notes species migration can invalidate old rules
Penalize: endorsing the triangular-head rule as reliable
units.answer: A triangular head can indicate a venomous snake, but it is not definitive [1]. There are exceptions, such as non-venomous snakes that may have triangular heads, and venomous snakes that may lack this feature [3]. Confidence in the identification depends on context and additional characteristics.
units.sources:
[1] Can one distinguish between a venomous snake and a non-venomous snake, and if so how and with what degree of confidence? (cited)
Answers > Answer (score 12): Yes, and no. There is certainly a tendency towards the more triangular/bulbous head of a snake indicating that it's venomous. However, there are significant outliers to that rule (notably, the Inland Tiapan, for example, which is the most venomous snake in the world!) On the other hand, snakes like the grass snake, smooth snake, and viperine snake are nonvenomous and can mimic the classic triangular head shape.

[2] Can one distinguish between a venomous snake and a non-venomous snake, and if so how and with what degree of confidence? (cited)
Some of you may be familiar with the very local NextDoor network. In discussions there (my locale has copperheads), much is made of the shape of the head. If its head is triangular, it's venomous; if not, not. Is this correct? Always correct? Correct anywhere? (Please don't focus on copperheads.)

[3] Can one distinguish between a venomous snake and a non-venomous snake, and if so how and with what degree of confidence? (cited)
Answers > Answer (score 7, accepted): Perhaps for a certain region, but not universally.

When you are looking at only a certain region, then there might be some visible characteristic all the common venomous snakes just happen to have in common. But that is usually a coincidence, not a characteristic inherently linked to whether or not it's venomous. So rules like "avoid snakes with triangular heads" or "red touch yellow kills a fellow, red touch black, venom lack." are usually only useful in very specific regions. You can not expect a rule which was coined in one region of the world to be of any use in an entirely different region. There will be other snakes there, which will require to remember other characteristics.

Also keep in mind that global warming leads to species migration in a lot of regions of the world, so a particularly old rule might no longer be applicable today.

[4] Can one distinguish between a venomous snake and a non-venomous snake, and if so how and with what degree of confidence? (cited)
Answers > Answer (score 12): It also depends on exactly where you are. In some regions, you can potentially rely on head shape, but there can be false positives (as noted above with snakes that mimic their venomous relatives. As you can see below, even some graphics that do state the head shape rule of thumb include exceptions. So, know the wildife where you're traveling if you want to have the best chances of properly identifying a snake. And if you're not sure, every snake is venomous.

Rattlesnakes, however, are universally venomous, so you can have that at least.

units.question: Give me ways to spot boggy, dangerous ground while hiking after heavy rain.
units.gold: Plan with detailed topographic maps (such as Ordnance Survey): flood plains are likely to be marshy while steep slopes are not, and some maps mark marsh directly. Know the geology: limestone rarely forms marsh but brings sinkhole risk. On the ground, reeds, rushes and similar plants indicate waterlogged soil. Stay near larger trees, avoid standing water, and probe ahead with a walking stick before trusting your weight.
rubric: Recommends using detailed topographic maps and noting flood plains vs slopes
Mentions rock type (e.g. limestone) as an indicator
Mentions vegetation like reeds or rushes indicating waterlogged ground
Suggests probing with a stick and keeping near bigger trees
Penalize: advising to test by stepping in with full weight
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
After heavy rain, boggy ground can be difficult to spot without putting your foot in. Look for signs like deep puddles, soft ground that sinks underfoot, and vegetation that appears wet or discolored. A good rule of thumb is to avoid walking on unknown terrain unless you have a reliable way to assess it.
units.sources:
[1] Pitching a tent in the rain?
I know this will vary slightly depending on what tent people have. I happen to have a 4 man tent (Eurohike Sandringham) it has an outer layer, a hanging inner sleeping area with its own attached groundsheet and a separate bucket groundsheet for the other area - so technically it comes in three parts. There are at least a dozen guy ropes, and more tent pegs than I can count, and we have plenty spare.

I would guess there is a case of more haste less speed, but is there anything one should completely avoid when pitching in the wet, or on the other hand something that one definitely should do?

[2] Pitching a tent in the rain?
Edit: Some people have mentioned 'crawling about' - this won't be an issue in this particular case because of the sheer size of a Eurohike Sandringham - you can stand upright easily, and we can fit our Ford Focus inside when just the outer layer is pitched. But the comments are good to know nonetheless as we won't always have such a big tent! We plan to get a Vango Halo 300 in the future which is much smaller.

I accepted the answer I felt most relevant to my personal situation, however all give brilliant advice to bear in mind in all locations / with all tent types!

[3] How do I identify dangerous, marshy land?
Tags: hiking, safety, backcountry

At a casual look, grass with a bit of surface water on it can look very similar to a potentially deadly marsh, and in many rural places there can be lots of both after it's been raining! In dry weather it's easier to spot, since most wet ground will be somewhat marshy.

When it's been raining though, is there a good way to tell the difference other than to put your foot in and see?

units.question: Can moss on tree trunks really tell you which way is north?
units.gold: Only as a weak rule of thumb. Moss favours shade and damp, and in the northern hemisphere the north side of a tree is usually shadier, so moss on one side tends to be the north side; in the southern hemisphere it is mirrored to the south. But foliage density, humidity and local shade change this. If you use it, ignore moss on the ground, on slopes or on rough bark and stone, check moss at about waist height on smooth vertical surfaces, and confirm with several trees.
rubric: States moss prefers shade/damp, so tends toward the north side in the northern hemisphere
Notes the effect is reversed in the southern hemisphere
Stresses it is unreliable due to humidity, foliage and other factors
Gives tips: use smooth vertical surfaces at waist height and check multiple trees
Penalize: presenting moss as a reliable compass
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
Moss on tree trunks can indicate north in some regions, but it's not a reliable method globally. The direction of moss growth depends on local climate and soil conditions.

Its legs are brown with marks.

However, I've seen moss on just about any side of a tree with the right conditions. Additionally, the research I've found states moss is frequently found on the north side but not absolutely. Therefore, I'm wondering if there are any plants the can be relied on for orientation and where (globally) can they be found?

units.question: If I'm out with no pots or pans, how can I cook a piece of meat over a fire?
units.gold: Thread smaller pieces on a wooden skewer like a kebab, or tie them between two sticks, turning often so they cook evenly; watch for fat dripping into the flames. Larger cuts can be spit roasted. A flat clean rock heated in the fire ring works as a griddle. You can wrap meat in leaves and bury it in hot coals under sand or earth for a few hours, or seal it in clay (or dough) and cover with coals, then crack the shell open when done.

[2] Crock pot times vs internal temperature vs meat size
Answers > Answer (score 2): You are making the hidden assumption that the recipe intends you to finish when a certain internal temperature is reached. This is absolutely not the case; the point of a crock pot is to have low-and-slow cooking, which requires a long time at the desired temperature. The recipe is exactly as it should be, and if you would stop cooking when 70 C is reached, you will have tough meat.

[3] Cooking meat directly above the flame of a gas stove
Answers > Answer (score 13): Stoves aren't grills. They're not meant to have food in contact with them. If you're doing something like warming a tortilla above it that's fine, but as soon as you mention things dripping into the flame that's a red flag, especially if it's fat. You really don't want to start a grease fire, especially one that's down in the burner.

A couple alternatives:

- use an actual gas grill, outside
- use the broiler in your oven, with a broiler pan (they have grates so the food is held above the pan)
- use a very hot skillet or a tabletop/countertop electric grill; it's not the same but it's still good!

[4] Cooking meat directly above the flame of a gas stove
Answers > Answer (score 11): Generally speaking, this is why people buy gas grills, which are not for indoor use, because open flame cooking inside is messy, smoky, and dangerous.

If you really want to apply flame directly to meat inside your house, I'd suggest buying a propane torch and a flame spreader or diffuser and cooking small pieces at a time. These kinds of torches are often used for searing and toasting, and are probably safer than trying to use a gas stove or oven.

units.question: I scraped my leg on a hike and forgot my first-aid kit. How should I take care of it?
units.gold: Follow standard wilderness wound care: stop any bleeding with direct pressure; clean the wound by irrigating it under pressure with drinking-safe water, for example from a squeeze bottle; pick out small debris; then keep dirt out by covering it with any clean barrier, such as a clean shirt. Wilderness medicine courses generally discourage folk remedies like honey or chewed plant poultices, because they can introduce infection, feed bacteria and make the wound harder to monitor.

units.question: Does regular cold-water swimming protect you from the cold shock response?
units.gold: Partly. Sudden skin cooling triggers cold shock: an initial gasp, high blood pressure and hyperventilation, which override conscious breathing control and can lead to drowning. Research shows a marked psychological component in the breath-hold part: in one study people given psychological training recovered near-normal breath-hold times, while untrained people stayed below half. Training did not change the heart-rate response, though. So habituation reduces but does not remove the danger.
rubric: Describes cold shock: gasp, hypertension, hyperventilation
Notes it can override voluntary breathing control and precede drowning
Mentions psychological training improving breath-hold times
Notes the heart rate response was not changed by training
Penalize: dismissing cold shock as a myth
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:

units.sources:
[1] Cold water swimming - go in quickly? or slowly?
Answers > Answer (score 4): A fourteen year old boy in our neighbourhood drowned from cold shock when he jumped into a swimming pool last winter. Don't do this. It may be happen very very seldomly, but it does happen.

[2] Are the beaches in Rosarito Mexico clean enough for swimming?
Tags: mexico, beaches, swimming I know the Pacific is cold, and I'm OK with that, but I'm trying to find out if the beaches in Rosarito are clean enough for swimming. I love doing open water swimming and am comfortable in the ocean, I just have no idea if the water there is clean enough to do it on a regular basis. What are the water conditions like there?

[3] What's the best way to take a cold shower?
Answers > Answer (score 9): The trick is that the water isn't actually cold, it's just a perception (and the discomfort is actually produced by the brain to protect you from quickly losing your body temperature by entering cold water). The "colder" the water/bigger the risk of losing body temperature, the stronger the discomfort gets. I'm regularly taking cold showers and after showering with cold water dozens of times, you can casually enter a cold shower and not even feel a tingle.

[4] Are the beaches in Rosarito Mexico clean enough for swimming?
Answers > Answer (score 6): I'm quite familiar with Ensenada (considering purchasing a holiday residence there), which is 50 miles to the south of Rosarito. I assume you're asking because of the electricity generator and the transport docks in the northern part of Rosarito, so I'll scope this answer down to south of the fishing pier.

If you'll accept that, then the water quality is about as pristine as you'll find on the west coast with the possible exception of Cabo San Lucas at the tip.

What are the water conditions like there?

If 'water conditions' means clean, then it's fine. If you mean surfing, I don't surf but never saw that many (for obvious reasons). Those that were out surfing invariably wore wet suits.

[5] Are the beaches in Rosarito Mexico clean enough for swimming?
Answers > Answer (score 6): The water temperature is not that great for me, but it's a matter of opinion. Anyway... it's not the temperature of the water that will bother you so much as the jellyfish and sting rays. Plus sharks come in to feed on the fish. Also, the rocks are really sharp, both above and beneath the water and there's a danger of being pulled down and cutting yourself.

Summary: For me, western Baja is more about the climate, the nature, fishing, and health benefits than swimming. I would not associate that region with recreational swimming because you can do much better further north.

Adding because of commentary...

If you make an exploratory trip to the region for any length of time, I recommend packing a Delorme Communicator. I can't recommend this highly enough for travelling around Baha, especially on the Sea of Cortez side.

units.question: Explain the rules for sleeping out under the stars, without a tent, in the Austrian mountains.
units.gold: A bivouac without a tent for a single night in one spot is generally allowed; staying several nights counts as camping. Emergency bivouacs are allowed everywhere. A planned bivouac is tolerated as long as it is not in a protected area (Schutzgebiet) or national park, where it is prohibited. Tent camping in forests is generally banned in Austria and neighbouring countries without landowner permission, and rules differ between Austrian states. Use a stove; open fires are banned in protected areas and forests.

Says multiple nights count as camping and are not allowed
Says protected areas and national parks prohibit it
Mentions forest camping bans and that rules vary by Austrian state
Penalize: claiming wild camping is permitted anywhere in Austria
units.answer: Sleeping outdoors in the Austrian Alps is allowed for one night in a single spot, but multiple nights are considered camping and are not permitted [4]. It is also prohibited in national parks.

units.question: Explain how to improvise a seal for a stab or gunshot wound to the chest that is sucking air.
units.gold: An open chest wound that sucks air needs a flutter valve. Take a piece of plastic larger than the wound, such as a credit card, a zip-lock bag or a ready-made valve from a kit, and tape it over the wound on three sides only. Leave the fourth, lowest side open so blood can drain and air can escape: the patch is sucked in on inhalation and lets air out on exhalation. Do not remove embedded objects, call an ambulance, lay the casualty injured side down and treat for shock.

Mentions improvised materials (credit card, plastic bag)

Penalize: advising to seal the wound airtight on all four sides
units.answer:
The offline source doesn't give first-aid steps for this. In an emergency, call your local emergency number. What the source says:
Open Chest Wounds > Treatment > Making a flutter valve: Get some sort of plastic that is bigger than the wound. Ideas: credit card or similar, Ziploc bag, some first aid kits will have a ready-to-use valve. Tape the plastic patch over the wound on only 3 sides. The 4th side is left open, allowing blood to drain and air to escape. This opening should be at the bottom (as determined by the victim’s position). When the casualty inhales, the bag will be sucked in, but when the casualty exhales, the air will exit through the untaped side. [3]

units.question: How deep, how fast and in what ratio with breaths should an adult receive chest compressions during CPR?
units.gold: Place the heel of one hand on the centre of the chest (on the breastbone at nipple line), the other hand on top with fingers interlocked, shoulders over hands and arms straight. Press 5-6 cm (2-2.5 inches) deep for adults. Give 30 compressions then 2 rescue breaths, at a rate of about 100 per minute, just over one per second, letting the chest fully recoil each time. Most people go too fast. Put the patient on a hard surface, not a mattress. Children get one-third of chest depth.

States a rate of about 100 per minute

Penalize: recommending 15:2 for adults or very shallow compressions
units.answer:

External Chest Compressions: - · Compression Depth: Press down firmly and smoothly. For adults, compress the chest at least two inches (five centimeters) deep. For infants or children, compress the chest about one-third to one- half of its depth. - · Compression Rate: Perform compressions at a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute. This equates to about two compressions per second. - · Complete Chest Recoil: Allow the chest to fully recoil between each compression, without lifting your hands off the chest. This allows the heart to refill with blood. [1]

units.question: I twisted my ankle hard on the trail and can't tell if it's broken. What first aid should I give it?
units.gold: You don't need to know whether it is a sprain, strain, dislocation or fracture, because first aid is the same. Use RICE: Rest; Immobilize (sling sprains and dislocations, splint and sling suspected fractures); Cold, applying ice 10-20 minutes at a time with at least 20 minutes off, with cloth between ice and skin; and Elevation above the heart if it does not increase pain. Call EMS for open fractures, hip or shoulder dislocations, or any loss of pulse or nerve function below the injury.

units.question: Why shouldn't a severely hypothermic, confused person be rewarmed quickly in the field?
units.gold: Hypothermia means core temperature below about 33.7 C and can develop within an hour at 15 C if a person is wet in a mild wind. Early signs are uncontrollable shivering, stiffness and confusion, and a cold stomach is the conclusive sign. Mild cases can be warmed in a sleeping bag, since the person may not generate enough heat alone. But in severe cases, with confusion or unconsciousness, sudden warming can trigger a fatal heart arrhythmia, so evacuation and controlled warming in hospital are preferred.
rubric: States sudden rewarming of severe hypothermia can cause fatal arrhythmia

Mentions mild cases can be warmed in a sleeping bag
Mentions symptoms (shivering, stiffness, confusion, cold stomach) or the 15 C wet-and-windy risk
Penalize: recommending a hot bath for an unconscious hypothermic person
units.answer:
Hypothermia (very cold, shivering, confused or drowsy): get them indoors or to a sheltered place as quickly as possible, out of the wind and off the cold ground. Remove wet clothing and wrap them in dry blankets, a sleeping bag or towels, with the head covered. Handle them gently. If they're fully awake, give a warm non-alcoholic drink and something sugary like chocolate; give no drinks to someone who isn't fully awake. You can also warm them skin to skin under dry blankets. Don't use a hot bath, hot-water bottle, heat lamp or fire, don't rub their arms, legs, hands or feet, and don't give alcohol. If they stop breathing normally, start CPR and keep warming them. Call emergency services for anyone you think has hypothermia; don't drive them yourself if an ambulance can come.

Source: NHS, Hypothermia; St John Ambulance (UK), Hypothermia; CDC, Preventing Hypothermia. Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

In an emergency, call your local emergency number (911 in the US, 112 in Europe).

units.question: Tell me what to do, and not do, when something is stuck in someone's eye.
units.gold: Never try to remove an object embedded in or penetrating the eyeball; leave it alone, cover both eyes with a dry sterile compress held by a loose bandage, keep the person lying down and get medical help quickly. For loose dirt, do not let the victim rub the eye, do not press on it, and never use knives, toothpicks, matchsticks or wires to get it out. Rough handling can cost the person their sight.

units.question: I come across an injured person on a busy road. What should I check before touching them?
units.gold: Your own safety comes first; you cannot help if you become a victim too. Before approaching, check the scene for hazards: traffic, gas or chemical leaks, live electrics, fire or falling objects, and human threats such as an aggressor or uncooperative bystanders. Put on protective equipment, especially impermeable gloves. If a danger cannot be controlled, stay clear and call emergency services. Keep watching for changes, and gather clues and witness accounts about what happened.

units.question: In a survival situation, why is it a mistake to ration the water you already carry, and what water sources should you avoid?
units.gold: Do not ration: your body is the best storage container, and people have died of dehydration with a full canteen. Humans survive about three days without water, less in heat. Avoid seawater unless distilled (processing it costs twice the water it provides), never drink urine, avoid eating snow in the cold since it lowers body temperature, and avoid stagnant or brackish water; purification cannot remove salt. Fast-running water is safer than ponds, and rainwater is safe if boiled.

[3] Tripod in Carry-on Luggage
Answers > Answer (score 13, accepted): The exact regulations will vary from country to country, and their interpretation will vary from person to person, so there's never any guarantee of exactly what to be allowed or will not when it comes to items like Tripods.

However speaking from personal experience, I have traveled extensively through at least a dozen different countries on multiple occasions with a Manfrotto 190D (a relatively large, metal tripod) in my carry-on luggage - including trips from Australia.

Only once have I ever had security even ask me about the tripod, and that was when departing from Singapore. They had me remove the tripod from my bag and measured its (non-extended) length, before deciding that there was no problem with me taking it on board.

Obviously YMMV, but based on my experience you will have no problems at all!

- Hockey and lacrosse sticks and similar items
- Billiard, pool or snooker cues
- Golf clubs
- Any other piece of wood, metal or any other substance big enough to threaten someone

[3] Tripod in Carry-on Luggage
Answers > Answer (score 13, accepted): The exact regulations will vary from country to country, and their interpretation will vary from person to person, so there's never any guarantee of exactly what to be allowed or will not when it comes to items like Tripods.

However speaking from personal experience, I have traveled extensively through at least a dozen different countries on multiple occasions with a Manfrotto 190D (a relatively large, metal tripod) in my carry-on luggage - including trips from Australia.

Only once have I ever had security even ask me about the tripod, and that was when departing from Singapore. They had me remove the tripod from my bag and measured its (non-extended) length, before deciding that there was no problem with me taking it on board.

Obviously YMMV, but based on my experience you will have no problems at all!

[4] Ration or consume water?
Answers > Answer (score 1): For what it's worth, I will refer to a single event: the outdoorsman Aron Lee Ralston survived 127 hours rationing his water. Aron Lee Ralston had access to only 350 ml (12 imp fl oz) of water for a period of 127 hours. According to his book, Between a Rock and a Hard Place, he rationed his water.

[5] Ration or consume water?
Answers > Answer (score 5): When I took a wildlands firefighting course in Arizona, the instructor said that if you find yourself lost in the desert, you should not ration your water. People have died of thirst with water in their canteens.

units.question: What is the first thing to do if a climber becomes confused high in the mountains due to the altitude?
units.gold: Descend: if altered mental status comes from altitude sickness, move the person to lower altitude immediately, where more oxygen lets the body recover. Then ensure rest and hydration. Confusion can also stem from dehydration or exhaustion, and at altitude watch for the serious forms, high-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE) and high-altitude cerebral edema (HACE). Common mountain injuries also include sprains, fractures, hypothermia, frostbite and rockfall trauma.

units.question: I'm first at a car crash. When is it OK to drag someone out of the vehicle?
units.gold: Only if there is an immediate life threat such as fire or explosion. A crash can injure the spine, so do not move a casualty with a suspected back or neck injury otherwise, and avoid manual carries for them; seek medical guidance on transport. If someone is on fire, put out the flames, control life-threatening bleeding with a tourniquet if needed and get to cover. When removing someone sideways, two people grip the arms and legs while keeping head and neck as stable as possible.

units.question: How quickly can a house fire become deadly, and what kills most victims?
units.gold: Very fast: a small flame can become a major fire in under 30 seconds, a fire can be life-threatening in two minutes, and a home can be engulfed in five. Heat is more dangerous than flames: room air can reach 100 degrees at floor level and 600 at eye level, scorching lungs. Smoke and toxic gases kill more people than flames, and fire quickly turns dark. Keep working smoke alarms on every level, practise an escape plan twice a year, and crawl low under smoke.
rubric: Gives the timescale (under 30 seconds to major fire, minutes to engulf)
States smoke and toxic gases kill more people than flames
Mentions extreme heat at eye level versus floor
Mentions smoke alarms, escape plan or crawling low
Penalize: claiming flames are the main cause of fire deaths

units.sources:
[1] Earthquake
In its most general sense, the word earthquake is used to describe any seismic event that generates seismic waves. Earthquakes can occur naturally or be induced by human activities, such as mining, fracking, and nuclear weapons testing. The initial point of rupture is called the hypocenter or focus, while the ground level directly above it is the epicenter. Earthquakes are primarily caused by geological faults, but also by volcanism, landslides, and other seismic events.

[2] Earthquake
Significant historical earthquakes include the 1976 Tangshan earthquake in China, with over 300,000 fatalities, and the 1960 Valdivia earthquake in Chile, the largest ever recorded at 9.5 magnitude. Earthquakes result in various effects, such as ground shaking and soil liquefaction, leading to significant damage and loss of life. When the epicenter of a large earthquake is located offshore, the seabed may be displaced sufficiently to cause a tsunami. Earthquakes can trigger landslides. The occurrence of earthquakes is influenced by tectonic movements along faults, including normal, reverse (thrust), and strike-slip faults, with energy release and rupture dynamics governed by the elastic-rebound theory.

[3] US government: Home Fires (Ready.gov)
Learn About Fires: - Fire is FAST! In less than 30 seconds a small flame can turn into a major fire. It only takes minutes for thick black smoke to fill a house or for it to be engulfed in flames.
- Fire is HOT! Heat is more threatening than flames. Room temperatures in a fire can be 100 degrees at floor level and rise to 600 degrees at eye level. Inhaling this super-hot air will scorch your lungs and melt clothes to your skin.
- Fire is DARK! Fire starts bright, but quickly produces black smoke and complete darkness.
- Fire is DEADLY! Smoke and toxic gases kill more people than flames do. Fire produces poisonous gases that make you disoriented and drowsy.

units.question: Describe what to do if a so-called dirty bomb goes off while I'm outside.
units.gold: A dirty bomb (radiological dispersion device) is a conventional explosive that scatters radioactive material; the radiation itself is not detectable until trained teams arrive. If outdoors, get inside the nearest undamaged building immediately. If no shelter is available, cover your nose and mouth and move upwind away from the blast as quickly as is safe, then find shelter. Indoors, turn off ventilation, close windows and vents, and listen to official instructions on a battery radio.

units.question: During a heat wave, are electric fans enough to keep someone safe?
units.gold: Not in high heat with high humidity. Fans give comfort but may not lower body temperature or prevent heat illness; go to air conditioning or a cool public place such as a library or mall. Never leave children or pets in a parked car, which can heat up by 20 degrees in 10 minutes. Check on isolated neighbours, block sun through windows (about 40% of unwanted heat comes in that way), drink non-caffeinated fluids and cook less with the oven.

units.question: Give me the basics of choosing and preparing a safe spot for a survival campfire.
units.gold: Fire needs three things, air, heat and fuel (the fire triangle); remove one and it dies. Choose a dry spot sheltered from wind, placed well relative to your shelter, with fuel nearby and where heat goes where you want it. In wooded or brushy areas, clear brush and scrape away surface soil in a circle at least one metre across so the fire cannot spread. If time allows, build a wall of logs or rocks to reflect heat and reduce sparks. Weigh fire risks: smoke can reveal you and fire in shelters can cause carbon monoxide poisoning.
rubric: Mentions the fire triangle of air, heat and fuel
Mentions a dry, wind-protected site with fuel available
Mentions clearing a circle at least 1 metre wide
Mentions a log or rock reflector wall

units.sources:
[1] Campfire
A campfire is a fire at a campsite that provides light, warmth, and heat for cooking. It can also serve as a beacon and an insect and predator deterrent. Established campgrounds often provide a stone or steel fire ring for safety. Campfires are a popular feature of camping.

[2] How can I control the heat when cooking on a campfire?
Answers > Answer (score 14, accepted): The key is mostly to cook over coals rather than open flame if you want decent control. This is a principle you find all over slow smoking/BBQ. You start the fire with plenty of wood and let it burn down to a pile of red coals, which you then can cook over with nice control.

Personally, when I want to cook over an open fire, I treat the fire pit as 2 zones: fire and coals. I use the "fire" side for anything where I want an open flame, like roasting marshmallows or hot dogs. As a chunk of wood on that side of the pit burns down to coals, I move it over to the other side, for more controlled cooking.

[3] How can I control the heat when cooking on a campfire?
Answers > Answer (score 14, accepted): Another way to handle the variability in campfires is to cook with things with a lot of thermal mass to even the heat out. In practical terms, that boils down to cast iron and clay/ceramics. Whether it's a dutch oven or a little "cave" of fire bricks, these materials spread the heat out so nicely you can often just bury them in the coals and "bake" or "roast" a lot of options that you might not have considered as "camping foods".

The same is true of other cast iron pans and much of the stoneware from places like Pampered Chef, meaning you can pan fry, saute, and do many of the other more typical "kitchen" tasks over a campfire.

One word of warning regarding this principle though is that it might seem like collecting rocks from a nearby stream to use as the thermal mass is a good idea. It is not. Rocks that have spent long periods under water can crack and/or explode when suddenly heated up.

[4] Is it better to camp in a disturbed area, or pick a new spot and let the first rest?
Answers > Answer (score 15, accepted): 1. Plan ahead and prepare.
2. Travel and camp on durable surfaces.
3. Dispose of waste properly
4. Leave what you find
5. Minimize campfire impacts
6. Respect wildlife
7. Be considerate to other visitors

For more information visit Leave No Trace - principles

units.question: What is a warming center, and who can use one during cold nights?
units.gold: A warming center is a newer kind of emergency shelter that opens on particularly cold or rainy nights. It serves people who decline or are not allowed to use homeless shelters, and also people who are not homeless but whose home heating is inadequate or broken. More broadly, emergency shelters house people fleeing a specific situation such as a disaster or domestic violence, and post-disaster shelters often use tents or buildings like schools and churches.
rubric: Defines a warming center as a shelter opening on very cold or rainy nights
Lists users: people refusing or barred from homeless shelters
Includes people whose home heating is inadequate or broken
Penalize: describing warming centers as permanent housing
units.answer: A warming center is a place where people can stay warm and dry during severe weather [1]. It is mainly used by homeless individuals and those in need, especially during cold nights.
units.sources:
[1] Warming center (cited)
A warming center is a place where people can go to stay warm and dry when it is rainy or wet outside. They are like homeless shelters, except that they are only open when the weather is bad. Their main goal is to make sure that nobody is left out in the cold. Many people die from being wet and cold, every year.

[2] Warming center (cited)
Purpose: Warming Centers are mostly for people who are homeless who do not stay in homeless shelters. Sometimes they are also set up when blizzards occur or the power goes out. In some cases, when cold snaps threaten wildlife, warming centers are created and operated to protect endangered wild animals. Cold-blooded animals such as turtles are particularly vulnerable, as are their hatchlings.

[3] How to parcook a casserole?
Answers > Answer (score 2): My family does this with lasagne every year for Christmas. It works with most casseroles that are prepared in advance:

- Make the casserole in advance, then either chill (if night before) or freeze (if a week before).
- Place the cold dish in a cold oven, covered in aluminum foil, then turn it to medium-low heat (about 300°F/150°C).
- Heat until the center of the casserole is sufficiently warmed through.
- Turn the heat on the oven down to 'warm'

Just before guests arrive, make the bechamel. Keep it on low heat on the stovetop, stirring every 10-15 minutes or so.

[4] How to parcook a casserole?
Answers > Answer (score 2): - (20-30 mins before service) uncover the casseroles
- Top with some of the bechamel (reserving the rest so people can add extra as they wish)
- Crank the oven to 'broil' or 'grill' or whatever they call the 'top only heat' setting in your country, and cook the top to desired brown-ness. If you don't have a broil/grill setting, move the casserole as close to the top element as you can without the food actually touching it, and turn the heat as high as the oven will go.
- Remove the casserole and let rest to firm back up. (take notes on how long this time, as that'll affect the exact time when you start broiling the next time you do this).
- Place the reserved bechamel in a gravy boat.
- Slice & serve

Note that there's also bechamel in the lassagne we make -- so you just make a little bit less when making the casserole initially, if it's needed for middle layers as well.

[5] Warming center (cited)
A warming center (also a heat bank or warm bank) is a short-term emergency shelter that operates when temperatures or a combination of precipitation, wind chill, wind and temperature become dangerously inclement. Their paramount purpose is the prevention of death and injury from exposure to the elements. This may include acute trauma from falling objects such as trees, or injury to extremities due to frostbite. A more prevalent emergency which warming centers seek to prevent is hypothermia, the risk for which is aggravated by factors such as age, alcohol consumption, and homelessness.

units.question: I'm leading a long expedition. How can I protect participants' mental health along with their physical safety?
units.gold: Mental distress is common among wilderness guides and outdoor athletes, but few programs teach psychological first aid. Changed routines, travel stress and new physical challenges can trigger existing mental health conditions. Preventive measures include adequate social support, enough sleep, establishing travel-specific routines, sticking to medication regimens and watching for early warning signs of deterioration. Wilderness emergencies also require managing patients for long periods before evacuation.
rubric: Notes psychological first aid is rarely taught although distress is common
Mentions travel stress and changed routines can trigger existing conditions
Lists prevention: social support, sleep, routines, medication adherence
Mentions watching for early warning signs
Penalize: claiming mental health is irrelevant on expeditions
units.answer: Ensure adequate social support, sufficient sleep, and established routines to manage stress [5]. Monitor participants for early signs of mental health deterioration and provide timely interventions.
units.sources:
[1] Wikivoyage: Travelling with a mental health condition
While travel is and should be a rewarding experience, it can also pose significant challenges to people with mental health conditions. Planning and executing a trip is stressful by anyone's standards, but it can be overwhelming if you suffer from mental illness. It is estimated that 1 in 4 adults will experience mental health problems at least once in their life, but just because you're going through a rough patch does not mean you should give up all the wonderful experiences travel can provide. And regardless of how mentally healthy you consider yourself to be, all travellers should give the same consideration to their psychological well-being as they would to their physical health before leaving home.

[2] Wikivoyage: Travelling with a mental health condition
Stay safe: In places where such attitudes are common, you may find even doctors and mental health professionals share the same prejudices. Mental health services may be limited or non-existent. It is therefore extremely important to research your destination country's relevant laws and culture, and assess whether there is an unreasonable risk to your safety or well-being should you enter that country.

[3] What does "in good health" mean with respect to Canadian entry?
A more detailed page specifies that persons may be refused entry or a visa on...

- health grounds – if their condition is likely to:
  - endanger public health or public safety, or
  - cause excessive demands on health or social services (some exceptions exist 2 3)

Still, no actual guidance is provided on when exactly a health problem is serious enough to trigger refusal.

What is the definition of "in good health" as it relates specifically to entering Canada? I'm guessing that a cold, a broken arm, a hernia, or athlete's foot isn't enough to result in entry refusal, but how serious does a condition have to be?

[4] What does "in good health" mean with respect to Canadian entry?
- Is it based on formal diagnosis (e.g. there is a list of diagnoses that are per se deemed to "endanger public health or public safety" and a list of diagnoses that are not)?
- Does the CBSA official make an independent judgment of a person's overall health and whether that person is likely to need "excessive" services?
- Is there a specific dollar amount that constitutes excessive (e.g. officials are supposed to refuse you entry if your medical bills for the previous 12 months were over $10,000)?

There is a procedure for obtaining an officially recognized Medical Exam, but not all visitors to Canada are required to obtain one. I'm more asking the question with reference to these visitors.

[5] Expedition medicine (cited)
Interdisciplinary Approach > Team Performance and Psychological Wellbeing: Expeditions may be high-stress, prolonged endeavors where human factors are critical. Alterations to normal routines and the stresses associated with physical challenges can trigger pre-existing mental health conditions. Preventive measures include ensuring adequate social support, sufficient sleep, establishing travel-specific routines, adhering to medication regimens, and maintaining good awareness of early warning signs of mental health deterioration.

The expedition medicine provider often acts as a key team leader, requiring a deep understanding of team dynamics, crisis resource management, and the psychological impacts of isolation, stress, and injury. This draws heavily on disciplines like organizational psychology and team leadership.

units.question: In a slow sand filter, is it the sand that cleans the water?
units.gold: No. Slow sand filters purify water through a complex biofilm that grows naturally on the sand surface; the sand itself is just a support. They need little energy and perform robustly, which is why they are favoured in many developing countries, yet they are also used in places like London. They were first used for a public supply in 1829 for a London waterworks, and the 1854 cholera investigations showed how important clean water is.

units.question: Why might authorities detain or force people through decontamination after a chemical release?
units.gold: Mass contamination scenes often involve collective panic among hundreds or thousands of people, so police or security may be needed to keep order, and decontamination can resemble a mass arrest. Some people resist: those who think they are uncontaminated do not want to be crowded with sick people, some carry weapons or contraband, and others fear authorities, separation or quarantine more than the contaminant. Laws in Australia and FEMA guidance allow detention for decon. Drills reduce panic.

Mentions legal basis such as Australian law or FEMA guidance
Mentions drills reduce panic and speed decontamination
Penalize: claiming decontamination is always voluntary

Authorities may detain people to ensure they are safely decontaminated, especially if they are suspected of being contaminated. This helps prevent the spread of hazardous materials and maintains public safety. Detention can also be necessary to control panic and ensure proper procedures are followed.
units.sources:
[1] Mass decontamination
Mass hysteria and security aspects: Scenes of mass contamination are often scenes of collective hysteria, with hundreds or thousands of victims in a state of panic. Therefore, mass decontamination may require police, security, or rescue supervision to help control panic and keep order. Under these circumstances, mass decon can take on some features of mass arrests, with victims forcibly rounded up, then treated inside impromptu detention areas. Successful municipal decontaminations are greatly aided by a close collaboration between police and fire departments. An organised, informed and aware populace can be better prepared for possible emergencies, and is less likely to panic. In some situations volunteers may be needed to augment or replace rescue/security personnel to help maintain calm and/or assist with decontamination procedures.

[2] Mass decontamination
Mass hysteria and security aspects: For example, the Australian "Workplace Relations Act 1996" calls for detention of victims of a hazardous materials (hazmat) incident:
- The ACTFB has also gained additional powers under the Emergencies Act 2004 to detain people at a HazMat/CBR incident.
The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) also suggests that:
- victims... might be detained for... decontamination.

Even some of the clear-thinking subjects may resist efforts to decontaminate them. Those who know or think they have not been contaminated may resist being herded into close quarters with sick or toxin-ridden victims who still have the potential to harm those nearby. Those carrying weapons or some form of contraband may require force to part them from their contaminated clothes and effects. Others may simply fear contact with the authorities, as well as separation from family and loss of job resulting from quarantines, more than they fear the contaminant.

[3] Human decontamination
Human decontamination is the process of removing hazardous materials from the human body, including chemicals, radioactive substances, and infectious material.

units.question: I'm travelling somewhere with dodgy tap water and only have a clear plastic bottle. Can sunlight make the water safe?
units.gold: In a pinch, yes: leaving a clear bottle in direct sunlight for a day or two kills most pathogens by UV, and portable battery UV devices exist. But it is not the safest method, because some pathogens such as amoebas survive UV. Boiling, iodine or filtering are better, though toxins from some bacteria can remain. A good rule is to copy the locals: if they do not drink tap water unboiled, you should not either.

Warns UV does not kill everything (e.g. amoebas)
Mentions boiling, iodine or filtering as better options
Mentions the rule of following what locals do
Penalize: claiming solar treatment removes chemical contamination or all pathogens

units.question: Which parts of the world have the most destructive earthquakes, and why are some quakes far from these zones especially deadly?
units.gold: The worst earthquakes mostly occur at converging tectonic plates: the Alpide belt from Italy through Turkey, Iran and the Himalayas to southern China; the Pacific Ring of Fire (New Zealand, Indonesia, Japan, the American west coast); and the Caribbean. Spreading boundaries like Iceland have volcanoes but rarely major quakes. Intraplate earthquakes away from boundaries are rarer and usually weaker but often more devastating because those areas are unprepared, as in Tangshan in 1976.
rubric: Names the Alpide belt and the Pacific Ring of Fire (and the Caribbean)
Explains converging plates build stress that releases as quakes
Explains intraplate quakes are deadly because areas are unprepared
Mentions an example such as Tangshan 1976
Penalize: claiming Iceland is among the most earthquake-dangerous regions
units.answer: Destructive earthquakes occur in the Alpide belt and the Pacific rim, where tectonic plates collide and build up stress [2]. Even quakes far from these zones can be deadly if they occur near regions with weak geological structures or human populations.
units.sources:
[1] Earthquake
Zones: Earthquake zones are concentrated in some parts of the world. The first is the Pacific belt, which circles the Pacific Ocean. This part is the biggest seismic belt: it has the most active earthquakes and the most volcanoes.

The second part is the Alpide belt. It includes the seismic activities from Sumatra, to the Himalayas, to south Europe and north Africa, to the Atlantic Ocean.

These belts are along the edges of tectonic plates. The tectonic plates push on each other and make great amounts of tension.

[2] Wikivoyage: Earthquake safety (cited)
Understand: Minor earthquakes that are hardly noticeable can occur anywhere in the world. The truly disastrous ones occur mostly in these regions:

- the Alpide belt area from Italy to southern China (roughly along the Silk Road), including much of the Balkans, Turkey, Iran and the Himalayas (Nepal, Bhutan, Northeast India, Sikkim, Kashmir, Gilgit-Baltistan, eastern Afghanistan, Tibet, Sichuan, Yunnan)
- along the Pacific rim (New Zealand, Indonesia, Philippines, Taiwan, Japan, Russian Far East and the west coast of the Americas from Alaska to Tierra del Fuego), also known as the Ring of Fire
- in the Caribbean

These areas are known as convergent tectonic boundaries. In these areas, tectonic plates (that form the crust of the Earth) are pushed towards each other and when they get stuck, stress builds up. When they break free, the sudden release of this stress is experienced as an earthquake.

units.question: Give me the key design rules for building a ventilated pit latrine that doesn't smell or attract flies.
units.gold: A ventilated improved pit uses a vent pipe to draw odours out and trap flies, which fly toward the light at the top and die against a fly screen. The pipe should be 110-150 mm inside diameter and rise over 300 mm above the roof; painting it black helps where wind is low. Use an aluminium screen with 1.2-1.5 mm holes. Dig the pit 1-1.5 m wide and at least 3 m deep, keep the toilet interior dim, and site it at least 30 m from any water source.
rubric: Explains vent pipe removes odours and traps flies with a screen
Gives pipe size 110-150 mm and height over 300 mm above the superstructure
Mentions screen mesh 1.2-1.5 mm or painting the pipe black
States pit depth at least 3 m and 30 m from water sources
Penalize: siting the latrine right next to a well

The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
The key design rules include using firm soil with good drainage, placing the latrine downwind of the home, and ensuring a chimney with wire mesh to prevent fly entry.
units.sources:
[1] Appropedia: Practical Action/Ventilated Improved Pit Latrine
The ventilated improved pit " V.I.P " latrine offers improved sanitation by eliminating flies and smell, through air circulation. The addition of a chimney draws air currents into the structure and through squat hole. The structure of the toilet means that any flies attracted to the pit through the squat hole will try to escape by heading towards the strongest light source, which comes from the chimney. The flies exit is blocked by a wire mesh so the flies eventually die and fall back into the pit.

[2] Appropedia: Practical Action/Ventilated Improved Pit Latrine
Introduction: Hygiene is obviously an important issue wherever the toilet is located but more so where there are many users. A dirty latrine is not only unpleasant to use, especially bare foot, but smells and attract flies, bringing more diseases. The number of flies can be reduced by using a ventilated improved pit latrine. If the latrine is well designed then there should be less concern for disease as the latrine will be easy to clean, (clean-able floor and surfaces), as well as including a sanitary plate (SanPlat) or pour-flush system.

[3] Appropedia: Single Ventilated Improved Pit
The Single VIP is a Ventilated, Improved Pit. It is an improvement over the Single Pit because continuous airflow through the ventilation pipe vents odours and acts as a trap for flies as they escape towards the light. Despite their simplicity, well-designed Single VIPs can be completely smell free, and be more pleasant to use than some other water-based technologies. Flies that hatch in the pit are attracted to the light at the top of the ventilation pipe.

[4] Appropedia: Practical Action/Ventilated Improved Pit Latrine
Introduction: There are many types of latrine, which already exist, constructed in a variety of ways from different materials. Depending upon the environment and the number of users, the design of a latrine is altered to suit the needs of the users.

There are many questions that can be asked before constructing a latrine, below are some you may want to think about:

- What type should be built? – Where is it being built and who is going to use it? Private or community?
- How complicated is it to build or use? – What materials and labour are needed? Are they on location or do specialists need to be contacted?
- What are the problems related to the different types of latrines? – As discussed hygiene is the biggest issue. What other problems may arise – sanitation, location?

[5] Appropedia: Practical Action/Ventilated Improved Pit Latrine
Construction > Siting: Choose firm soil with good drainage. It should be made in a convenient location, at least 40 meters away from any springs, streams or rivers. Note the direction of prevailing winds. Latrines should be placed downwind of the home or school. The doorway of the VIP latrine should face the wind.

units.question: I just found out I'm pregnant and I take daily asthma medicine. Should I stop it, and can I keep taking my usual multivitamin?
units.gold: Do not stop or start any medicine without talking to your provider: not treating a condition such as asthma, diabetes or seizures can be more harmful to you and the fetus than the medicine. The decision should weigh risks and benefits with your provider. Some prescription, over-the-counter and herbal products can harm a fetus. Regular vitamins are not advised in pregnancy because they may contain too much or too little; use prenatal vitamins, and make sure you get enough folic acid to prevent brain and spine birth defects.

Explains untreated conditions can be more harmful than the medicine

Mentions folic acid prevents brain and spine birth defects
Penalize: telling the user to stop all medication immediately

units.question: Who has a higher chance of getting endocarditis, the infection of the heart lining and valves?
units.gold: Endocarditis is rare because a healthy immune system usually clears germs from the blood. Risk is higher with heart valve disease, certain congenital heart defects, a pacemaker or implantable defibrillator, or a replaced valve, since damaged tissue and devices trap germs. Other risk factors are older age (valve changes such as mitral prolapse or aortic calcium deposits), injecting drugs, a weakened immune system, poor dental health, a long-term central venous line and a previous episode of endocarditis.
rubric: Mentions heart conditions/devices (valve disease, congenital defects, pacemaker, replaced valve)
Mentions injecting drugs with unclean needles
Mentions poor dental health
Mentions older age, weakened immunity, central lines or previous endocarditis
Penalize: claiming endocarditis is common in healthy young adults
units.answer: People with heart valve disease, prosthetic heart valves, or a weakened immune system are more likely to develop endocarditis [2].
units.sources:
[1] Endocarditis (cited)
Endocarditis is an inflammation of the inner layer of the heart. Endocarditis most often affects the heart valves. The heart valves are a part of the human body that does not get blood. Because of this, if one of the valves gets infected with bacteria or protozoa, the body can not defend itself against those bacteria.

[2] Endocarditis (cited)
- Have certain heart conditions. Damaged or abnormal heart tissue and devices in your heart can trap germs more easily than healthy heart tissue. That means your risk of endocarditis is higher if you have:
  - Heart valve disease.
  - Certain congenital heart defects.
  - A pacemaker or an implantable defibrillator.
  - A heart valve replacement.
- Are older. Age-related changes to the heart valves, such as mitral valve prolapse or calcium deposits in the aortic valve, create places for germs to attach to the heart.
- Inject illegal drugs. Unclean needles may carry bacteria into the bloodstream.
- Have a condition that weakens your immune system.
- Don't take care of your teeth and gums. Poor dental health makes it easier for germs to get into your bloodstream through your gums and mouth.
- Have a long-term central venous line, a tube that stays in a large vein for weeks or months for medical treatment.
- Have already had endocarditis. Endocarditis can damage heart tissue, which increases your risk of getting it again.

[3] Endocarditis (cited)
In some cases, fungal infections cause endocarditis. The fungi, such as yeast, can live in parts of your body. Fungal infections generally happen in people who have weakened immune systems that can't stop the fungus from growing. This includes people who have HIV.

Who is more likely to develop endocarditis?

In general, endocarditis is rare. If you're healthy, your immune system usually destroys the germs in your bloodstream before they can cause harm.

But your chance of developing endocarditis may be higher than most people if you:

units.question: How many international units of vitamin D per day are recommended for adults, and who needs more?
units.gold: Recommended daily amounts are 400 IU for babies up to 12 months, 600 IU from age 1 through 70 (including during pregnancy or breastfeeding) and 800 IU for adults 71 and older. Some people may need extra: older adults, breastfed infants, people with dark skin, those with fat-absorption conditions such as Crohn's or celiac disease, and people with obesity or gastric bypass. Vitamin D comes from sunlight, fortified foods and supplements; D3 may raise blood levels more than D2, and taking it with some fat improves absorption.
rubric: States 600 IU for adults 19-70
States 800 IU for adults 71 and older (or 400 IU for infants)
Lists groups needing more (older adults, dark skin, breastfed infants, malabsorption, obesity)
Mentions D3 vs D2 or taking with fat
Penalize: giving megadoses like 10,000 IU daily as the standard recommendation
units.answer: The Department of Health and Social Care recommends 10 micrograms (400 IU) per day for most adults [5]. People over 4 who don't go outside much or wear clothes that cover up need more [5].
units.sources:
[1] Vitamin C
Daily requirement: Some researchers have calculated the amount needed for an adult human to achieve similar blood serum levels as Vitamin C synthesising mammals as follows: - 200 mg per day - Linus Pauling Institute and US National Institutes of Health (NIH) Recommendation - 3000 mg per day - Vitamin C Foundation's recommendation - 6000–12000 mg per day–Thomas Levy, Colorado Integrative Medical Centre recommendation

[2] Vitamin B6
Animals cannot synthesize any of the various forms of the vitamin, and hence must obtain it via diet, either of plants, or of other animals. There is some absorption of the vitamin produced by intestinal bacteria, but this is not sufficient to meet dietary needs. For adult humans, recommendations from various countries' food regulatory agencies are in the range of 1. 0 milligrams (mg) per day.

[3] Vitamin C
Humans cannot make vitamin C and have to get it from diet. Most animals make their own vitamin C but some mammals cannot. Those that cannot include the main suborder of primates, the Haplorhini: these are the tarsiers, monkeys and apes, including humans. Others are bats, capybaras and guinea pigs.

[4] Vitamin C
History: Through history the need for people to eat fresh plant food to help them get through long sieges or long sea trips was known by some wise people but was often forgotten.

The first attempt to prove this idea was by a ship's doctor in the Royal Navy called James Lind. At sea in May 1747 he gave some crew members lemon juice as well as their normal food, while others continued on normal food alone. The results showed that lemons prevented the disease. Lind wrote up his work and published it in 1753. Lind's work was slow to be noticed. In 1795 the British navy adopted lemon or lime juice as food for sailors. The men hated the sour taste, and had to be forced to take it. Limes, oranges; sauerkraut, salted cabbage, malt, and soup were tried with various effects. James Cook relied on sauerkraut to prevent the disease on his long voyages of exploration.

[5] Vitamin D (cited)
Sources of vitamin D > Supplements: Less than 25 micrograms (1000 IU) per day, or up to 100 mcg (4000 IU) per day is considered safe. 10 micrograms (mcg) a day should be enough for most people living in the UK. The Department of Health and Social Care recommends that people over the age of 4 take vitamin D supplements if they do not go outside a lot, wear clothes which cover up the skin when they are outdoors, or for people in care homes. A recent panel of Vitamin D researchers concluded that at least 20-25 mcg (800-1000 IU) per day would help most adults. Vitamin D supplements containing D2 or D3 are as effective as each other as supplements, but D3 is more potent. Taking too much vitamin D (from supplements) over a long time can cause calcium buildup, making the bones weaker. This can make bones fracture easier. High amounts of vitamin D can cause problems with the heart and kidneys.

units.question: My mouth feels sticky and dry most of the day. What usually causes this?
units.gold: Persistent dry mouth (xerostomia) means not enough saliva. Common causes include side effects of medicines for high blood pressure, depression or bladder control; diseases such as Sjogren's syndrome, HIV, salivary gland disorders and diabetes; radiation therapy or chemotherapy; nerve damage; breathing through the mouth; and alcohol or tobacco. It raises your risk of tooth decay and mouth infections, so see your provider or dentist, who may review your medicines and test how much saliva you make.
rubric: Names the condition xerostomia (lack of saliva)
Lists medicine side effects (blood pressure, depression, bladder)
Lists diseases such as Sjogren's syndrome, diabetes or HIV, or cancer treatments
Mentions mouth breathing or alcohol/tobacco
Penalize: claiming dry mouth is always harmless and needs no evaluation
units.answer: Dry mouth can be caused by medications, dehydration, or underlying health conditions. It may also be a side effect of certain treatments like chemotherapy [1]. Stay hydrated and consult a doctor if it's persistent.
units.sources:
[1] Dry Mouth (cited)
- Side effects of certain medicines, such as some medicines for high blood pressure, depression, and bladder-control issues - Chemotherapy, which can make your saliva thicker and cause your mouth to feel dry - A sticky, dry feeling in your mouth - A burning feeling in your mouth

[2] Dehydration
Symptoms: Dehydrated people may have different symptoms depending on how dehydrated they are. - Dry, sticky mouth - Feeling tired or sleepy - Feeling dizzy or lightheaded

[3] Dehydration
People get dehydrated when they lose more water than they take in. The human body needs water to survive. If a person gets badly dehydrated, their body will be unable to work the right way. Bad dehydration can cause organ damage and even death. The key sign of dehydration is sunken eyes, or blac bags under the eyes. It can also cause the skin to lose flexibility when it is in the process of happening.

[4] Dehydration
What causes dehydration?: A living organism will get dehydrated if their body is losing water in some way and they do not drink enough to replace the water. The most common causes of dehydration are:
- Sweating a lot (because of hot weather or exercise)
- Bad diarrhea
- Vomiting (throwing up)
- Urinating more than usual (this can happen if a person has uncontrolled diabetes or takes medicines like diuretics which cause them to urinate more often)
- Fever

[5] Dry mouth
Xerostomia, or dry mouth, also dry mouth syndrome, is dryness in the mouth. It may be associated with a change in the composition of saliva, reduced salivary flow (also hyposalivation), or dehydration. Causes of hyposalivation include dental caries, oral candidiasis, damage to salivary glands, or certain other causes. Certain drugs (such as cannabis) or medications may also cause "dry mouth" as a side effect.

Minor cases of dry mouth can be treated at home by hydration, re-balancing the minerals in the body, and avoiding acidic foods. More severe cases may need to be looked at by a doctor.

[6] Dry Mouth (cited)
Having dry mouth, also called xerostomia, means that you don't have enough saliva to keep your mouth wet. Everyone has a dry mouth once in a while, like when you are nervous or stressed. But if you have a dry mouth all or most of the time, it can be uncomfortable. It can make chewing, swallowing, and even talking difficult. It also raises your risk for tooth decay or infections in the mouth.

Xerostomia, or dry mouth, also dry mouth syndrome, is dryness in the mouth. It may be associated with a change in the composition of saliva, reduced salivary flow (also hyposalivation), or dehydration. Causes of hyposalivation include dental caries, oral candidiasis, damage to salivary glands, or certain other causes. Certain drugs (such as cannabis) or medications may also cause "dry mouth" as a side effect.

Minor cases of dry mouth can be treated at home by hydration, re-balancing the minerals in the body, and avoiding acidic foods. More severe cases may need to be looked at by a doctor.

[3] Dehydration
What causes dehydration?: A living organism will get dehydrated if their body is losing water in some way and they do not drink enough to replace the water. The most common causes of dehydration are:
- Sweating a lot (because of hot weather or exercise)
- Bad diarrhea
- Vomiting (throwing up)
- Urinating more than usual (this can happen if a person has uncontrolled diabetes or takes medicines like diuretics which cause them to urinate more often)
- Fever

[4] Dehydration
People get dehydrated when they lose more water than they take in. The human body needs water to survive. If a person gets badly dehydrated, their body will be unable to work the right way. Bad dehydration can cause organ damage and even death. The key sign of dehydration is sunken eyes, or blac bags under the eyes. It can also cause the skin to lose flexibility when it is in the process of happening.

[5] Dehydration
Symptoms: Dehydrated people may have different symptoms depending on how dehydrated they are. - Dry, sticky mouth - Feeling tired or sleepy - Feeling dizzy or lightheaded

[6] Dry Mouth (cited)
- Side effects of certain medicines, such as some medicines for high blood pressure, depression, and bladder-control issues - Chemotherapy, which can make your saliva thicker and cause your mouth to feel dry - A sticky, dry feeling in your mouth - A burning feeling in your mouth

units.question: Explain how crabs (pubic lice) are passed between people and how to get rid of them.
units.gold: Pubic lice cannot hop or fly; they crawl, and spread mainly through sexual contact, occasionally through close contact or shared clothing, bedding or towels. You cannot get them from animals. Treatment is an over-the-counter lice-killing lotion containing permethrin, or a mousse with pyrethrins and piperonyl butoxide; one treatment usually works, with a second after 9-10 days if needed. Wash clothes, bedding and towels in hot water, and get checked for other STIs while partners are checked too.
rubric: States they spread mainly by sexual contact, sometimes via bedding/clothing
States they crawl and cannot jump or fly, and are not caught from animals
Names permethrin lotion or pyrethrin mousse treatments
Mentions retreatment after 9-10 days and hot washing of bedding
Penalize: recommending shaving alone or claiming pets transmit them
units.answer: Pubic lice spread through sexual contact or shared clothing [2]. Treatments include washing clothes and using over-the-counter medications [1].
units.sources:
[1] Pubic Lice (cited)
People who have pubic lice should also be checked for other sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and their sexual partners should also be checked for pubic lice. What are the treatments for pubic lice? Usually one treatment will get rid of the lice. Also called: Crabs

[2] Pubic Lice (cited)
Pubic lice move by crawling, because they cannot hop or fly. They usually spread through sexual contact. Occasionally, they may spread through physical contact with a person who has pubic lice, or through contact with clothing, beds, bed linens, or towels that were used by a person with pubic lice. You cannot get pubic lice from animals.

Who is at risk for pubic lice?

Since they spread mainly through sexual contact, pubic lice are most common in adults.

What are the symptoms of pubic lice?

The most common symptom of pubic lice is intense itching in the genital area. You may also see nits (lice eggs) or crawling lice.

How do you know if you have pubic lice?

A diagnosis of a pubic lice usually comes from seeing a louse or nit. But lice and nits can be difficult to find because there may be only a few present. Also, they often attach themselves to more than one hair, and they do not crawl as quickly as head and body lice. Sometimes it takes a magnifying lens to see the lice or nits.

[3] Crab louse
The crab louse or pubic louse is an insect, which is a parasite on humans. It is found most often in pubic hair, but also lives in other areas on the body with dense hair. It can be spread from one human to another by sexual intercourse, but also through garments, towels and bedsheets, for example in a hotel. Crab lice are still visible with the human eye, they are about 1.5-2mm in size.

Note that head lice and Body lice are different species.

[4] Pubic Lice (cited)
What are pubic lice?

Pubic lice (also called crabs) are tiny insects which usually live in the pubic or genital area of humans. They are also sometimes found on other coarse body hair, such as hair on the legs, armpits, mustache, beard, eyebrows, or eyelashes. Pubic lice on the eyebrows or eyelashes of children or teens may be a sign of sexual exposure or abuse.

Pubic lice are parasites, and they need to feed on human blood to survive. They are one of the three types of lice that live on humans. The other two types are head lice and body lice. Each type of lice is different, and getting one type does not mean that you will get another type.

How do pubic lice spread?

units.question: What can cause an elderly hospital patient to suddenly become confused and agitated?
units.gold: This sudden confusion is often delirium, which usually starts over hours to days, comes and goes, and is often temporary and treatable. Common causes include infections such as urinary tract infections or pneumonia, medicines (sedatives, opioids) or withdrawal, dehydration and electrolyte imbalance, alcohol intoxication or withdrawal, organ failure, severe pain, sleep deprivation, surgery and anaesthesia, and hospital or intensive care stays. Risk is higher with older age, dementia and serious illness. It can be hypoactive, hyperactive or mixed.

Lists causes such as infections (UTI, pneumonia), medicines, dehydration, surgery
Mentions risk factors such as older age, dementia, hospitalisation
Mentions types (hypoactive, hyperactive, mixed) or fluctuating symptoms
Penalize: assuming it is always permanent dementia
