units.question: I'm pregnant and planning a holiday somewhere with a Zika outbreak. What's the risk and what does the CDC advise?
units.gold: Zika is spread mostly by mosquitoes, but also from mother to baby, sexually and possibly via transfusions. Most infected people never feel ill; about one in five get mild fever, rash, joint pain or pink eye. The danger in pregnancy is that Zika can cause microcephaly and other birth defects. The CDC recommends that pregnant women do not travel to outbreak areas; if you go anyway, talk to your doctor first and prevent bites with repellent, covering clothing and air-conditioned or screened rooms.
rubric: States the CDC advises pregnant women not to travel to Zika outbreak areas
Mentions microcephaly or birth defects
Mentions transmission mainly by mosquitoes (and sexual/maternal)
Lists bite prevention: repellent, covering clothes, screens or air conditioning
Penalize: saying there is a vaccine or cure for Zika
units.answer: The CDC advises pregnant women to avoid traveling to areas with active Zika virus outbreaks [1]. The risk includes potential transmission to the fetus, leading to birth defects such as microcephaly. Pregnant women should consult their healthcare provider for personalized advice.
units.sources:
[1] Zika virus (cited)
2016 outbreak: In January 2016, the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) published advice for how to avoid getting Zika fever. They suggested that when traveling to places where Zika virus lives: - Pregnant women should think about not traveling to these areas Colombia, the Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, and Jamaica advised women not to get pregnant until scientists know more about the risks of Zika virus to pregnant women.

[2] Zika fever
Efforts to prevent bites include the use of insect repellent, covering much of the body with clothing, mosquito nets, and getting rid of standing water where mosquitoes reproduce. Health officials recommended that women in areas affected by the 2015–16 Zika outbreak consider putting off pregnancy and that pregnant women not travel to these areas.

[3] Thailand Zika Travel and Pregnant?
Tags: health, thailand, pregnancy, zika I'm having a hard time understanding what the advice is surrounding current Zika outbreaks in Thailand. The cost of the holiday is obviously quite expensive (about 5k GBP) and if the advice is just advisory because there IS a risk, well that is something to factor. I just can't find any stats about how many outbreaks per week~, is the risk high, meaning, 2% chance?..

[4] Zika virus (cited)
Background: Zika virus is related to West Nile virus and the viruses that cause dengue fever, yellow fever, and Japanese encephalitis. Zika virus causes an illness that is like a mild form of dengue fever. It is treated by rest. As of 2016, there is no medication or vaccine that can prevent the Zika virus.

Pregnant women who get the Zika virus can spread the virus to their fetuses. When they are born, these newborns may be more likely to have microcephaly. In places where the Zika virus lives, people are more likely to have birth defects, neurological problems like Guillain-Barré syndrome, and autoimmune diseases.

[5] How to decide on travel to possible Zika zone while pregnant
Answers > Answer (score 6): The CDC and WHO are always (understandably) over-cautious, they don't want to risk an outbreak or be accused of not warning people.

Indeed, as recently as last year there was a Zika case in Buenos Aires. While previously it was contained to the Tucumán province, it doesn't mean it couldn't spread or be transmitted in an airport, for example.

While any first hand info is going to be merely anecdotal, if you're pregnant, you should speak to your clinician/doctor about preventative methods, as they'll have the latest information, or access to it at least, as this is a reasonably quickly changing situation. They may advise against it, or provide you with some preventative measures.

Remember, not getting medical advice, or going against government/medical advice can cause some insurance policies to decline any claims, so best to check with your travel insurance as well as to what they recommend, as opposed to a random first hand knowledge on the internet.

Hope that helps a little.

units.question: What are the warning signs of high blood sugar, and why does it happen in people with diabetes?
units.gold: Hyperglycemia means high blood glucose. In diabetes the body makes too little insulin or cannot use it well, so glucose stays in the blood. It happens when food, physical activity and medicines are out of balance, for example eating too much, missing medicines or skipping exercise, and also with stress or illness. Symptoms are thirst, tiredness or weakness, headaches, frequent urination and blurred vision. Untreated it causes long-term complications, and very high levels can lead to diabetic ketoacidosis.
rubric: Lists symptoms: thirst, fatigue, headache, frequent urination, blurred vision
Explains insufficient or ineffective insulin keeps glucose in the blood
Mentions triggers: diet, missed medicines, inactivity, stress or illness
Mentions complications such as diabetic ketoacidosis
Penalize: confusing it with low blood sugar symptoms such as needing sugar
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
High blood sugar can cause thirst, frequent urination, fatigue, and blurry vision. It happens in people with diabetes due to insulin resistance or insufficient insulin production, leading to the body's inability to use sugar effectively.
units.sources:
[1] Type 2 diabetes
Type 2 diabetes (T2D), formerly known as adult-onset diabetes, is a form of diabetes mellitus that is characterized by high blood sugar, insulin resistance, and relative lack of insulin. Common symptoms include increased thirst, frequent urination, fatigue and unexplained weight loss. Other symptoms include increased hunger, having a sensation of pins and needles, and sores (wounds) that heal slowly.

[2] Diabetes
Diabetes mellitus, commonly known as diabetes, is a group of common endocrine diseases characterized by sustained high blood sugar levels. Diabetes tends to progress in severity, and is due to either a reduced production of the hormone insulin by the pancreas or unresponsiveness of bodily cells to insulin's effects. Classic symptoms include the three Ps: polydipsia (excessive thirst), polyuria (excessive urination), and polyphagia (excessive hunger), together with weight loss and blurred vision.

[3] Type 2 diabetes
Long-term complications from high blood sugar include heart disease; stroke; diabetic retinopathy, which can result in blindness; kidney failure; and poor blood flow in the lower limbs, which may lead to amputations. Type 2 diabetes primarily occurs as a result of obesity and lack of exercise. Some people are genetically more at risk than others. Type 2 diabetes makes up about 90% of cases of diabetes, with the other 10% due primarily to type 1 diabetes and gestational diabetes.

[4] Type 1 diabetes
Type 1 diabetes (T1D), or type 1 diabetes mellitus, is an autoimmune disease that occurs when the body's immune system destroys beta cells in the pancreas that produce the hormone insulin. Insulin is used by the body to store and convert blood sugar into energy. T1D results in high blood sugar levels in the body prior to treatment due to the lack of insulin.

[5] Blood sugar
Hyperglycemia: Hyperglycemia is high blood sugar. Some of the signs of high blood sugar are:

- Thirstiness
- Being extra hungry
- Peeing more often
- Headache
- Blurry eyesight

Some signs of long time high blood sugar can be:

- Being very tired
- Losing weight
- Infections of the skin
- Cuts and sores heal slowly
Another sickness that is caused by high blood sugar is ketoacidosis. This sickness is because of a lack of insulin and a high amount of chemicals called ketones in the blood.

[6] Insulin resistance
Signs and symptoms: - High blood sugar levels (hyperglycemia)
- Fatigue, and sleepiness, especially after meals.
- Brain fogginess and inability to focus (can't think clearly).
- Weight gain, fat storage, difficulty losing weight.
- High blood pressure (hypertension)
- Increased thirst (called polydipsia) and hunger (called polyphagia)

units.question: Tell me why radon in a house matters and when I should test for it.
units.gold: Radon is an invisible, odourless radioactive gas from uranium and thorium in soil and rock. It enters through cracks in foundations, some building materials and well water, and is highest in basements and ground floors and in tightly sealed homes. Breathing its decay products damages lung cells and it is the second leading cause of lung cancer deaths after smoking, especially in smokers. Testing is the only way to know: test if never tested, when buying or selling, around renovations, or before using a basement more. Short-term kits run 2-90 days, long-term over 90.
rubric: States radon is the second leading cause of lung cancer after smoking
Explains it is an invisible, odourless gas entering from the ground
Says testing is the only way to know and lists when to test
Mentions short-term (2-90 days) vs long-term (over 90 days) kits
Penalize: claiming you can smell radon or that it only matters outdoors
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
Radon is a radioactive gas that can seep into homes and pose a health risk, particularly for those with respiratory conditions. You should test for radon if you're buying a house, especially in areas where radon levels are known to be high.
units.sources:
[1] What will my typical radiation exposure be for one week in Bad Gastein?
Answers > Answer (score 4): While most radon-related deaths are due to radon gas accumulated in houses from seepage through cracks in the foundation, 30 to 1,800 deaths per year in the United States are attributed to radon from household water. So drinking water contamination is a potential issue. I live in an area where radon is an issue and that doing a radon test is part of the inspection when buying a house. I know it can be mitigated with various pumping and sealing techniques, but as I said at the top, I know nothing about what you will encounter in Bad Gastein

[2] How do Inspection Contingencies work if the seller offers to fix the problem?
Answers > Answer (score 1): First, radon is common in some areas of New Jersey. Before you back out of this house, you should consider if you can find a different place to live that does not have a radon issue. You should be able to find someone who does radon testing specifically. Such a company should be able to check that neither the gas nor the particulates (on walls, etc.) are present in the house after the mitigation.

[3] What will my typical radiation exposure be for one week in Bad Gastein?
Answers > Answer (score 15): Are you aware that people actually live and work there 24/7/365 and apparently don't keel over from radiation poisoning ?

From: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/248212139_Investigation_of_cancer_mortality_in_the_Gastein_Valley_an_area_of_high-level_natural_radiation

Furthermore, the number of all cancer cases, especially lung cancer, in Badgastein is lower than the expected value for the province of Salzburg, despite the annual doses being four times higher.

It seems to be fine for the locals, so I highly doubt that a stay of one week will have any meaningful impact at all.

units.question: I've been on antibiotics for two weeks and now have watery diarrhea and a fever. Could it be C. diff?
units.gold: Possibly. C. diff infections usually happen while taking antibiotics, which kill the protective gut bacteria; the effect can last months, and risk rises with courses longer than a week, age 65 or more, recent hospital or nursing-home stays and weak immunity. Symptoms are several days of watery diarrhea, fever, belly pain, poor appetite and nausea. See your provider, who will test a stool sample. Treatment uses specific antibiotics; about 1 in 6 people get it again within 2 to 8 weeks.
rubric: Links C. diff to recent antibiotic use killing protective bacteria
Lists symptoms: watery diarrhea, fever, abdominal pain, nausea
Advises seeing a provider for a stool test
Mentions recurrence in about 1 in 6 within 2-8 weeks or other risk factors
Penalize: advising to treat it at home with anti-diarrhea medicine only

units.question: What are the common types and causes of a shaking hand tremor?
units.gold: A tremor is involuntary rhythmic shaking from muscle contractions, usually in the hands. The most common type is essential tremor, affecting both hands and arms during movement. Parkinsonian tremor typically affects the hands at rest, and dystonic tremor occurs with dystonia. It stems from problems in deep brain areas controlling movement, often of unknown cause and sometimes inherited. Other causes: MS, stroke or brain injury, some medicines (asthma drugs, steroids, chemotherapy), alcohol use or withdrawal, heavy metal poisoning, overactive thyroid, anxiety and too much caffeine.

Mentions Parkinsonian tremor at rest
Lists causes such as medicines, alcohol withdrawal, hyperthyroidism, caffeine or neurologic disease
Notes cause is often unknown and some types run in families
Penalize: stating every tremor means Parkinson's disease

units.question: My lab report lists a VLDL value but I never had a direct VLDL test. How was it calculated and what level is healthy?
units.gold: VLDL cannot be measured directly. Labs estimate it from your triglyceride level: VLDL is roughly one-fifth of triglycerides, although this estimate fails when triglycerides are very high. A healthy VLDL is below 30 mg/dL; higher levels raise your risk of heart disease and stroke because VLDL, like LDL, contributes to artery plaque. Since VLDL mainly carries triglycerides, lowering triglycerides through weight loss, diet, exercise, healthier fats and less sugar and alcohol lowers it.
rubric: States VLDL is estimated from triglycerides rather than measured directly

States a healthy level is below 30 mg/dL

[1] Can a lab collection requisition be used in two different labs and still be covered by the health insurance?
Tags: united-states, health-insurance For example, let's assume that a lab collection requisition lists two tests: test A and test B (e.g., test A and test B can be some blood tests). Can the patient do test A in one lab and test B in another lab, and still be covered by the health insurance? Or does the patient need to have two distinct lab collection requisition?

[2] Can a lab collection requisition be used in two different labs and still be covered by the health insurance?
Answers > Answer (score 3): In the united states the insurance company decides which lab testing company will be used to perform the test.

My spouse works in a doctors office, in the lab. Some small quick tests can be done in the office, others have to be sent out. Each insurance company decides how test A and test B are done, in the office or out of the office. Some companies even dictate that the sample be collected at a specific drawing center which means the patient has to go someplace else to get the blood collected.

If they have to send it out-of-the-office the insurance company dictates which external lab company will perform the test. The patient doesn't pick, and the doctor doesn't know. The lab staff collect the ample, check the insurance records, package the sample, generate the order, and put it in the pickup box. The transport company picks up samples at the end of the day. The lab staff then checks periodically for updated results on the website.

[3] Can a lab collection requisition be used in two different labs and still be covered by the health insurance?
Answers > Answer (score 3): Exceptions to this are if the sample is collected in an emergency at an ER or hospital. More tests will be done in the on site hospital lab.

So If doctor X says get test A and test B done. Where the blood goes is out of the patients control. If the office messed up and Test B was done by an out-of-network lab, then complain. Of course if Doctor X is out of network, it is possible that your tests are also done by an out-of-network lab, and that can be very expensive.

Why is out-of-network always way more expensive? I had recent lab work done:

- $305 the Rate they would charge without insurance
- $15 the negotiated rate between the lab company and the insurance company
- $0 what I was charged in-network, because I had met my in-network deductible.

If I had gone out-of-network, I would have had to pay the lab company $305, and only $15 would have counted towards my higher out-of-network deductible.

units.question: Which irregular heart rhythm do doctors see most often, and what test usually picks it up?
units.gold: An arrhythmia is a problem with the rate or rhythm of the heartbeat: too fast (tachycardia), too slow (bradycardia) or with early extra beats. The most common type is atrial fibrillation, causing a fast irregular heartbeat. Many people have no symptoms; others feel fluttering, pounding or skipped beats, dizziness, fainting, chest discomfort or breathlessness. The usual test is an electrocardiogram (EKG), which records the heart's electrical activity. Chest pain or breathlessness warrant emergency care.
rubric: Names atrial fibrillation as the most common arrhythmia
Defines tachycardia and bradycardia
States an electrocardiogram (EKG) is the most common diagnostic test
Lists symptoms or notes it may be symptomless
Penalize: claiming all arrhythmias are harmless
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
The most common irregular heart rhythm is atrial fibrillation, and an electrocardiogram (EKG) is usually used to detect it.
units.sources:
[1] Arrhythmia
Some arrhythmias are harmless, such as when your heart rate speeds up during exercise and slows down when you sleep. But if you have a frequent irregular rhythm, it may mean your heart isn't pumping enough blood into your body. Getting treatment and following a heart-healthy lifestyle can help control arrhythmias. It may also help prevent heart damage that can trigger some heart arrhythmias.

What causes an arrhythmia?

Many factors can affect your heart's rhythm, such as having had a heart attack, smoking, congenital heart defects, and stress. Other factors that could increase your risk for some types of arrhythmias could include if you:

- Have a family history of arrhythmias
- Have certain health conditions, which can include heart and blood vessel diseases, lung diseases, kidney diseases, obesity, and sleep apnea
- Are an older adult
- Have had recent surgery for your heart, lungs, or throat
- Take certain medicines for other health conditions
- Use illegal drugs

[2] Arrhythmia
If you have risk factors, some situations that make your heart work harder, raise your blood pressure, or cause strong emotional stress may trigger an arrhythmia.

What are the symptoms of an arrhythmia?

You may not have any noticeable symptoms of an arrhythmia. Your provider may find an arrhythmia during your routine checkup. Symptoms of an arrhythmia can include:

- Fast or slow heartbeat
- Skipping, fluttering, or pounding heartbeats
- Chest pain or discomfort
- Dizziness or fainting
- Shortness of breath
- Sweating
- Tiredness or weakness

Seek emergency medical care if you have chest pain, shortness of breath, or think you are having a heart attack.

How is an arrhythmia diagnosed?

To find out if you have an arrhythmia, your health care provider may order an electrocardiogram (EKG). This test records your heart's electrical activity and is the most common for finding an arrhythmia. Your provider may also:

units.question: List the risk factors and typical symptoms of cataracts.
units.gold: Cataracts are very common with age: by 80, more than half of Americans have one or have had surgery. Risk also rises with diabetes, family history, eye injury or surgery, steroid medicines, smoking, heavy drinking and lots of sun exposure. Symptoms develop slowly: blurry or cloudy vision, faded colours, glare and halos around lights, poor night vision, double vision and frequent prescription changes. A dilated eye exam diagnoses them, and surgery is needed once daily life is affected.
rubric: Mentions ageing, with more than half of Americans affected by 80
Lists risk factors such as diabetes, smoking, steroids, sun exposure, eye injury
Lists symptoms: cloudy vision, faded colours, glare/halos, poor night vision
Mentions diagnosis by dilated eye exam or treatment by surgery
Penalize: claiming cataracts spread from one eye to the other
units.answer: Risk factors include aging, diabetes, corticosteroid use, and smoking [1]. Typical symptoms include cloudy vision, sensitivity to light, and faded colors [4].
units.sources:
[1] Cataract (cited)
Cataracts are most commonly due to aging but may also be caused by trauma to the eye, radiation exposure, conditions present from birth or complications from other conditions. Risk factors include diabetes, longstanding use of corticosteroid medication, obesity, other eye conditions, dietary deficiencies, smoking tobacco, prolonged exposure to sunlight and alcohol use. Cataract formation is primarily driven by oxidative stress and aging. Over time, the systems within the eye that keep the lens clear don't work as well, leading to the lens clouding.

[2] Cataract (cited)
Causes of Cataract: Some people may inherit a predisposition to cataracts or have genetic conditions that increase their risk. - Eye Trauma or Injury: Trauma to the eye, such as blunt force trauma or penetrating injuries, can damage the lens and increase the risk of developing cataracts. - Certain Medications: Long-term use of certain medications, such as corticosteroids or medications used to treat conditions like psoriasis or rheumatoid arthritis, may increase the risk of cataracts. - Congenital Factors: Some infants are born with cataracts or develop them in childhood due to genetic factors, infections during pregnancy, or other congenital conditions.

[3] Cataract (cited)
Signs and symptoms: Cataracts develop gradually over time, so symptoms may not be immediately noticeable. However, as the condition progresses, the following signs and symptoms may become apparent:

[4] Cataract (cited)
Signs and symptoms: - Cloudy or Blurry Vision: This is one of the most common symptoms of cataracts. Vision may become increasingly cloudy, hazy, or blurry, making it difficult to see clearly.
- Sensitivity to Light: Individuals with cataracts may experience increased sensitivity to bright lights, glare from headlights, lamps, or sunlight.
- Fading or Yellowing of Colors: Colors may appear faded or less vibrant than usual. Some people with cataracts also experience a yellowing or browning of colors.
- Poor Night Vision: Cataracts can cause difficulty seeing in dim or low-light conditions, which may result in problems with night driving or navigating in darkened rooms.
- Frequent Changes in Eyeglass Prescription: As cataracts progress, changes in vision may necessitate frequent changes in prescription eyeglasses or contact lenses.
- Double Vision: Cataracts can cause double vision in one eye, which may disappear when the affected eye is closed.
- Halos Around Lights: Some individuals with cataracts may see halos or circles around lights, particularly at night.
- Difficulty with Reading and/or Watching Television: Cataracts can make it challenging to focus on close-up tasks like reading or watching television.
- Increased Near-Sightedness (Myopia) or Far-Sightedness (Hyperopia): As the lens becomes increasingly clouded, it may cause changes in refractive error, leading to near-sightedness or far-sightedness.

units.question: My son bumped his head at football practice. Which signs after a concussion mean we should get help urgently?
units.gold: Concussion symptoms can appear days or weeks after the injury, typically headache, neck pain, nausea, ringing ears, dizziness or tiredness. Get medical help if symptoms worsen or serious ones appear: seizures, drowsiness or not waking up, a worsening persistent headache, weakness or numbness, repeated vomiting, confusion, slurred speech or loss of consciousness. Most people recover fully; rest is key, with limited physical and concentration-heavy activities (studying, screens) at first, then a gradual return when the provider agrees.
rubric: Lists red-flag signs: seizures, cannot wake, worsening headache, repeated vomiting, slurred speech, weakness
Notes symptoms may start days or weeks later
Advises rest and limiting physical and mental exertion
Mentions gradual return to activities with provider approval
Penalize: saying a concussion is always trivial if there was no loss of consciousness
units.answer:
From the offline source:
It happens when a hit to the head or body causes your head and brain to move rapidly back and forth. This sudden movement can cause the brain to bounce around or twist in the skull, creating chemical changes in your brain. Sometimes it can also stretch and damage your brain cells. Sometimes people call a concussion a "mild" brain injury. It is important to understand that while concussions may not be life-threatening, they can still be serious. Concussions are a common type of sports injury. Other causes of concussions include blows to the head, bumping your head when you fall, being violently shaken, and car accidents. [1]

In an emergency, call your local emergency number (911 in the US, 112 in Europe).

units.question: Which sudden eye symptoms point to an emergency type of glaucoma?
units.gold: Sudden intense eye pain, blurred vision, red eyes or nausea may signal angle-closure glaucoma, a less common type where fluid builds up quickly in the eye; go to an eye care provider or emergency room at once. The common open-angle type usually has no early symptoms and slowly erodes side vision, like looking through a tunnel, which is why regular dilated eye exams matter. Pressure tolerance varies: some people with high pressure never get glaucoma, others get it at normal pressure.
rubric: Lists acute symptoms: intense eye pain, blurred vision, red eye, nausea
Identifies angle-closure glaucoma and urgent care
Contrasts with symptomless open-angle glaucoma and peripheral vision loss
Mentions regular dilated eye exams
Penalize: telling the user to wait and see with sudden severe eye pain
units.answer: Sudden eye pain, blurry vision, red eyes, or an upset stomach (nausea) point to an emergency type of glaucoma [1]. These symptoms require immediate attention to prevent vision loss.
units.sources:
[1] Glaucoma (cited)
Not everyone with high eye pressure develops glaucoma. What are the symptoms of glaucoma? If you have sudden symptoms of intense eye pain, blurry vision, red eyes, or an upset stomach (nausea), you need to go to your eye care provider or an emergency room right away. This less common type of glaucoma causes fluid to build up quickly in your eye.

[2] Glaucoma (cited)
A comprehensive eye exam can tell if you have glaucoma. This would include:

- A dilated eye exam. This involves getting eye drops that dilate (widen) your pupils. This allows more light to enter your eye. Your eye care provider examines your eyes using a special magnifying lens. This provides a clear view of important tissues at the back of your eye to check for glaucoma or other eye problems. For a few hours after the exam your vision may be blurry and sensitive to light, so you will need someone to take you home.
- Visual field testing. This check of your peripheral (side) vision allows your eye care provider to find out how well you can see objects off to the side of your vision without moving your eyes.
- Tonometry. This measures the pressure inside your eye.

If you're at higher risk for glaucoma, you should get comprehensive eye exams every one to two years. You're at higher risk if you:

[3] Glaucoma (cited)
What is glaucoma?

Glaucoma is a group of diseases that can damage the optic nerve of one, or both, of your eyes. This can result in vision loss. There are different types of glaucoma, but the most common type is open-angle glaucoma. Other less common types include angle-closure glaucoma, and congenital glaucoma.

You may not have any symptoms of glaucoma. Regular eye exams by an eye care provider can check for glaucoma and other eye problems to help protect your vision. Treatments that lower eye pressure help slow the disease. Without treatment, glaucoma can eventually lead to blindness.

What causes glaucoma?

Medical experts aren't sure what causes glaucoma, but the most common types usually happen when the fluid pressure inside your eye slowly rises, damaging the optic nerve. Other types of glaucoma may be caused by medical conditions, or a baby may be born with it.

units.question: With a stomach bug, when should an adult stop waiting it out and contact a provider?
units.gold: Gastroenteritis is usually mild, but call a provider right away for: a change in mental state such as irritability or lack of energy, diarrhea lasting more than 2 days, high fever, frequent vomiting, six or more loose stools a day, severe abdominal or rectal pain, black tarry or bloody stools, or dehydration signs (thirst, dry mouth, headache, dark urine, urinating less). Pregnant women, older adults, infants and people with weak immunity should seek care early. Note 'stomach flu' is not caused by influenza.

units.question: Explain what a PSA blood test can and cannot tell a man about prostate cancer.
units.gold: PSA is a protein made by the prostate. A high blood level may indicate prostate cancer but does not prove it, because an enlarged prostate (BPH), other prostate problems and certain medicines also raise PSA. Generally the higher the PSA, the likelier cancer is, yet a low PSA does not guarantee you are cancer-free. Screening only flags possible cancer; further tests diagnose it. It is unclear whether early detection lowers the risk of dying, so discuss benefits and harms with your provider.
rubric: States a high PSA is not proof of cancer
Lists other causes: enlarged prostate (BPH), other prostate problems, medicines
States a low PSA does not rule out cancer
Mentions uncertainty whether screening reduces deaths and the need to discuss with a provider
Penalize: claiming a PSA test alone diagnoses prostate cancer
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
A PSA blood test can indicate high levels of prostate-specific antigen, which may suggest prostate cancer, but it cannot definitively diagnose it. It also cannot confirm the presence of cancer alone; further tests like a biopsy are needed.
units.sources:
[1] Prostate cancer
Prostate cancer is the uncontrolled growth of cells in the prostate, a gland in the male reproductive system below the bladder. Abnormal growth of prostate tissue is usually detected through screening tests, typically blood tests that check for prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels. Those with high levels of PSA in their blood are at increased risk for developing prostate cancer. Diagnosis requires a biopsy of the prostate.

[2] Prostate Cancer Screening
Prostate cancer is most common in people over age 50. What tests screen for prostate cancer? - A prostate-specific antigen test, also called a PSA blood test. A high level of PSA in your blood may mean you have prostate cancer, but it's not proof of cancer.

[3] Prostate cancer
Medical imaging is performed to look for cancer that has spread outside the prostate. Based on the Gleason score, PSA levels, and imaging results, a cancer case is assigned a stage 1 to 4. A higher stage signifies a more advanced, more dangerous disease. These are managed with active surveillance, monitoring the tumor with regular tests to ensure it has not grown.

[4] Prostatitis
Nomenclature: The term prostatitis refers in its strictest sense to histological (microscopic) inflammation of the tissue of the prostate gland, although historically the term has loosely been used as a rubric to describe a set of quite different conditions. To try to remedy this, the National Institutes of Health (NIH) devised a new classification system in 1999.

[5] Prostatitis
Classification: According to the 1999 National Institute of Health (NIH) Classification, there are four categories of prostatitis:

- Category I: Acute prostatitis (bacterial)
- Category II: Chronic bacterial prostatitis
- Category III: Chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome (CP/CPPS), Pelvic Myoneuropathy
Subdivisions of IIIa (inflammatory) and IIIb (non-inflammatory) exist based on levels of pus cells in expressed prostatic secretions, but these subcategories are of limited use clinically
- Category IV: Asymptomatic inflammatory prostatitis

[6] Prostate Cancer
- A digital rectal exam (DRE). In this exam, your provider feels your prostate for lumps or anything unusual by inserting a lubricated, gloved finger into your rectum.
- A prostate-specific antigen (PSA) blood test. A high PSA blood level may be a sign of prostate cancer. But many other things can cause high PSA levels, too.
- Imaging tests. These tests may use ultrasound or MRI to make pictures of your prostate.

If these tests show that you might have prostate cancer, the next step is usually a prostate biopsy. A biopsy is the only way to diagnose prostate cancer.

During a biopsy, a doctor uses a hollow needle to remove some prostate tissue. The tissue is studied under a microscope to look for cancer cells.

What are the treatments for prostate cancer?

Your treatment options usually depend on your age, your general health, and how serious the cancer is. Your treatment may include one or more options:

units.question: Tell me what to keep in the car before driving during a winter storm.
units.gold: Carry an emergency car kit: an ice scraper and shovel, cat litter or sand for traction, water and snacks, extra warm clothing, jumper cables, a first aid kit with any needed medicines and a pocketknife, a battery radio with flashlight and spare batteries, emergency flares or distress flags, and waterproof matches with a can to melt snow for water. Winter storms also bring frostbite, hypothermia, icy roads, power failures and carbon monoxide risks from heaters, so have a family plan and CO detector at home.

Lists survival basics: water, snacks, warm clothes, first aid kit

units.question: I'm nervous about vaccinating my kids. How common are serious side effects, and is there a link to autism?
units.gold: Most vaccine side effects are minor, such as a sore arm, tiredness or mild fever, and go away within a few days; they often show the body is building immunity. Serious side effects such as severe allergic reactions can happen but are very rare. Many scientific studies have found no link between vaccines and autism spectrum disorder. US vaccines undergo years of testing: lab work, then clinical trials that grow from 20-100 volunteers to thousands, before FDA approval and continued monitoring.
rubric: States common side effects are minor and short-lived
States serious side effects (e.g. severe allergic reactions) are very rare
States studies found no link between vaccines and autism
Mentions extensive testing via lab work and clinical trials before FDA approval
Penalize: suggesting vaccines cause autism
units.answer: Vaccines have serious side effects, but they are generally rare and mild [1]. There is no credible scientific evidence linking vaccines to autism. The benefits of vaccination far outweigh the risks.
units.sources:
[1] Vaccination (cited)
Safety of vaccination: Today in modern countries almost all people are vaccinated, which has caused many serious diseases to become rare. However, some people argue against vaccination, as they are worried about possible side effects from the vaccination. Vaccinations do have some side effects. As well as these real side effects of vaccinations, some people believe that vaccines cause other serious problems like autism, brain damage, or diabetes.

[2] Do vaccines cause autism?
Answers > Answer (score 61, accepted): [15] WebMD - Autism-Vaccine Link: Evidence Doesn't Dispel Doubts [16] When do children usually show symptoms of autism spectrum disorder (ASD)?

[3] Vaccination (cited)
Vaccination versus immunization: Another word used for vaccines is immunization. These words mean things that are a little different. Vaccination is when a person is given something to make the immune system learn to fight an infectious disease.

Immunization is when a person's immune system learns to fight an infection. Immunization can happen from vaccination. But immunization can also happen from getting the infection. For example, a person can be immune to hepatitis B if he gets sick with hepatitis B. After a person gets hepatitis B and then gets well, he is immunized from getting it again. A person can also be immunized from hepatitis B by taking the hepatitis B vaccination.

So vaccination and immunization have meanings that are a little different. But when people say these words, they usually mean the same thing.

[4] Vaccination (cited)
Herd immunity: Herd immunity is an important part of how vaccines work. A herd is a group of animals. Herd immunity happens when most of the animals in a group are immune to an infection. If most animals are immune they cannot get the disease. If they do not get the disease, they cannot give it to other animals. So even one animal who is not immune is safer. If none of the other animals in a herd get the infection, they cannot give the infection to the one who is non immune.

This is important in people too. If 95% of people in a place are immune to a disease, the other 5% are safer. They are not near infected people, so they won't get infected.

units.question: I'm reading up on Kyrgyzstan before a trip. What is its capital, roughly how many people live there, and just how mountainous is the land?
units.gold: Kyrgyzstan's capital is Bishkek. The population is about 6.2 million (6,219,751, 2025 estimate), spread over roughly 200,000 sq km (199,951 sq km). The country is landlocked and almost entirely mountainous, dominated by the Tien Shan range: 94% of its territory lies above 1,000 m and the average elevation is about 2,750 m, with many high peaks, glaciers and alpine lakes. Most people live in rural areas, with the densest settlement in the north around Bishkek and around Osh in the west.

units.question: How big is Malta, what is its capital, and how many of its islands have permanent residents?
units.gold: Malta is a small archipelago of 316 sq km, a little less than twice the size of Washington, D.C. Its capital is Valletta. Only the three largest islands are inhabited: Malta itself, Gozo (Ghawdex) and Comino (Kemmuna); the rest are uninhabited. About 522,000 people live in the country (2025 estimate), most of them on the eastern half of the main island of Malta.

units.answer: Malta is an island in Southern Europe, with a total area of 316 sq km [8]. Its capital is Valletta, and it has only one island, Gozo, that has permanent residents.

units.question: Give me the head count and the capital of the Cocos (Keeling) Islands, and tell me which of the islands people actually live on.
units.gold: The Cocos (Keeling) Islands, an Australian territory in the Indian Ocean, are tiny: about 14 sq km of land and only 593 residents (2021 estimate). The capital is West Island. The group has 27 coral islands, mostly arranged as a horseshoe-shaped atoll around a lagoon, with North Keeling lying about 30 km away, but only two islands are populated: Home Island and West Island.
rubric: Population about 593 (2021 est.)
Capital is West Island
Only Home Island and West Island are populated
27 coral islands forming an atoll
Penalize: a population in the thousands or naming Home Island as the capital
units.answer: The Cocos (Keeling) Islands have a population of approximately 593 people, with West Island as the capital [5]. Only two of the 27 islands are inhabited: West Island and Home Island [1].
units.sources:
[1] Cocos (Keeling) Islands (cited)
The territory's dual name (official since the islands' incorporation into Australia in 1955) reflects that the islands have historically been known as either the Cocos Islands or the Keeling Islands, the latter of which is still a common short name. The territory consists of two atolls made up of 27 coral islands, of which only two – West Island and Home Island – are inhabited. The population of around 600 people consists mainly of Cocos Malays, who mostly practise Sunni Islam and speak a dialect of Malay as their first language.

[2] Cocos (Keeling) Islands (cited)
Cocos (Keeling) Islands: Nationality: Cocos (Keeling) Islands' nationality (noun) is Cocos Islander(s). Cocos (Keeling) Islands' nationality (adjective) is Cocos Islander.

[3] Wikivoyage: Cocos (Keeling) Islands
For the island in Costa Rica, see Cocos Island National Park. units.question: A friend told me Bhutan's capital got its name from a legend. Which city is it, how many people live in Bhutan, and what's the story?
units.gold: Bhutan's capital is Thimphu. The country has about 893,000 people (892,877, 2025 estimate) on 38,394 sq km. The origin of the name is not certain, but the traditional explanation, going back to the 14th century, says 'thim' means dissolve and 'phu' means rock: a local deity is said to have dissolved before a traveller's eyes and become part of the rock on which the city now stands.

units.question: Who is Curacao's capital city named after, and roughly how large is the island in land and people?
units.gold: Curacao's capital, Willemstad, means 'William's Town' in Dutch; it was named after Prince Willem of Orange (1533-84), the first stadtholder of the United Provinces of the Netherlands. The island covers 444 sq km, a bit more than twice the size of Washington, D.C., and has about 153,000 inhabitants (2024 estimate). Most people live in and around Willemstad, which has about 144,000 people.

units.question: I heard Paraguay gets nearly all its power from dams. Is that right, what money do they use, and what are its main exports?
units.gold: Yes. Hydroelectricity accounts for about 99.4% of Paraguay's installed generating capacity (2023), with biomass making up almost all the rest, and electricity is itself one of its top exports. The currency is the guarani (PYG), at roughly 7,560 per US dollar in 2024. The leading exports are soybeans, beef, electricity, corn and soybean meal. Real GDP per capita was about $16,300 in 2024.

units.answer: Paraguay gets nearly all its power from dams, and it uses the Paraguayan currency, the "Paraguay Peso" (PYP). Its main exports are soybeans and beef [1].

units.question: How did the Mauritian economy grow out of its plantation past, and what currency and income level does the island have now?
units.gold: Mauritius was built as a sugar economy: from 1722 the French ran profitable sugar-cane plantations worked by enslaved Africans, and after abolition in 1835 the British brought contract labourers from the Indian subcontinent. Since independence in 1968 it has stayed a stable democracy, attracted heavy foreign investment and now has one of Africa's highest per capita incomes, about $27,300 real GDP per head (2024). Sugar milling, textiles and tourism remain key industries. The currency is the Mauritian rupee (MUR).

Currency: Mauritian rupee (MUR)

units.answer: The Mauritian economy transitioned from plantation-based agriculture to a diversified economy with focus on tourism, finance, and information services [4]. The island's currency is the Mauritian rupee (MUR), and its income level is upper middle-income.

units.question: Describe how Bahrain has worked to rely less on oil, and tell me its currency and output per person.
units.gold: Falling oil output and reserves since 1970 pushed Bahrain to diversify. It built up petroleum processing and refining, aluminium production, hospitality and retail, and has tried to become a leading regional banking centre, especially for Islamic finance. The currency is the Bahraini dinar (BHD), held at about 0.376 per US dollar. Real GDP per capita was about $59,100 in 2024.

units.answer: Bahrain has diversified its economy by investing in sectors like tourism, finance, and renewable energy to reduce reliance on oil. The Bahraini dinar (BHD) is the official currency, and its output per person is approximately $59,100 (2024 est [2].).

units.question: What sectors drive Hong Kong's economy, and what has the Hong Kong dollar been worth against the US dollar lately?
units.gold: Hong Kong is an international financial and trading centre. Its main industries are trading and logistics, financial services, professional services and tourism, plus cultural and creative industries, shipping and electronics. The Hong Kong dollar (HKD) has stayed very stable, around 7.76-7.83 per US dollar from 2020 to 2024 (7.804 in 2024). Real GDP per capita was about $66,200 in 2024.
rubric: Trading/logistics, finance, professional services, tourism
HKD about 7.8 per US dollar
Stable rate across 2020-2024
GDP per capita about $66,200
Penalize: saying the HKD floats widely or giving a rate far from 7.8
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
Hong Kong's economy is driven by finance, trade, and services, with the financial sector being the largest contributor. The Hong Kong dollar (HKD) has been weak against the US dollar, losing value over the past year.

units.question: I'm confused about who runs Western Sahara. Who controls it today, and why did the planned independence vote never happen?
units.gold: Western Sahara is a non-self-governing territory whose sovereignty is unresolved. After Spain left its colony in 1976, Morocco annexed the northern two-thirds and later claimed the rest when Mauritania withdrew in 1979. A guerrilla war with the Polisario Front ended in a 1991 ceasefire and a UN peacekeeping operation. The UN planned a referendum offering independence or integration with Morocco, but it never took place because the sides could not agree on who was eligible to vote. Morocco controls about three-quarters of the territory, west of a 1,600 km sand berm.
rubric: Status unresolved; contested by Morocco and Polisario Front
Morocco annexed it after Spain left in 1976
1991 ceasefire; UN referendum never held over voter eligibility
Morocco controls about three-quarters, west of the berm
Penalize: stating Western Sahara is an independent recognized state or that the referendum took place
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
Morocco controls most of Western Sahara, including major cities and natural resources, while the Polisario Front controls smaller areas in the east. The planned independence vote never occurred because the Spanish withdrawal led to the Madrid Accords, which transferred control to Morocco and Mauritania, and the Polisario Front launched a war against both countries.
units.sources:
[1] Western Sahara
Western Sahara: Demographic profile (2): Western Sahara (continued): and the construction of the defensive berm separating Moroccan- and Polisario-controlled (Sahrawi liberalization movement) areas. Morocco supported rapid urbanization to facilitate surveillance and security. ++ Today more than 80% of Western Sahara's population lives in urban areas.

[2] Western Sahara
Spain attempted to transfer its administration to Morocco and Mauritania despite an advisory opinion of the International Court of Justice that those countries had no sovereignty over Western Sahara; a war erupted and the pro-independence Polisario Front proclaimed the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic (SADR). Mauritania withdrew its claims in 1979, and Morocco secured de facto control of most of the territory, including all major cities and most natural resources. The SADR established a government-in-exile in Tindouf, Algeria.

[3] Polisario Front
History > Founding: The Polisario Front was founded on May 10 1973, by a group of Sahrawi students and activists. At the time, Western Sahara was under Spanish control. The group began in Mauritania but had supporters throughout Western Sahara. Their objective was to fight for independence and to put an end to Spanish Colonial Rule. The first military action taken by the Polisario Front took place on May 20 1973, when they attacked a Spanish military post. This date is remembered as the beginning of their armed struggle.

[4] Polisario Front
History > Founding > Spanish withdrawal and regional conflict: In 1975. after many years of pressure, the Spanish Government agreed to withdraw from Western Sahara. Instead of granting it independence, Spain signed the Madrid Accords, granting control over the territory over to Morocco and Mauritania. This decision was not accepted by the Sahrawi people or the Polisario Front. The group went on to start a war against both Morocco and Mauritania. On February 27 1976, the Polisario Front declared the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic (SADR), which is still a government in exile today. In 1979 Mauritania signed a peace treaty with the Polisario Front and surrendered its claim to the Southern part of the Western Sahara. However Morocco quickly took over that area. Since then Morocco has controlled about 80% of Western Sahara. While the Polisario Front controls much smaller parts in the East. The SADR government is located in refugee camps in Tindouf Algeria.

[5] Western Sahara
Western Sahara: Suffrage: Western Sahara's suffrage is none; (residents of Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara participate in Moroccan elections).

units.question: When and by what process did Eritrea become independent, and who has led the country since then?
units.gold: Eritrea became independent from Ethiopia on 24 May 1993. Ethiopia had annexed it as a province in 1962, starting a 30-year armed struggle that ended in 1991 when Eritrean fighters defeated government forces; Eritreans then overwhelmingly approved independence in a 1993 referendum. Isaias Afwerki has been the only president since independence, and his rule has been highly autocratic, with indefinite mandatory national service.
rubric: Independence 24 May 1993 from Ethiopia
Approved in a 1993 referendum after a 30-year war ending 1991
Isaias Afwerki only president since
Autocratic rule, indefinite conscription
Penalize: dating independence to 1991 alone or naming a different leader
units.answer: Eritrea became independent on May 24, 1993, after a popular vote [4]. ISAIAS Afwerki has been the only president since independence [3].

[1] Horn of Africa

Borders: There are four countries in the Horn of Africa. They are Eritrea, Ethiopia, Somalia and Djibouti. The northernmost areas of the Horn are Ras Kasar in the west, settled by the Rashaida tribe, and Alula in the east, settled by Dishiishe. The easternmost area is Ras Hafun, settled by Somalis, and the southernmost in Ras Kamboni, settled by Somalis.

[3] Eritrea (cited)
Eritrea: background: Eritrea won independence from Italian colonial control in 1941, but the UN only established it as an autonomous region within the Ethiopian federation in 1952, after a decade of British administrative control. Ethiopia's full annexation of Eritrea as a province 10 years later sparked a violent 30-year conflict for independence that ended in 1991 with Eritrean fighters defeating government forces. Eritreans overwhelmingly approved independence in a 1993 referendum. ISAIAS Afwerki has been Eritrea's only president since independence; his rule, particularly since 2001, has been characterized by highly autocratic and repressive actions.

[4] Eritrea (cited)
History: Eritrea became an independent country on May 24, 1993. It is one of the newest countries in the world.

Many different countries have ruled the land that is now called Eritrea. Between 1885 and 1941 it was a colony of Italy. Between 1941 and 1952, the United Nations put it under the protection of the United Kingdom. After 1952, Eritrea became a part of Ethiopia. This was the reason for a long civil war between the Eritreans and the government of Ethiopia.

Eventually, in 1993, Eritrea became an independent country after a vote by its people.

units.question: Summarize when Trinidad and Tobago became independent and from whom, and name the industry that has dominated its economy for more than a century.
units.gold: Trinidad and Tobago gained independence from the United Kingdom on 31 August 1962 and is a parliamentary republic. Oil was discovered on Trinidad in 1910 and petroleum remains the dominant industry; together with natural gas production and processing it has made the country one of the most prosperous in the Caribbean. Earlier, the economy rested on sugar and cocoa worked by enslaved people and later by contract workers from India.
rubric: Independence 31 August 1962 from the UK
Parliamentary republic
Oil discovered 1910; petroleum and gas dominate
Penalize: naming Spain as the power it became independent from or sugar as today's main industry
units.answer:

units.question: We want to hike near volcanoes in New Zealand. Which natural hazards there should we be aware of?
units.gold: New Zealand has frequent earthquakes, though they are usually not severe, and significant volcanism on the North Island. Ruapehu (2,797 m) has had large eruptions within the past century, and Taranaki could produce dangerous avalanches and lahars (volcanic mudflows). Other historically active volcanoes include Okataina, Raoul Island, Tongariro and White Island. The climate is temperate with sharp regional contrasts.
rubric: Earthquakes common but usually not severe
Significant volcanism on North Island
Ruapehu large eruptions; Taranaki avalanche/lahar risk
Other active volcanoes e.g. Tongariro, White Island
Penalize: saying New Zealand has no active volcanoes or placing the volcanism on the South Island
units.answer: New Zealand's natural hazards include earthquakes and volcanic activity, with Ruapehu and other volcanoes posing risks [1]. Stay informed about warnings and follow safety measures for hiking near active volcanoes.

New Zealand's ethnic groups are European 64.1%, Maori 16.5%, Chinese 4.9%, Indian 4.7%, Samoan 3.9%, Tongan 1.8%, Cook Islands Maori 1.7%, English 1.5%, Filipino 1.5%, New Zealander 1%,…. New Zealand's life expectancy at birth is 82.9 years (2024 est.).

[4] US government: Volcanoes (Ready.gov)
A volcanic eruption can:

- Contaminate water supplies.

- Damage machinery.

- Reduce visibility through smog and harmful gases that may threaten low-lying areas.

- Make it hard to breathe and irritate the skin, eyes, nose and throat.

IF YOU ARE UNDER A VOLCANO WARNING:

- Listen for emergency information and alerts.

- Follow evacuation or shelter orders. If advised to evacuate, do so early.

- Reduce your ash exposure by doing the following:

- Limit your time outdoors and use a dust mask or cloth mask as a last resort if you must be outside.

- Avoid areas downwind and river valleys downstream of the volcano.

- Take temporary shelter from volcanic ash in the location where you are.

- Cover ventilation openings and seal doors and windows.

- Avoid driving in heavy ash. If you must drive, keep the windows up and do not use the air conditioning system.

- Do not get on your roof to remove ash.

- Stay indoors until authorities say it is safe to go outside.

units.question: Why does Guatemala face both volcanic and storm risks, and which of its volcanoes stand out?
units.gold: Guatemala lies on the Pacific Ring of Fire, the belt holding about 75% of the world's volcanoes and up to 90% of its earthquakes, so its mountains contain many volcanoes and it suffers occasional violent earthquakes. Notable volcanoes include Pacaya, one of the most active with frequent eruptions since 1965, Santa Maria, named a Decade Volcano for its explosive history, and Fuego; Tajumulco (4,220 m) is the highest point in Central America.

units.question: Explain what the volcano on Montserrat did to the island's capital and its people from the mid-1990s on.
units.gold: The Soufriere Hills volcano on Montserrat began erupting in 1995 and devastated much of the island; about two-thirds of the population left for abroad. A massive eruption in 1997 destroyed most of the capital, Plymouth, and left about half of the island uninhabitable. Volcanic activity continued for years, with the last eruption in 2013. The island also faces severe hurricanes from June to November.

Montserrat is a Caribbean island and a British Overseas Territory. Officially, the capital is Plymouth, but the government has moved to Brades after Chances Peak erupted, destroying Plymouth in 1995.

Montserrat was colonised mostly by Irish Catholics. They brought many black slaves to the island and forced them to work on sugar plantations. The work the slaves made many plantations grow wealthy. When slavery was made illegal in the 1830s, the British Empire paid all the slave owners.

units.question: Which mother tongues are most common in Pakistan, and what part does English play there?
units.gold: By mother tongue, Punjabi is the largest language in Pakistan at about 38.8%, followed by Pashto (18.2%), Sindhi (14.6%), Saraiki (12.2%) and Urdu (7.1%), with smaller shares of Balochi, Hindko and Brahui. English is an official language and serves as the lingua franca of the elite and of most government ministries. The population is overwhelmingly Muslim (96.4%).

[2] Mahajir (Pakistan)
Mahajirs/Mohajir/Muhajir () constitute about 8 percent of the population. They are Muslims who settled in Pakistan after the end of British India in 1947. Unlike other cultural ethnic groups of Pakistan, they do not have a tribe-based cultural identity. Urdu, the official language of Pakistan, is their native tongue, though many muhajirs speak other languages such as Gujarati, Memoni, Marwari etc as their mother tongue. Mohajirs were the vanguard of the Pakistan Movement, which advocated the partition of British India in order to create the independent nation of Pakistan for Indian Muslims. After the partition of India a large number of Muslims migrated from various urban centers of India to live in the new nation of Pakistan. These migrants later identified themselves as mohajirs.

A large number of Mohajirs settled in the cities of Sindh Province, particularly Karāchi and Hyderābād. Today they remain mostly urban.

units.question: Compare the Maldives and the Seychelles on how high their land rises and which natural hazards each one faces.
units.gold: The Maldives is extremely low-lying: its highest point is just 5 m (a golf-course tee on Villingi Island) and its mean elevation about 2 m, so it is exposed to tsunamis and very sensitive to sea level rise. The Seychelles is much higher, rising to 905 m at Morne Seychellois. It lies outside the cyclone belt, so severe storms are rare, and its main hazard is occasional short droughts.

Climate: The Maldives has a tropical monsoon climate (Am) under the Köppen climate classification, which is affected by the large landmass of South Asia to the north. Because the Maldives has the lowest elevation of any country in the world, the temperature is constantly hot and often humid. The presence of this landmass causes differential heating of land and water. These factors set off a rush of moisture-rich air from the Indian Ocean over South Asia, resulting in the southwest monsoon. Two seasons dominate Maldives' weather: the dry season associated with the winter northeastern monsoon and the rainy season which brings strong winds and storms.

units.question: I'm choosing between living in Austria or Ireland. Which one produces more per person, and how do their landscapes compare in height?

[3] As a young person in Austria, what steps should I take so that I can buy a house someday
Answers > Answer (score 2): Given your income, expenses and the provided property prices, you don't need to do much to afford a house. Just leaving the money in your bank account while you save should be enough to afford a house in your area within 5 years, even if you had no pay raise.

For the rest, ask your bank, and go to a second one to see what they suggest. I don't think any other place makes sense because they will not provide a better / cheaper offering and you need a bank for your loan anyways. A bank can show you ways to save money in a secure way, explain if a so called Bausparer is beneficial, can help with funding (Kredit) and know details about potential tax benefits and state funded support (cheaper loans etc). Your local bank will also know the local housing market well.

A few things to consider:

[4] As a young person in Austria, what steps should I take so that I can buy a house someday
Answers > Answer (score 2): - Don't buy stocks, (bond) ETFs, funds: chances are you may actually make a lot of money in 5 years, but it may also drop 30% - 40% just before you would want to buy a house
- Try to get a good interest rate on a term deposit (Spareinlage / Sparbuch in Austria; the latter likely has higher fees, so try to avoid it). 20.000 at 3% for five years will return about 23.185. in total, you will be way above the required 80k at the time of writing if you save 20k per year, for 5 years, and get interest. Realistically, it will be around 110k.
- Alternatively, buy bonds (Anleihen) from companies with a low chance of default. They should pay about 4 percent interest at the time of writing. Make sure they expire at a time you want to start to look for houses on the market(e.g. in 5 years).

With regards to the housing market, the market conditions don't matter too much. It's difficult to predict what will happen. Also, you cannot buy now, and you don't want to wait too long either it seems.

units.question: Why can't heat flow by itself from a cold object to a warmer one, and how did Clausius and Kelvin each phrase this rule?
units.gold: This is the second law of thermodynamics: in a closed system, entropy (disorder) increases, so differences in temperature, pressure and density tend to even out. Clausius stated it as heat cannot by itself pass from a colder to a hotter body; equivalently, no device can do nothing except move heat from a cooler to a hotter body. Kelvin's equivalent version says it is impossible for the only result of a process to be turning heat taken from a constant-temperature source entirely into work. The law describes likely behaviour of large systems.
rubric: Second law: entropy in a closed/isolated system increases
Clausius: heat cannot of itself pass from colder to hotter body
Kelvin: cannot convert heat from one constant-temperature source wholly into work as the only result
Applies to large systems (statistical)
Penalize: saying the law forbids refrigerators or heat pumps outright, or swapping hot and cold
units.answer: Heat cannot flow by itself from a colder to a warmer object due to the second law of thermodynamics [4]. Clausius stated this as "Heat cannot of itself pass from a colder to a hotter body," while Kelvin stated it as "It is impossible to construct a device that produces no other effect than the transfer of heat from a lower temperature body to a higher temperature body [4]."
units.sources:
[1] Kelvin's circulation theorem
The differential operator D {\displaystyle \mathrm {D} } is a substantial (material) derivative moving with the fluid particles. Stated more simply, this theorem says that if one observes a closed contour at one instant, and follows the contour over time (by following the motion of all of its fluid elements), the circulation over the two locations of this contour remains constant. This theorem does not hold in cases with viscous stresses, nonconservative body forces (for example the Coriolis force) or non-barotropic pressure-density relations.

[2] First law of thermodynamics
People can use the changes to do work that is useful. Examples of forms of energy in classical mechanics include heat, light, kinetic (movement) or potential energy. However, in modern physics it is considered that there are only two types of energy - mass and kinetic energy, although this may not be helpful to those not familiar with more complex physics.

The law means that the total energy of the universe (or any Closed system) is a constant. However, energy can be transferred from one part of the universe to another.

The most common wording of the first law of thermodynamics used by scientists is:

[3] First law of thermodynamics
History: James Prescott Joule was the first person who found out by experiments that heat and work are convertible.

The first statement of the first law of thermodynamics was given by Rudolf Clausius in 1850: "There is a state function E, called 'energy', whose differential equals the work exchanged with the surroundings during an adiabatic process."

[4] Second law of thermodynamics (cited)
The second law of thermodynamics says that when energy changes from one form to another form, or matter moves freely, entropy (disorder) in a closed system increases.

Differences in temperature, pressure, and density tend to even out after a while. Due to the force of gravity, density and pressure do not even out vertically. Density and pressure on the bottom will be more than at the top.

Entropy is a measure of spread of matter and energy to everywhere they have access.

The most common wording for the second law of thermodynamics is essentially due to Rudolf Clausius: It is impossible to construct a device that produces no other effect than transfer of heat from lower temperature body to higher temperature body

In other words, everything tries to maintain the same temperature over time.

There are many statements of the second law which use different terms, but all mean the same thing. Another statement by Clausius is: Heat cannot of itself pass from a colder to a hotter body.

units.question: I keep reading that the Standard Model is incomplete. What exactly can't it explain, and how do physicists fill that gap?
units.gold: The Standard Model is the main theory of particles and fundamental forces. It explains three of the four fundamental forces (electromagnetism, the weak interaction and the strong interaction) very well, but it cannot explain gravity. To describe the whole universe, physicists combine it with general relativity, the separate theory of gravity; together they are the most accepted explanation of how the universe works. Theoretical particle physicists keep working on improved theories, many of which predict particles not yet discovered.
rubric: Explains three of four forces (electromagnetic, weak, strong)
Cannot explain gravity
Combined with general relativity
Ongoing theoretical work; predicted undiscovered particles
Penalize: claiming the Standard Model explains gravity or that it has been replaced
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
The Standard Model fails to explain dark matter, the matter-antimatter asymmetry, and the origin of mass. Physicists fill this gap by exploring theories beyond the Standard Model, such as supersymmetry or extra dimensions.
units.sources:
[1] Standard Model
Bosons: Bosons are the second type of elementary particle in the standard model. All bosons have an integer spin (1, 2, 3, etc..) so many of them can be in the same place at the same time. There are two types of elementary bosons: gauge bosons and the Higgs boson. The word "boson" honors the Indian physicist Satyendra Nath Bose.

[2] Physics beyond the Standard Model
Another problem lies within the mathematical framework of the Standard Model itself: the Standard Model is inconsistent with that of general relativity, and one or both theories break down under certain conditions, such as spacetime singularities like the Big Bang and black hole event horizons.

[3] Standard Model
Since then, proof of the top quark (1995), the tau neutrino (2000), and the Higgs boson (2012) have added further credence to the Standard Model. In addition, the Standard Model has predicted with great accuracy the various properties of weak neutral currents and the W and Z bosons. Although the Standard Model is believed to be theoretically self-consistent and has demonstrated some success in providing experimental predictions, it leaves some physical phenomena unexplained and so falls short of being a complete theory of fundamental interactions.

[4] Physics beyond the Standard Model
Physics beyond the Standard Model (BSM) is the theoretical developments needed to explain the deficiencies of the Standard Model, such as the inability to explain the fundamental parameters of the Standard Model, the strong CP problem, neutrino oscillations, matter–antimatter asymmetry, and the nature of dark matter and dark energy.

[5] Standard Model
Fermions: Fermions are particles that join together to make up all "matter" we see. Examples of groups of fermions are the proton and the neutron. Fermions have properties, such as charge and mass, which can be seen in everyday life. They also have other properties, such as spin, weak charge, hypercharge, and color charge, whose effects do not usually appear in everyday life. These properties are given numbers called quantum numbers.

Fermions are particles whose spin numbers equal an odd, positive number times one half: 1/2, 3/2, 5/2, etc. We say that fermions have "half integer spin."

An important fact about fermions is that they follow a rule called the Pauli exclusion principle. This rule says that no two fermions can be in the same "place" at the same time, because no two fermions in an atom can have the same quantum numbers at the same time. Fermions also obey a theory called Fermi-Dirac statistics. The word "fermion" honors the physicist Enrico Fermi.

[6] Standard Model
Fermions: There are 12 different types of fermions. Each type is called a "flavor." Their names are:

- Quarks — up, down, strange, charm, top, bottom
- Leptons — electron, muon, tau, electron neutrino, muon neutrino, tau neutrino. The electron is the best known lepton.

Quarks are grouped into three pairs. Each pair is called a "generation." The first quark in each pair has charge 2/3, and the second quark has charge -1/3. The three kinds of neutrino have a charge of 0. The electron, muon, and tau have charge -1.

Matter is made of atoms, and atoms are made of electrons, protons, and neutrons. Protons and neutrons are made of up and down quarks. You can find one lepton by itself, but you can never find quarks alone. This is because quarks are held together by the color force.

units.question: Explain how cosmogony differs from cosmology, and why science still cannot describe the very first instant of the universe.
units.gold: Cosmogony is any theory of how the universe (or things like the Solar System or the Earth-Moon system) originated; cosmology studies the universe in general and can do so without asking about its origin. The leading scientific account is the Big Bang, in which the universe began as an expanding singularity. Science cannot yet model the earliest moments, the Planck time, because there is no testable theory of quantum gravity, although string theory, M theory and loop quantum cosmology offer ideas. Myths offer other cosmogonies.
rubric: Cosmogony = theories of origin; cosmology = study of universe generally
Big Bang from a singularity is the accepted model
Earliest moments (Planck time) unexplained
Reason: no testable theory of quantum gravity
Penalize: treating cosmogony and cosmology as the same field
units.answer: Cosmogony focuses on the origin of the universe, while cosmology studies the universe in general [1]. Science cannot describe the first instant of the universe due to the lack of a testable theory of quantum gravity [4].
units.sources:
[1] Cosmogony (cited)
It is not the same as cosmology: Cosmology studies the universe in general. You can still study the universe without thinking about its origin, which is what cosmonogy studies specifically.

[2] Cosmology
In the science of astronomy, physical cosmology is concerned with the study of the chronology of the universe, the observable universe's origin, its large-scale structures and dynamics, and the ultimate fate of the universe, including the physical laws that govern these areas. Physical cosmology is a sub-branch of astronomy that is concerned with the universe as a whole.

[3] Cosmogony (cited)
Examples > Physics: In astronomy, cosmogony is the study of the origin of things like the universe, the Solar System, or the Earth–Moon system. The popular cosmological model for the birth of the universe is the Big Bang theory.

It is generally accepted that the universe began as a singularity, and when the singularity of the universe started to expand, the Big Bang occurred, which began the universe.

People disagree on the origins of the singularity.

It may be like a black hole, which is a singularity sincegravity in a black hole becomes boundless.

Others like Stephen Hawking say "time" did not exist and was only born with the universe. Hence the universe does not have an origin story. Time did not exist before the creation of the universe.

[4] Cosmogony (cited)
Examples > Physics: There is currently no theoretical model that explains the earliest moments of the universe's existence (during the Planck time). This is because we lack a testable theory of quantum gravity. Still, some researchers in string theory, M theory, and loop quantum cosmology have some ideas.

[5] Cosmogony (cited)
Cosmogony is any theory of the origin of the universe.

[6] Universe
Theoretical models > Big Bang model: Other observations are not clearly answered by known physics. According to the prevailing theory, a slight imbalance of matter over antimatter was present in the universe's creation, or developed very shortly thereafter. Although the matter and antimatter mostly annihilated one another, producing photons, a small residue of matter survived, giving the present matter-dominated universe.

Several lines of evidence also suggest that a rapid cosmic inflation of the universe occurred very early in its history (roughly 10−35 seconds after its creation). Recent observations also suggest that the cosmological constant (Λ) is not zero, and that the net mass-energy content of the universe is dominated by a dark energy and dark matter that have not been characterized scientifically. They differ in their gravitational effects. Dark matter gravitates as ordinary matter does, and thus slows the expansion of the universe; by contrast, dark energy serves to accelerate the universe's expansion.

units.question: How is one joule defined in mechanics, and how does it relate to the watt?
units.gold: The joule (J) is the SI unit of energy, named after the English physicist James Prescott Joule. In classical mechanics, 1 J is the energy transferred when a force of 1 newton acts on an object over a distance of 1 metre (1 J = 1 N x 1 m, or 1 kg m2/s2). Power is linked to it through the watt: one watt is one joule of energy transferred per second. In electricity, 1 J is the work done when 1 ampere flows through 1 ohm of resistance for one second.
rubric: SI unit of energy named after James Prescott Joule
1 J = 1 N x 1 m
1 W = 1 J per second
Penalize: calling the joule a unit of power or of force
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
One joule is the work done when a force of 1 newton is applied over a distance of 1 meter, and one watt is the rate of energy transfer, measured in joules per second. The watt is directly related to the joule through the equation power equals work divided by time.
units.sources:
[1] Joule
Classical mechanics: 1 J is defined as the amount of energy transferred to an object when a force of 1 newton (kg m s-2) is exerted on it over a distance of 1 metre (1 J = 1 N × 1 m), which is related to the W, a unit of power (P): One watt is defined as one joule per second of energy transfer. Algebraically, work done in classical mechanics (W) can be expressed as:

[2] Joule
Electromagnetism > Electronics: 1 J is defined as the work done for one ampere of electric current to pass through an electric circuit with external resistance equivalent to one ohm per second. It can be illustrated by the following equations:

E = C V — (1)V = I R — (2)P = V I — (3)E = P t — (4)Combining (2), (3) and (4),E = I2 R t

where V is the voltage, E is the electrical energy, C is the charge, I is the current, R is the resistance, P is the power and t is the time of energy transfer.

[3] Watt
Definition: Watt is a unit of power, joule is a unit of work and energy, and time is a unit of time. An equation for solving Power, Work and Time is Power = Work ÷ Time, Work = Power × Time, or Time = Work ÷ Power.

[4] Joule's laws
Joule's laws are two: first about heat produced by an electric current, and second about how the energy of a gas relates to pressure, volume.

Joule's first law shows the relation between heat generated by an electric current flowing through a conductor. It is named after James Prescott Joule and shown as:

Q = I^2 \cdot R \cdot t

Where Q is the amount of heat, I is the electric current flowing through a conductor, R is the amount of electric resistance present in the conductor, and t is the amount of time that this happens for.

Joule's second law says that the internal energy of an ideal gas does not change if volume and pressure change, but does change if temperature changes.

Joule's law is important.
