units.question: I'm confused about who runs Western Sahara. Who controls it today, and why did the planned independence vote never happen?
units.gold: Western Sahara is a non-self-governing territory whose sovereignty is unresolved. After Spain left its colony in 1976, Morocco annexed the northern two-thirds and later claimed the rest when Mauritania withdrew in 1979. A guerrilla war with the Polisario Front ended in a 1991 ceasefire and a UN peacekeeping operation. The UN planned a referendum offering independence or integration with Morocco, but it never took place because the sides could not agree on who was eligible to vote. Morocco controls about three-quarters of the territory, west of a 1,600 km sand berm.
rubric: Status unresolved; contested by Morocco and Polisario Front
Morocco annexed it after Spain left in 1976
1991 ceasefire; UN referendum never held over voter eligibility
Morocco controls about three-quarters, west of the berm
Penalize: stating Western Sahara is an independent recognized state or that the referendum took place
units.answer: Morocco controls approximately 80% of Western Sahara, while the Polisario Front controls smaller areas in the east [4]. The planned independence vote never happened due to ongoing conflict and territorial disputes.
units.sources:
[1] Western Sahara
A UN-sponsored ceasefire agreement was reached in 1991, though a planned referendum monitored by the UN's MINURSO mission has since stalled. Approximately 30% of the Western Sahara is controlled by the Polisario Front and the remaining 70% is occupied by Morocco. Morocco maintains the Berm, a 2,700 km-long (1,700 mi) wall lined with land mines that splits the territory. The Polisario Front is recognized by the UN as the legitimate representative of the people of Western Sahara and is primarily supported by Algeria.

[2] Western Sahara
Spain attempted to transfer its administration to Morocco and Mauritania despite an advisory opinion of the International Court of Justice that those countries had no sovereignty over Western Sahara; a war erupted and the pro-independence Polisario Front proclaimed the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic (SADR). Mauritania withdrew its claims in 1979, and Morocco secured de facto control of most of the territory, including all major cities and most natural resources. The SADR established a government-in-exile in Tindouf, Algeria.

[3] Polisario Front (cited)
History > Founding: The Polisario Front was founded on May 10 1973, by a group of Sahrawi students and activists. At the time, Western Sahara was under Spanish control. The group began in Mauritania but had supporters throughout Western Sahara. Their objective was to fight for independence and to put an end to Spanish Colonial Rule. The first military action taken by the Polisario Front took place on May 20 1973, when they attacked a Spanish military post. This date is remembered as the beginning of their armed struggle.

[4] Polisario Front (cited)
History > Founding > Spanish withdrawal and regional conflict: In 1975. after many years of pressure, the Spanish Government agreed to withdraw from Western Sahara. Instead of granting it independence, Spain signed the Madrid Accords, granting control over the territory over to Morocco and Mauritania. This decision was not accepted by the Sahrawi people or the Polisario Front. The group went on to start a war against both Morocco and Mauritania. On February 27 1976, the Polisario Front declared the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic (SADR), which is still a government in exile today. In 1979 Mauritania signed a peace treaty with the Polisario Front and surrendered its claim to the Southern part of the Western Sahara. However Morocco quickly took over that area. Since then Morocco has controlled about 80% of Western Sahara. While the Polisario Front controls much smaller parts in the East. The SADR government is located in refugee camps in Tindouf Algeria.

units.question: When and by what process did Eritrea become independent, and who has led the country since then?
units.gold: Eritrea became independent from Ethiopia on 24 May 1993. Ethiopia had annexed it as a province in 1962, starting a 30-year armed struggle that ended in 1991 when Eritrean fighters defeated government forces; Eritreans then overwhelmingly approved independence in a 1993 referendum. Isaias Afwerki has been the only president since independence, and his rule has been highly autocratic, with indefinite mandatory national service.
rubric: Independence 24 May 1993 from Ethiopia
Approved in a 1993 referendum after a 30-year war ending 1991
Isaias Afwerki only president since
Autocratic rule, indefinite conscription
Penalize: dating independence to 1991 alone or naming a different leader
units.answer: Eritrea became independent on May 24, 1993, through a vote by its people [3]. Since then, the country has been led by a president elected in regular elections.
units.sources:
[1] Horn of Africa
Pan-Hornism: Some people said that its a good idea for Horn Africans to help each other with making money and politics. Or in general This aim is sometimes called Pan-Hornism.

[2] Horn of Africa
Borders: There are four countries in the Horn of Africa. They are Eritrea, Ethiopia, Somalia and Djibouti. The northernmost areas of the Horn are Ras Kasar in the west, settled by the Rashaida tribe, and Alula in the east, settled by Dishiishe. The easternmost area is Ras Hafun, settled by Somalis, and the southernmost in Ras Kamboni, settled by Somalis.

[3] Eritrea (cited)
History: Eritrea became an independent country on May 24, 1993. It is one of the newest countries in the world.

Many different countries have ruled the land that is now called Eritrea. Between 1885 and 1941 it was a colony of Italy. Between 1941 and 1952, the United Nations put it under the protection of the United Kingdom. After 1952, Eritrea became a part of Ethiopia. This was the reason for a long civil war between the Eritreans and the government of Ethiopia.

Eventually, in 1993, Eritrea became an independent country after a vote by its people.

[4] Eritrean–Ethiopian War
Eritrea's war of independence lasted for 30 years, on and off; it was started in 1961 and finished in 1991 when Eritrea finally became independent. While this was going on, there was also a civil war in Ethiopia, which began in 1975. This war was started by Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) as a rebellion to overthrow the Marxist military dictatorship of Derg (a military committee that had overthrown Emperor Haile Selassie in 1974). TPLF and the Eritrean People's Liberation Front were formidable allies during the civil war, but then Ethiopia and Eritrea could not agree on where the border was after Eritrea's independence. One of the main areas of conflict was focused on Badme.

units.question: Summarize when Trinidad and Tobago became independent and from whom, and name the industry that has dominated its economy for more than a century.
units.gold: Trinidad and Tobago gained independence from the United Kingdom on 31 August 1962 and is a parliamentary republic. Oil was discovered on Trinidad in 1910 and petroleum remains the dominant industry; together with natural gas production and processing it has made the country one of the most prosperous in the Caribbean. Earlier, the economy rested on sugar and cocoa worked by enslaved people and later by contract workers from India.
rubric: Independence 31 August 1962 from the UK
Parliamentary republic
Oil discovered 1910; petroleum and gas dominate
Penalize: naming Spain as the power it became independent from or sugar as today's main industry
units.answer: Trinidad and Tobago gained independence from the UK on August 31, 1962, and became a republic in 1976. Its economy is primarily industrial, with oil and gas reserves playing a significant role [1].
units.sources:
[1] Trinidad and Tobago (cited)
Trinidad and Tobago obtained independence in 1962, and became a republic in 1976. Unlike most Caribbean countries and territories, which rely heavily on tourism, the economy is primarily industrial, based on large reserves of oil and gas. The country sees fewer hurricanes than most of the Caribbean because it is farther south.

[2] Reema Harrysingh-Carmona
Early Life: Reema Carmona was born in Hoboken, New Jersey, in the United States.
Her father, Cobee Harrysingh, was an engineer. Her mother is Savitri Seeteram-Harrysingh. She comes from an Indo-Trinidadian family. She went to school in Siparia, in Trinidad and Tobago. She studied at St. Brigid's Girls' Roman Catholic School and Iere High School. She passed her O-Level exams.
Later, she moved to Canada. She went to Cairine Wilson High School in Ottawa. She also studied at the University of Ottawa. She got a degree in Economics.
She is married to Anthony Carmona. They have two children.
She lived in the United States and Canada before she moved to Trinidad.

[3] Reema Harrysingh-Carmona
Career: After 11 years in Canada, Harrysingh-Carmona went back to Trinidad and Tobago. She worked at Point Lisas Industrial Port Development Corporation and also at the Small Business Development Corporation.

[4] Trinidad and Tobago (cited)
Trinidad and Tobago (officially called the Republic of Trinidad and Tobago) is a country in the south Caribbean Sea. It is 11 km (7 miles) away from Venezuela. The country has two bigger islands, Trinidad and Tobago, and many smaller islands. The capital is Port-of-Spain. The country has about 1,262,366 people in it.

Trinidad and Tobago received independence from the United Kingdom on August 31, 1962. Before that, it was ruled by the U.K. Right now, the head of state (person who is in charge of the country) is Ms Paula-Mae Weekes. The head of government (person who is in charge of the government) are Prime Minister Keith Rowley and President Paula-Mae Weekes.

units.question: We want to hike near volcanoes in New Zealand. Which natural hazards there should we be aware of?
units.gold: New Zealand has frequent earthquakes, though they are usually not severe, and significant volcanism on the North Island. Ruapehu (2,797 m) has had large eruptions within the past century, and Taranaki could produce dangerous avalanches and lahars (volcanic mudflows). Other historically active volcanoes include Okataina, Raoul Island, Tongariro and White Island. The climate is temperate with sharp regional contrasts.
rubric: Earthquakes common but usually not severe
Significant volcanism on North Island
Ruapehu large eruptions; Taranaki avalanche/lahar risk
Other active volcanoes e.g. Tongariro, White Island
Penalize: saying New Zealand has no active volcanoes or placing the volcanism on the South Island
units.answer:

Hiking near volcanoes in New Zealand involves awareness of volcanic activity, ash clouds, and potential eruptions. Always check volcanic alerts and stay updated on safety information. Avoid areas near active volcanoes and follow local guidelines for safety.

[1] Hazards on road trip through Italian Alps
Tags: italy, switzerland, nature-and-wildlife, national-parks, alps I am planning to spend about a week in Italian Alps in late October. I have done this kind of thing a lot in New Zealand, and also a bit of Canada and the US, but never in Europe. What potential hazards are there?

[2] Hazards on road trip through Italian Alps
Answers > Answer (score 4, accepted): At this time of the year, the risk of heavy snowfall is low, but you never know. Of course, the risk increases as you go higher, so it depends on your actual route.

Many of the passes and roads on or near the border are well over 2000 meters high, and some may be closed as early as October. Grand St Bernard Pass and Stilfser Joch / Passo dello Stelvio are examples of passes that are open only until September (though not everybody seems to agree on the exact dates). Note that some passes described as "open all year" may actually close based on current conditions.

Another possible risk (though very low) is that a road would be closed due to falling rocks, mudslides, or other obstructions. Not dangerous per se (the chance you would be caught in the event itself is really really low), but you might get stuck somewhere you hadn't planned.

You probably want to:

[3] Hazards on road trip through Italian Alps
Answers > Answer (score 4, accepted): - have a car with snow tires
- have chains in your car (and know how to use them)
- always have enough food and drink in your car to last a day, just in case
- make sure you always have a charged mobile phone (note that you may not always have a signal, though)
- download the detailed maps for your area in Google maps
- have a paper map of the appropriate level of detail
- make sure you always know your position
- let people know of your travel plans, and update them if they change.

If you actually go trekking/hiking/climbing in the mountains, you definitely want to make sure you have the right equipment to do so (nobody wants to see someone trying to climb the Matterhorn wearing flip-flops). You may want to consider buying or renting a Personal Locator Beacon in case of an emergency (if you fall and get injured somewhere along the way). See this discussion for some recommendations.

You may want to check The Great Outdoors SE for additional recommendations.

units.question: Why does Guatemala face both volcanic and storm risks, and which of its volcanoes stand out?
units.gold: Guatemala lies on the Pacific Ring of Fire, the belt holding about 75% of the world's volcanoes and up to 90% of its earthquakes, so its mountains contain many volcanoes and it suffers occasional violent earthquakes. Its Caribbean coast is highly exposed to hurricanes and tropical storms. Notable volcanoes include Pacaya, one of the most active with frequent eruptions since 1965, Santa Maria, named a Decade Volcano for its explosive history, and Fuego; Tajumulco (4,220 m) is the highest point in Central America.
rubric: On the Ring of Fire
Caribbean coast exposed to hurricanes
Pacaya very active since 1965; Santa Maria a Decade Volcano
Occasional violent earthquakes
Penalize: placing the hurricane exposure on the Pacific coast only or denying volcanic activity
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
Guatemala faces volcanic and storm risks due to its location along the Central American Volcanic Arc and its proximity to the Pacific Ocean. The most active volcanoes are Pacaya and Santa María, with Santa María being a key focus for lava flow studies.
units.sources:
[1] What is the most active volcano in Central America?
Answers > Answer (score 6, accepted): There are probably two acceptable answers here:

1. Pacaya - an active volcano in Guatemala, it's erupted 23 times since the Spanish conquest of Guatemala. It then erupted in 1965 and has been erupting basically continuously since then.

1. Santa Maria - also in Guatemala (which makes it easy for you), which appears on this list of 10 most active volcanoes in the world. While currently the most activity is lahars (mud flows) there are also regular lava flows.

[2] What is the most active volcano in Central America?
Answers > Answer (score 1): I'd suggest Volcán de Fuego near Antigua in Guatemala. It's active all the time but only at a low level -- great if you want to reliably check out some lava flows without making the evening news. It's just outside of town too, very easy to get to from Antigua which is a great place to visit. Volcán de Agua is also very near by but it's been inactive since the 1500's.

[3] Where can someone see flowing lava at roughly Easter time?
Answers > Answer (score 18): Towering over Guatemala’s Pacific coastal plain, Santa Maria is a 12,375-foot (3,772-meter) tall stratovolcano consisting of alternating layers of hardened ash, lava and rock. A catastrophic eruption in 1902, one of the largest eruptions of the 20th century, caused severe damage throughout southwestern Guatemala and carved a crater on the volcano's flank. Since 1922, a lava-dome complex, Santiaguito, has formed in the 1902 crater. Santa María is part of the Sierra Madre range of volcanoes, which extends along the western edge of Guatemala, separated from the Pacific Ocean by a broad plain. The volcanoes are formed by the subduction of the Cocos Plate under the Caribbean Plate, which led to the formation of the Central America Volcanic Arc. Santa Maria’s most recent eruption occurred in March of 2011.

Piton de la Fournaise – Reunion Island

It's active all the time but only at a low level -- great if you want to reliably check out some lava flows without making the evening news. It's just outside of town too, very easy to get to from Antigua which is a great place to visit. Volcán de Agua is also very near by but it's been inactive since the 1500's.

[3] What is the most active volcano in Central America?
Answers > Answer (score 6, accepted): There are probably two acceptable answers here:

1. Pacaya - an active volcano in Guatemala, it's erupted 23 times since the Spanish conquest of Guatemala. It then erupted in 1965 and has been erupting basically continuously since then.

1. Santa Maria - also in Guatemala (which makes it easy for you), which appears on this list of 10 most active volcanoes in the world. While currently the most activity is lahars (mud flows) there are also regular lava flows.

units.question: Explain what the volcano on Montserrat did to the island's capital and its people from the mid-1990s on.
units.gold: The Soufriere Hills volcano on Montserrat began erupting in 1995 and devastated much of the island; about two-thirds of the population left for abroad. A massive eruption in 1997 destroyed most of the capital, Plymouth, and left about half of the island uninhabitable. Volcanic activity continued for years, with the last eruption in 2013. The island also faces severe hurricanes from June to November.

About half the island uninhabitable
Penalize: saying the capital was unaffected or confusing the island with another Caribbean territory

units.question: Which mother tongues are most common in Pakistan, and what part does English play there?
units.gold: By mother tongue, Punjabi is the largest language in Pakistan at about 38.8%, followed by Pashto (18.2%), Sindhi (14.6%), Saraiki (12.2%) and Urdu (7.1%), with smaller shares of Balochi, Hindko and Brahui. English is an official language and serves as the lingua franca of the elite and of most government ministries. The population is overwhelmingly Muslim (96.4%).

About 96% Muslim
Penalize: saying Urdu is the most common mother tongue
units.answer: Urdu is the national language of Pakistan and is widely spoken as a mother tongue [2]. English is an official language and is widely used in education and administration. Muhajirs, who are Muslim migrants, speak various languages including Urdu, Gujarati, and Memoni as their mother tongues [2].

[1] Modern Standard Arabic
It is a pluricentric standard language taught throughout the Arab world in formal education, differing significantly from many vernacular varieties of Arabic that are commonly spoken as mother tongues in the area; these are only partially mutually intelligible with both MSA and with each other depending on their proximity in the Arabic dialect continuum.

[2] Mahajir (Pakistan) (cited)
Mahajirs/Mohajir/Muhajir () constitute about 8 percent of the population. They are Muslims who settled in Pakistan after the end of British India in 1947. Unlike other cultural ethnic groups of Pakistan, they do not have a tribe-based cultural identity. Urdu, the official language of Pakistan, is their native tongue, though many muhajirs speak other languages such as Gujarati, Memoni, Marwari etc as their mother tongue. Mohajirs were the vanguard of the Pakistan Movement, which advocated the partition of British India in order to create the independent nation of Pakistan for Indian Muslims. After the partition of India a large number of Muslims migrated from various urban centers of India to live in the new nation of Pakistan. These migrants later identified themselves as mohajirs.

A large number of Mohajirs settled in the cities of Sindh Province, particularly Karāchi and Hyderābād. Today they remain mostly urban.

Pakistani English is the type of the English Language as it is spoken in Pakistan. It is recognised as one of the official languages of the country.

units.question: Compare the Maldives and the Seychelles on how high their land rises and which natural hazards each one faces.
units.gold: The Maldives is extremely low-lying: its highest point is just 5 m (a golf-course tee on Villingi Island) and its mean elevation about 2 m, so it is exposed to tsunamis and very sensitive to sea level rise. The Seychelles is much higher, rising to 905 m at Morne Seychellois. It lies outside the cyclone belt, so severe storms are rare, and its main hazard is occasional short droughts.
rubric: Maldives highest point about 5 m
Maldives at risk from tsunamis and sea level rise
Seychelles highest point 905 m (Morne Seychellois)
Seychelles outside cyclone belt; occasional droughts
Penalize: swapping the two countries' elevations or saying the Seychelles is often hit by cyclones
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
The Maldives have an average elevation of 1.5 metres above sea level, while the Seychelles has a higher elevation. The Maldives face tsunamis, while the Seychelles faces hurricanes and tropical storms.
units.sources:
[1] Maldives
Its land area is only 298 square kilometres (115 sq mi), but this is spread over roughly 90,000 square kilometres (35,000 sq mi) of the sea, making it one of the world's most spatially dispersed sovereign states. With a population of 515,132 in the 2022 census, it is the second least populous country in Asia and the ninth-smallest country by area, but also one of the most densely populated countries. The Maldives has an average ground-level elevation of around 1. 5 metres (4 ft 11 in) above sea level, and a highest natural point of only 2.

[2] Maldives
The Maldives are a group of islands in the Indian Ocean. They are southwest of India. They are made up of the Maldive and Suadive archipelagos, with over 1,200 islands. The highest point in the Maldives is only high above the level of the sea.

[3] Maldives
Climate: The Maldives has a tropical monsoon climate (Am) under the Köppen climate classification, which is affected by the large landmass of South Asia to the north. Because the Maldives has the lowest elevation of any country in the world, the temperature is constantly hot and often humid. The presence of this landmass causes differential heating of land and water. These factors set off a rush of moisture-rich air from the Indian Ocean over South Asia, resulting in the southwest monsoon. Two seasons dominate Maldives' weather: the dry season associated with the winter northeastern monsoon and the rainy season which brings strong winds and storms.

[4] Tsunami
Tsunami waves do not resemble normal undersea currents or sea waves because their wavelength is far longer. Rather than appearing as a breaking wave, a tsunami may instead initially resemble a rapidly rising tide. For this reason, it is often referred to as a tidal wave, although this usage is not favoured by the scientific community because it might give the false impression of a causal relationship between tides and tsunamis. Tsunamis generally consist of a series of waves, with periods ranging from minutes to hours, arriving in a so-called "wave train". Wave heights of tens of metres can be generated by large events. Although the impact of tsunamis is limited to coastal areas, their destructive power can be enormous, and they can affect entire ocean basins. The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami was among the deadliest natural disasters in human history, with at least 230,000 people killed or missing in 14 countries bordering the Indian Ocean.

units.question: Explain how to improvise a seal for a stab or gunshot wound to the chest that is sucking air.
units.gold: An open chest wound that sucks air needs a flutter valve. Take a piece of plastic larger than the wound, such as a credit card, a zip-lock bag or a ready-made valve from a kit, and tape it over the wound on three sides only. Leave the fourth, lowest side open so blood can drain and air can escape: the patch is sucked in on inhalation and lets air out on exhalation. Do not remove embedded objects, call an ambulance, lay the casualty injured side down and treat for shock.

Penalize: advising to seal the wound airtight on all four sides

units.question: How deep, how fast and in what ratio with breaths should an adult receive chest compressions during CPR?
units.gold: Place the heel of one hand on the centre of the chest (on the breastbone at nipple line), the other hand on top with fingers interlocked, shoulders over hands and arms straight. Press 5-6 cm (2-2.5 inches) deep for adults. Give 30 compressions then 2 rescue breaths, at a rate of about 100 per minute, just over one per second, letting the chest fully recoil each time. Most people go too fast. Put the patient on a hard surface, not a mattress. Children get one-third of chest depth.

units.question: I come across an injured person on a busy road. What should I check before touching them?
units.gold: Your own safety comes first; you cannot help if you become a victim too. Before approaching, check the scene for hazards: traffic, gas or chemical leaks, live electrics, fire or falling objects, and human threats such as an aggressor or uncooperative bystanders. Put on protective equipment, especially impermeable gloves. If a danger cannot be controlled, stay clear and call emergency services. Keep watching for changes, and gather clues and witness accounts about what happened.

units.answer:
From the offline source:
Answers > Answer (score 3): If both legs are OK and there is no way they could have a spinal injury, you may well find it is quicker to get them to hospital in your car. Drive very slowly over bumps and around corners, do not accelerate fast and leave plenty of stopping distance for slow braking. This would be my preferred option for a minor injury to an arm, hand, shoulder or foot. In any other situation, call an ambulance and follow the phone operator's instructions to the letter. Do NOT try to be clever or show initiative about treating the casualty - you could easily make things worse! [1]

In an emergency, call your local emergency number (911 in the US, 112 in Europe).

units.question: In a survival situation, why is it a mistake to ration the water you already carry, and what water sources should you avoid?
units.gold: Do not ration: your body is the best storage container, and people have died of dehydration with a full canteen. Humans survive about three days without water, less in heat. Avoid seawater unless distilled (processing it costs twice the water it provides), never drink urine, avoid eating snow in the cold since it lowers body temperature, and avoid stagnant or brackish water; purification cannot remove salt. Fast-running water is safer than ponds, and rainwater is safe if boiled.

Penalize: recommending drinking urine or seawater

units.sources:
[1] Ration or consume water?
Answers > Answer (score 5): When I took a wildlands firefighting course in Arizona, the instructor said that if you find yourself lost in the desert, you should not ration your water. People have died of thirst with water in their canteens.

[2] Ration or consume water?
Answers > Answer (score 1): For what it's worth, I will refer to a single event: the outdoorsman Aron Lee Ralston survived 127 hours rationing his water. Aron Lee Ralston had access to only 350 ml (12 imp fl oz) of water for a period of 127 hours. According to his book, Between a Rock and a Hard Place, he rationed his water.

[3] Tripod in Carry-on Luggage
Answers > Answer (score 13, accepted): The exact regulations will vary from country to country, and their interpretation will vary from person to person, so there's never any guarantee of exactly what to be allowed or will not when it comes to items like Tripods.

However speaking from personal experience, I have traveled extensively through at least a dozen different countries on multiple occasions with a Manfrotto 190D (a relatively large, metal tripod) in my carry-on luggage - including trips from Australia.

Only once have I ever had security even ask me about the tripod, and that was when departing from Singapore. They had me remove the tripod from my bag and measured its (non-extended) length, before deciding that there was no problem with me taking it on board.

Obviously YMMV, but based on my experience you will have no problems at all!

[4] Tripod in Carry-on Luggage
Answers > Answer (score 7): There is a comprehensive list of items that are prohibited to be carried on-board by the Australian Government Agencies. The list that of prohibited and Dangerous goods do not list tripod as an item, however, there is a general clause that your tripod may fit under and though most information from forums such as Whirlpool and Overclockers points to the fact that it will be allowed it is in the discretion of the individual doing the checking whether they want to apply the following clause to it:

Blunt objects that can be used to bludgeon or threaten someone, such as:

- Baseball, softball, and cricket bats, and similar items
- Hockey and lacrosse sticks and similar items
- Billiard, pool or snooker cues
- Golf clubs
- Any other piece of wood, metal or any other substance big enough to threaten someone

When it comes to Dubai there is no information like the one above you can probably look at Etihad's list of dangerous or prohibited items to verify.

units.question: How quickly can a house fire become deadly, and what kills most victims?
units.gold: Very fast: a small flame can become a major fire in under 30 seconds, a fire can be life-threatening in two minutes, and a home can be engulfed in five. Heat is more dangerous than flames: room air can reach 100 degrees at floor level and 600 at eye level, scorching lungs. Smoke and toxic gases kill more people than flames, and fire quickly turns dark. Keep working smoke alarms on every level, practise an escape plan twice a year, and crawl low under smoke.
rubric: Gives the timescale (under 30 seconds to major fire, minutes to engulf)
States smoke and toxic gases kill more people than flames
Mentions extreme heat at eye level versus floor
Mentions smoke alarms, escape plan or crawling low
Penalize: claiming flames are the main cause of fire deaths
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
House fires can become deadly rapidly, often within minutes, as flames and heat spread quickly. Most victims die from smoke inhalation or direct heat injury, not from the fire itself.

Many heads of state have expressed condolences, including António Guterres, General Secretary of the United Nations. There have also been donations and massages sent to victims of the arson attack.

On 25 January 2024, the man who perpetrated the arson attack was sentenced to death for the killings.

[2] In a house on fire, do children faint more easily than the adults?
Answers > Answer (score 0, accepted): There's a reason why, in a house fire, the phrase to remember is "Get down low and go, go, go"

The most common ailment of someone in a house fire is from smoke inhalation. As smoke rises, the closer you are to the floor, the less smoke you will breathe in (until the entire room is filled with smoke in which case you're dead anyway).

From this perspective, as long as the child stays away from the flame, they are actually more likely to last longer than an adult, purely because they are smaller, lower to the ground and not breathing in as much smoke.

[3] In a house on fire, do children faint more easily than the adults?
My explanation is that this character is not risking his life if he knows the person-to-save would most likely die even after being rescued when other (possibly more important) lives are concurrently in danger. So my question is this: If a house is on fire, are young children more prone to faint since they have a more underdeveloped body system than adults, or, due to their size, can they stay safe from smoke and large fires by sticking themselves into corners until their rescue arrives?

units.question: What is a warming center, and who can use one during cold nights?
units.gold: A warming center is a newer kind of emergency shelter that opens on particularly cold or rainy nights. It serves people who decline or are not allowed to use homeless shelters, and also people who are not homeless but whose home heating is inadequate or broken. More broadly, emergency shelters house people fleeing a specific situation such as a disaster or domestic violence, and post-disaster shelters often use tents or buildings like schools and churches.
rubric: Defines a warming center as a shelter opening on very cold or rainy nights
Lists users: people refusing or barred from homeless shelters
Includes people whose home heating is inadequate or broken
Penalize: describing warming centers as permanent housing
units.answer: A warming center is a place where people can stay warm and dry during rain or cold weather [1]. It is mainly used by homeless individuals and others who cannot stay in shelters.
units.sources:
[1] Warming center (cited)
A warming center is a place where people can go to stay warm and dry when it is rainy or wet outside. They are like homeless shelters, except that they are only open when the weather is bad. Their main goal is to make sure that nobody is left out in the cold. Many people die from being wet and cold, every year.

[2] Warming center (cited)
Purpose: Warming Centers are mostly for people who are homeless who do not stay in homeless shelters. Sometimes they are also set up when blizzards occur or the power goes out. In some cases, when cold snaps threaten wildlife, warming centers are created and operated to protect endangered wild animals. Cold-blooded animals such as turtles are particularly vulnerable, as are their hatchlings.

[3] How to parcook a casserole?
Answers > Answer (score 2): My family does this with lasagne every year for Christmas. It works with most casseroles that are prepared in advance:

- Make the casserole in advance, then either chill (if night before) or freeze (if a week before).
- Place the cold dish in a cold oven, covered in aluminum foil, then turn it to medium-low heat (about 300°F/150°C).
- Heat until the center of the casserole is sufficiently warmed through.
- Turn the heat on the oven down to 'warm'

Just before guests arrive, make the bechamel. Keep it on low heat on the stovetop, stirring every 10-15 minutes or so.

[4] How to parcook a casserole?
Answers > Answer (score 2): - (20-30 mins before service) uncover the casseroles
- Top with some of the bechamel (reserving the rest so people can add extra as they wish)
- Crank the oven to 'broil' or 'grill' or whatever they call the 'top only heat' setting in your country, and cook the top to desired brown-ness. If you don't have a broil/grill setting, move the casserole as close to the top element as you can without the food actually touching it, and turn the heat as high as the oven will go.
- Remove the casserole and let rest to firm back up. (take notes on how long this time, as that'll affect the exact time when you start broiling the next time you do this).
- Place the reserved bechamel in a gravy boat.
- Slice & serve

[1] How to parcook a casserole?
Answers > Answer (score 2): - (20-30 mins before service) uncover the casseroles
- Top with some of the bechamel (reserving the rest so people can add extra as they wish)
- Crank the oven to 'broil' or 'grill' or whatever they call the 'top only heat' setting in your country, and cook the top to desired brown-ness. If you don't have a broil/grill setting, move the casserole as close to the top element as you can without the food actually touching it, and turn the heat as high as the oven will go.
- Remove the casserole and let rest to firm back up. (take notes on how long this time, as that'll affect the exact time when you start broiling the next time you do this).
- Place the reserved bechamel in a gravy boat.
- Slice & serve

Note that there's also bechamel in the lassagne we make -- so you just make a little bit less when making the casserole initially, if it's needed for middle layers as well.

[2] How to parcook a casserole?
Answers > Answer (score 2): My family does this with lasagne every year for Christmas. It works with most casseroles that are prepared in advance:

- Make the casserole in advance, then either chill (if night before) or freeze (if a week before).
- Place the cold dish in a cold oven, covered in aluminum foil, then turn it to medium-low heat (about 300°F/150°C).
- Heat until the center of the casserole is sufficiently warmed through.
- Turn the heat on the oven down to 'warm'

Just before guests arrive, make the bechamel. Keep it on low heat on the stovetop, stirring every 10-15 minutes or so.

Purpose: Warming Centers are mostly for people who are homeless who do not stay in homeless shelters. Sometimes they are also set up when blizzards occur or the power goes out. In some cases, when cold snaps threaten wildlife, warming centers are created and operated to protect endangered wild animals. Cold-blooded animals such as turtles are particularly vulnerable, as are their hatchlings.

[4] Warming center (cited)
A warming center is a place where people can go to stay warm and dry when it is rainy or wet outside. They are like homeless shelters, except that they are only open when the weather is bad. Their main goal is to make sure that nobody is left out in the cold. Many people die from being wet and cold, every year.

units.question: I'm leading a long expedition. How can I protect participants' mental health along with their physical safety?
units.gold: Mental distress is common among wilderness guides and outdoor athletes, but few programs teach psychological first aid. Changed routines, travel stress and new physical challenges can trigger existing mental health conditions. Preventive measures include adequate social support, enough sleep, establishing travel-specific routines, sticking to medication regimens and watching for early warning signs of deterioration. Wilderness emergencies also require managing patients for long periods before evacuation.

Mentions travel stress and changed routines can trigger existing conditions
Lists prevention: social support, sleep, routines, medication adherence
Mentions watching for early warning signs
Penalize: claiming mental health is irrelevant on expeditions
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
Protecting participants' mental health requires proactive strategies like regular check-ins, creating a supportive environment, and ensuring access to mental health resources. Prioritize physical safety by following all travel guidelines and ensuring proper equipment and training.
units.sources:
[1] Wikivoyage: Travelling with a mental health condition
While travel is and should be a rewarding experience, it can also pose significant challenges to people with mental health conditions. Planning and executing a trip is stressful by anyone's standards, but it can be overwhelming if you suffer from mental illness. It is estimated that 1 in 4 adults will experience mental health problems at least once in their life, but just because you're going through a rough patch does not mean you should give up all the wonderful experiences travel can provide. And regardless of how mentally healthy you consider yourself to be, all travellers should give the same consideration to their psychological well-being as they would to their physical health before leaving home.

[2] Wikivoyage: Travelling with a mental health condition
Stay safe: In places where such attitudes are common, you may find even doctors and mental health professionals share the same prejudices. Mental health services may be limited or non-existent. It is therefore extremely important to research your destination country's relevant laws and culture, and assess whether there is an unreasonable risk to your safety or well-being should you enter that country.

[3] What does "in good health" mean with respect to Canadian entry?
A more detailed page specifies that persons may be refused entry or a visa on...

- health grounds – if their condition is likely to:
  - endanger public health or public safety, or
  - cause excessive demands on health or social services (some exceptions exist 2 3)

Still, no actual guidance is provided on when exactly a health problem is serious enough to trigger refusal.

What is the definition of "in good health" as it relates specifically to entering Canada? I'm guessing that a cold, a broken arm, a hernia, or athlete's foot isn't enough to result in entry refusal, but how serious does a condition have to be?

[4] What does "in good health" mean with respect to Canadian entry?
- Is it based on formal diagnosis (e.g. there is a list of diagnoses that are per se deemed to "endanger public health or public safety" and a list of diagnoses that are not)?
- Does the CBSA official make an independent judgment of a person's overall health and whether that person is likely to need "excessive" services?
- Is there a specific dollar amount that constitutes excessive (e.g. officials are supposed to refuse you entry if your medical bills for the previous 12 months were over $10,000)?

There is a procedure for obtaining an officially recognized Medical Exam, but not all visitors to Canada are required to obtain one. I'm more asking the question with reference to these visitors.

units.question: Why might authorities detain or force people through decontamination after a chemical release?
units.gold: Mass contamination scenes often involve collective panic among hundreds or thousands of people, so police or security may be needed to keep order, and decontamination can resemble a mass arrest. Some people resist: those who think they are uncontaminated do not want to be crowded with sick people, some carry weapons or contraband, and others fear authorities, separation or quarantine more than the contaminant. Laws in Australia and FEMA guidance allow detention for decon. Drills reduce panic.

Mentions legal basis such as Australian law or FEMA guidance
Mentions drills reduce panic and speed decontamination
Penalize: claiming decontamination is always voluntary

Authorities may detain or force decontamination to prevent exposure to hazardous chemicals, ensuring public safety and preventing health risks. This measure helps contain the chemical spread and protects those involved in response efforts.

[1] Eritrea
Eritrea: Military and security forces: Eritrea's military and security forces are Eritrean Defense Forces (EDF): Eritrean Ground Forces, Eritrean Navy, Eritrean Air Force; People's Militia (aka People's Army or Hizbawi Serawit) (2024). Note on Eritrea's military and security forces: police are responsible for maintaining internal security, but the government sometimes uses the armed forces, reserves, demobilized soldiers, or civilian militia to meet domestic as well as external security requirements; the armed forces have authority to arrest and detain civilians.

Eritrea: capital, population and area: Eritrea's official name is State of Eritrea. Eritrea's capital is Asmara. Eritrea's time zone is UTC+3. [3] Eritrea
Eritrea: languages, religions and people: Eritrea's religions are Eritrean Orthodox, Roman Catholic, Evangelical Lutheran, Sunni Muslim. Eritrea's ethnic groups are Tigrinya 50%, Tigre 30%, Saho 4%, Afar 4%, Kunama 4%, Bilen 3%, Hedareb/Beja 2%, Nara 2%, Rashaida 1% (2021 est.). Eritrea's life expectancy at birth is 67.5 years (2024 est.).

[4] Chemical Emergencies
When a hazardous chemical has been released, it may harm people's health. Chemical releases can be unintentional, as in the case of an industrial accident. They could also be planned, as in the case of a terrorist attack with a chemical weapon.

Some hazardous chemicals have been developed by military organizations for use in warfare. Examples are nerve agents such as sarin and VX. Many hazardous chemicals are used in industry - for example, chlorine, ammonia, and benzene. Some can be made from everyday items such as household cleaners.

Although there are no guarantees of safety during a chemical emergency, you can take actions to protect yourself. You should have a disaster plan. Being prepared can help reduce fear, anxiety, and losses. If you do experience a disaster, it is normal to feel stressed. You may need help in finding ways to cope.

Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

Topic groups: Disasters

units.question: Which parts of the world have the most destructive earthquakes, and why are some quakes far from these zones especially deadly?
units.gold: The worst earthquakes mostly occur at converging tectonic plates: the Alpide belt from Italy through Turkey, Iran and the Himalayas to southern China; the Pacific Ring of Fire (New Zealand, Indonesia, Japan, the American west coast); and the Caribbean. Spreading boundaries like Iceland have volcanoes but rarely major quakes. Intraplate earthquakes away from boundaries are rarer and usually weaker but often more devastating because those areas are unprepared, as in Tangshan in 1976.

Explains converging plates build stress that releases as quakes
Explains intraplate quakes are deadly because areas are unprepared
Mentions an example such as Tangshan 1976
Penalize: claiming Iceland is among the most earthquake-dangerous regions
units.answer:

The Pacific Ring of Fire has the most destructive earthquakes due to frequent tectonic activity. Some quakes are deadly even outside these zones because they occur in tectonically active areas where stress builds up and is released suddenly.
units.sources:
[1] Earthquake
Zones: Earthquake zones are concentrated in some parts of the world. The first is the Pacific belt, which circles the Pacific Ocean. This part is the biggest seismic belt: it has the most active earthquakes and the most volcanoes.

The second part is the Alpide belt. It includes the seismic activities from Sumatra, to the Himalayas, to south Europe and north Africa, to the Atlantic Ocean.

These belts are along the edges of tectonic plates. The tectonic plates push on each other and make great amounts of tension.

[2] Earthquake
History: Earthquakes sometimes hit cities and kill hundreds or thousands of people. Most earthquakes happen along the Pacific Ring of Fire but the biggest ones mostly happen in other places. Tectonically active places are places where earthquakes or volcanic eruptions are regularly repeated.

units.question: Give me the key design rules for building a ventilated pit latrine that doesn't smell or attract flies.
units.gold: A ventilated improved pit uses a vent pipe to draw odours out and trap flies, which fly toward the light at the top and die against a fly screen. The pipe should be 110-150 mm inside diameter and rise over 300 mm above the roof; painting it black helps where wind is low. Use an aluminium screen with 1.2-1.5 mm holes. Dig the pit 1-1.5 m wide and at least 3 m deep, keep the toilet interior dim, and site it at least 30 m from any water source.

States pit depth at least 3 m and 30 m from water sources
Penalize: siting the latrine right next to a well

units.question: Who has a higher chance of getting endocarditis, the infection of the heart lining and valves?
units.gold: Endocarditis is rare because a healthy immune system usually clears germs from the blood. Risk is higher with heart valve disease, certain congenital heart defects, a pacemaker or implantable defibrillator, or a replaced valve, since damaged tissue and devices trap germs. Other risk factors are older age (valve changes such as mitral prolapse or aortic calcium deposits), injecting drugs, a weakened immune system, poor dental health, a long-term central venous line and a previous episode of endocarditis.

units.question: My mouth feels sticky and dry most of the day. What usually causes this?
units.gold: Persistent dry mouth (xerostomia) means not enough saliva. Common causes include side effects of medicines for high blood pressure, depression or bladder control; diseases such as Sjogren's syndrome, HIV, salivary gland disorders and diabetes; radiation therapy or chemotherapy; nerve damage; breathing through the mouth; and alcohol or tobacco. It raises your risk of tooth decay and mouth infections, so see your provider or dentist, who may review your medicines and test how much saliva you make.
rubric: Names the condition xerostomia (lack of saliva)
Lists medicine side effects (blood pressure, depression, bladder)
Lists diseases such as Sjogren's syndrome, diabetes or HIV, or cancer treatments
Mentions mouth breathing or alcohol/tobacco
Penalize: claiming dry mouth is always harmless and needs no evaluation
units.answer: Dehydration is a common cause of dry mouth [5]. Saliva production can be reduced by certain medications or medical conditions. Hydration and maintaining a healthy lifestyle can help alleviate symptoms.
units.sources:
[1] Dehydration
Symptoms: Dehydrated people may have different symptoms depending on how dehydrated they are. - Dry, sticky mouth - Feeling tired or sleepy - Dry skin

[2] My pasta keeps sticking together
Answers > Answer (score 1): Your pasta may be too wet to begin with. If it feels sticky when you roll and cut, it is too sticky. Also, try allowing the rolled sheets to air dry on your counter for 15-30 minutes per side before cutting. Sticking or clumping usually happens early in the cooking process, if it is going to happen.

[3] Dehydration
People get dehydrated when they lose more water than they take in. The human body needs water to survive. If a person gets badly dehydrated, their body will be unable to work the right way. Bad dehydration can cause organ damage and even death. The key sign of dehydration is sunken eyes, or blac bags under the eyes. It can also cause the skin to lose flexibility when it is in the process of happening.

[4] Dehydration
What causes dehydration?: A living organism will get dehydrated if their body is losing water in some way and they do not drink enough to replace the water. The most common causes of dehydration are:
- Sweating a lot (because of hot weather or exercise)
- Bad diarrhea
- Vomiting (throwing up)
- Urinating more than usual (this can happen if a person has uncontrolled diabetes or takes medicines like diuretics which cause them to urinate more often)
- Fever

[5] Dry mouth (cited)
Xerostomia, or dry mouth, also dry mouth syndrome, is dryness in the mouth. It may be associated with a change in the composition of saliva, reduced salivary flow (also hyposalivation), or dehydration. Causes of hyposalivation include dental caries, oral candidiasis, damage to salivary glands, or certain other causes. Certain drugs (such as cannabis) or medications may also cause "dry mouth" as a side effect.

Minor cases of dry mouth can be treated at home by hydration, re-balancing the minerals in the body, and avoiding acidic foods. More severe cases may need to be looked at by a doctor.

[6] Long term effects of chewing on cheek?
Tags: dermatology, oral-health

When I'm concentrating hard or anxious I unconsciously start biting my cheeks, sometimes biting off the topmost layer of skin. I don't bleed, but the sensation of the skin is bumpy instead of smooth.

I have done some googling, but can't seem to get anything else than articles related to peeling of the skin inside the mouth (e.g. http://www.webdental.com/profiles/blogs/the-inside-of-my-mouth-is-peeling-what-s-going-on), which is definitely not similar to my situation.

Has anyone heard of this kind of fixation, and is there any potential health risks associated with it?

units.question: Explain how crabs (pubic lice) are passed between people and how to get rid of them.
units.gold: Pubic lice cannot hop or fly; they crawl, and spread mainly through sexual contact, occasionally through close contact or shared clothing, bedding or towels. You cannot get them from animals. Treatment is an over-the-counter lice-killing lotion containing permethrin, or a mousse with pyrethrins and piperonyl butoxide; one treatment usually works, with a second after 9-10 days if needed. Wash clothes, bedding and towels in hot water, and get checked for other STIs while partners are checked too.
rubric: States they spread mainly by sexual contact, sometimes via bedding/clothing
States they crawl and cannot jump or fly, and are not caught from animals
Names permethrin lotion or pyrethrin mousse treatments
Mentions retreatment after 9-10 days and hot washing of bedding
Penalize: recommending shaving alone or claiming pets transmit them
units.answer: Crab lice are passed through direct or indirect contact with an infected person [3]. To get rid of them, clean and treat affected areas with soap and water, and use over-the-counter or prescription medications.
units.sources:
[1] Crab louse
The crab louse or pubic louse is an insect, which is a parasite on humans. It is found most often in pubic hair, but also lives in other areas on the body with dense hair. Crab lice are still visible with the human eye, they are about 1.5-2mm in size. Note that head lice and Body lice are different species.

[2] Crab louse
The crab louse or pubic louse (Pthirus pubis) is an insect that is an obligate ectoparasite of humans, feeding exclusively on blood. The crab louse usually is found in the person's pubic hair. Humans are the only known hosts of the crab louse, although a closely related species, Pthirus gorillae, infects gorillas.

[3] Under what wilderness conditions is becoming infested with lice a possibility and what precautions should one take to avoid it? (cited)
Answers > Answer (score 11, accepted): Lice are passed on by one of two manners. Either by direct contact or indirect contact with someone who is infected with lice.

The chances of coming in contact with lice in the wilderness is exceedingly remote. A camp site that has been abandoned for several days would be free of lice if it was actually occupied by an infested person.

First of all, there is no need to spray your home and belongings with potentially dangerous insecticides. Lice are known as “obligate parasites,” meaning they don’t survive very long without their human host. They need us to live, and they die within 24 to 48 hours after removal from a human host. - How to Keep Lice from Spreading—and Coming Back!

Here is how people actually get lice:

[4] Louse
Lice and humans: Humans are unique in that they host three different species of lice: head lice, body lice (which live mainly in clothing), and pubic lice. The DNA differences between head lice and body lice provide corroborating evidence that humans started wearing clothes at approximately 70,000 BCE.

Recent DNA evidence suggests that pubic lice spread to the ancestors of humans approximately 3.3 million years ago from the ancestors of gorillas by sharing the same bed or other communal areas with them, and are more closely related to lice endemic to gorillas than to other lice species infesting humans.

Humans are the only known hosts of the crab louse, although a closely related species, Pthirus gorillae, infects gorillas.

[4] Crab louse
The crab louse or pubic louse is an insect, which is a parasite on humans. It is found most often in pubic hair, but also lives in other areas on the body with dense hair. Crab lice are still visible with the human eye, they are about 1.5-2mm in size. Note that head lice and Body lice are different species.

units.question: Which irregular heart rhythm do doctors see most often, and what test usually picks it up?
units.gold: An arrhythmia is a problem with the rate or rhythm of the heartbeat: too fast (tachycardia), too slow (bradycardia) or with early extra beats. The most common type is atrial fibrillation, causing a fast irregular heartbeat. Many people have no symptoms; others feel fluttering, pounding or skipped beats, dizziness, fainting, chest discomfort or breathlessness. The usual test is an electrocardiogram (EKG), which records the heart's electrical activity. Chest pain or breathlessness warrant emergency care.
rubric: Names atrial fibrillation as the most common arrhythmia
Defines tachycardia and bradycardia
States an electrocardiogram (EKG) is the most common diagnostic test
Lists symptoms or notes it may be symptomless
Penalize: claiming all arrhythmias are harmless
units.answer: Doctors most commonly see ventricular tachycardia, which is detected via an electrocardiogram (ECG) [3]. This test reveals abnormal electrical activity in the heart, specifically when the atria do not initiate the heartbeat properly.
units.sources:
[1] Is it normal to feel your heart beat in your chest?
Answers > Answer (score 11, accepted): Is it normal for a person to at times feel their heart beat in their chest without actually placing their hand on their chest, while at other times not be able to...?

Yes, this is normal.

Normally, people do not feel their heart beating in their chest at rest. It is one of those things similar to breathing - it's happening, but we're not often aware of it (which is good as it might be very distracting otherwise.)

However, an alteration in the steady background of the beating heart is often perceived. Sometimes the alteration is due to increased rate or force of contractions. If so, the sensation of feeling your heart beating (normally under the circumstances) is called physiological palpitations (i.e. normal.) If they are a result of an "abnormal" rate or rhythm, the phenomenon is known as "palpitations".

[2] Is it normal to feel your heart beat in your chest?
Answers > Answer (score 11, accepted): In normal resting conditions, the activity of the heart is generally not perceived by the individual. However, during or immediately after intense physical activity or emotional stress, it may be quite normal to become aware of one's own heartbeat for brief periods; these sensations are regarded as physiological palpitations, in that they represent the normal or expected response to a certain challenge or activity leading to an increase in the frequency and strength of the contraction of the heart. Outside of such situations, instead, palpitations are perceived as abnormal.2

The sensory mechanisms responsible for palpitation are unknown.1

[3] Ventricular tachycardia (cited)
Diagnosis: A doctor can diagnose ventricular tachycardia by doing an electrocardiogram (also called an ECG or an EKG). This is a test that shows the electrical activity in the heart. The doctor will be able to see that the electrical signals that tell the atria to squeeze first are not working.

units.question: My son bumped his head at football practice. Which signs after a concussion mean we should get help urgently?
units.gold: Concussion symptoms can appear days or weeks after the injury, typically headache, neck pain, nausea, ringing ears, dizziness or tiredness. Get medical help if symptoms worsen or serious ones appear: seizures, drowsiness or not waking up, a worsening persistent headache, weakness or numbness, repeated vomiting, confusion, slurred speech or loss of consciousness. Most people recover fully; rest is key, with limited physical and concentration-heavy activities (studying, screens) at first, then a gradual return when the provider agrees.
rubric: Lists red-flag signs: seizures, cannot wake, worsening headache, repeated vomiting, slurred speech, weakness
Notes symptoms may start days or weeks later
Advises rest and limiting physical and mental exertion
Mentions gradual return to activities with provider approval
Penalize: saying a concussion is always trivial if there was no loss of consciousness
units.answer:
Head injury: if they might have hurt their neck (a fall from height, a high-speed hit) or aren't responding, don't move them unless they're in danger; support the head so the head, neck and spine stay in a straight line. If they're not responding and not breathing normally, call emergency services and start CPR. If they're not responding but breathing normally, and they're vomiting or their breathing sounds blocked or gurgling, turn them on their side, keeping the head and spine in line. For a bump, hold an ice pack or frozen peas wrapped in a tea towel on it for short periods; never put ice directly on the skin. An adult should stay with them for the first 24 hours. They should rest, avoid alcohol until they feel better, and avoid contact sport for 3 weeks. Get urgent medical advice if they've been sick once, feel dizzy, take blood thinners, or had been drinking; if told to go to hospital, don't drive yourself. Call emergency services if they were knocked out and haven't woken, can't stay awake, have a seizure, vomit more than once, fell more than 1 metre or 5 stairs, were hit at high speed, have problems seeing, hearing, speaking, walking or with balance, new weakness or numbness, clear fluid from the ears or nose, bleeding from the ears, or changed behaviour.

Source: St John Ambulance (UK), Spinal injury; St John Ambulance (UK), Head injury; St John Ambulance (UK), CPR; British Heart Foundation, How to do CPR; St John Ambulance (UK), Recovery position; NHS, Head injury and concussion; British Red Cross, Head injury; healthdirect (AU), Head injuries. Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

In an emergency, call your local emergency number (911 in the US, 112 in Europe).

units.question: Which sudden eye symptoms point to an emergency type of glaucoma?
units.gold: Sudden intense eye pain, blurred vision, red eyes or nausea may signal angle-closure glaucoma, a less common type where fluid builds up quickly in the eye; go to an eye care provider or emergency room at once. The common open-angle type usually has no early symptoms and slowly erodes side vision, like looking through a tunnel, which is why regular dilated eye exams matter. Pressure tolerance varies: some people with high pressure never get glaucoma, others get it at normal pressure.
rubric: Lists acute symptoms: intense eye pain, blurred vision, red eye, nausea
Identifies angle-closure glaucoma and urgent care
Contrasts with symptomless open-angle glaucoma and peripheral vision loss
Mentions regular dilated eye exams
Penalize: telling the user to wait and see with sudden severe eye pain
units.answer: Sudden eye pain, blurred vision, and nausea point to an emergency like closed-angle glaucoma [1].
units.sources:
[1] Glaucoma (cited)
This elevated pressure can reduce vascular perfusion in the vitreous chamber and can damage the optic nerve and peripheral glial tissues. In closed-angle glaucoma, the drainage of the eye becomes suddenly blocked, leading to a rapid increase in intraocular pressure. This may lead to intense eye pain, blurred vision, and nausea. Closed-angle glaucoma is an emergency requiring immediate attention.

[2] Glaucoma (cited)
Glaucoma is a disease that causes damage to the eye. If a person who has glaucoma does not get help from a doctor, they will not be able to see. This disease happens because of increased pressure in the eye. The pressure causes damage to the optic nerve.

[3] Glaucoma (cited)
Genetic component: There is often a hereditary tendency to glaucoma. A family history of glaucoma is a risk factor. The relative risk of having what is called "primary open-angle glaucoma" (POAG) is increased about two- to four-fold for people who have a sibling with glaucoma. Glaucoma, particularly primary open-angle glaucoma, is associated with mutations in several different genes

Also, the likelihood of it happening is different in different populations. Glaucoma is the leading cause of blindness in African Americans, who have higher rates of primary open angle glaucoma.

[4] When someone with glaucoma sees rainbows around lights, what exactly is happening physically?
Answers > Answer (score 9, accepted): Basically, this can happen in other forms of high-tension glaucoma or ocular hypertension with momentarily raised intraocular pressure (IOP), too. Note that it only does in forms where the IOP rises quickly, whereas in a slow and constant rise (as it happens in many forms of chronic glaucoma) the endothelial cells can adapt and still drain the cornea from the excess water. So basically, the same happens in an attack of angle-closure glaucoma, just with the difference being that angle-closure glaucomas often don't go away without medical treatment, whereas in early adulthood IOP spikes due to MDS the halos often are the only symptom which is often triggered by exercise or in dim ambience light situations. This is due to the fact that when the iris moves (as in widened pupils due to adrenaline reactions when performing sports or whe the lights are dim) in a patient with MDS, it rubs against the lens, loses pigment by erosion and this then clogs the eye's drain (in the anterior chamber angle).

units.question: Explain what a PSA blood test can and cannot tell a man about prostate cancer.
units.gold: PSA is a protein made by the prostate. A high blood level may indicate prostate cancer but does not prove it, because an enlarged prostate (BPH), other prostate problems and certain medicines also raise PSA. Generally the higher the PSA, the likelier cancer is, yet a low PSA does not guarantee you are cancer-free. Screening only flags possible cancer; further tests diagnose it. It is unclear whether early detection lowers the risk of dying, so discuss benefits and harms with your provider.
rubric: States a high PSA is not proof of cancer
Lists other causes: enlarged prostate (BPH), other prostate problems, medicines
States a low PSA does not rule out cancer
Mentions uncertainty whether screening reduces deaths and the need to discuss with a provider
Penalize: claiming a PSA test alone diagnoses prostate cancer
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
A PSA blood test measures prostate-specific antigen levels, which can indicate elevated levels associated with prostate cancer. However, it cannot definitively diagnose cancer and may falsely suggest it. The test also cannot detect all forms of cancer or determine the exact stage of the disease.
units.sources:
[1] Prostate cancer
Prostate cancer is the uncontrolled growth of cells in the prostate, a gland in the male reproductive system below the bladder. Abnormal growth of prostate tissue is usually detected through screening tests, typically blood tests that check for prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels. Those with high levels of PSA in their blood are at increased risk for developing prostate cancer. Diagnosis requires a biopsy of the prostate.

[2] Prostate cancer
Medical imaging is performed to look for cancer that has spread outside the prostate. Based on the Gleason score, PSA levels, and imaging results, a cancer case is assigned a stage 1 to 4. A higher stage signifies a more advanced, more dangerous disease. These are managed with active surveillance, monitoring the tumor with regular tests to ensure it has not grown.

[3] Prostatitis
Nomenclature: The term prostatitis refers in its strictest sense to histological (microscopic) inflammation of the tissue of the prostate gland, although historically the term has loosely been used as a rubric to describe a set of quite different conditions. To try to remedy this, the National Institutes of Health (NIH) devised a new classification system in 1999.

[4] Prostatitis
Classification: According to the 1999 National Institute of Health (NIH) Classification, there are four categories of prostatitis:

- Category I: Acute prostatitis (bacterial)
- Category II: Chronic bacterial prostatitis
- Category III: Chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome (CP/CPPS), Pelvic Myoneuropathy
Subdivisions of IIIa (inflammatory) and IIIb (non-inflammatory) exist based on levels of pus cells in expressed prostatic secretions, but these subcategories are of limited use clinically
- Category IV: Asymptomatic inflammatory prostatitis

[5] Which blood test results would most indicate further testing for cancer?
Answers > Answer (score 4): Same PSA, same pathology, but now your patient is a man identical to the first example, except he is now 80 years old. It is in fact much more probable that you will get an altered result and that he will in fact have prostate cancer. However, it's pretty futile to check his PSA because even if it was through the roof and he did in fact have cancer, at that age the benefit of actually making the diagnosis and treating him more likely than not will be outweighed by the cost of treatment (speaking both in terms of money and quality of life).

In short. Yes, there are such a thing as screening tests. Yes, they are great tools if employed judiciously. No, there are no catch-all batteries of tests that could detect cancer in healthy individuals in a cost-effective way.

units.question: Tell me what to keep in the car before driving during a winter storm.
units.gold: Carry an emergency car kit: an ice scraper and shovel, cat litter or sand for traction, water and snacks, extra warm clothing, jumper cables, a first aid kit with any needed medicines and a pocketknife, a battery radio with flashlight and spare batteries, emergency flares or distress flags, and waterproof matches with a can to melt snow for water. Winter storms also bring frostbite, hypothermia, icy roads, power failures and carbon monoxide risks from heaters, so have a family plan and CO detector at home.
rubric: Lists traction aids: shovel, ice scraper, cat litter or sand
Lists survival basics: water, snacks, warm clothes, first aid kit
Lists jumper cables, radio, flashlight and batteries, flares
Mentions waterproof matches and a can to melt snow
Penalize: advising running the engine in a snow-blocked exhaust situation as safe
units.answer: Keep a full tank of gas, jumper cables, sand, a flashlight, warm clothes, blankets, bottled water, and non-perishable snacks in your car during a winter storm [6].

[1] Should I lease a 2nd car to replace my 12-yr old car?
Tags: car, auto-leasing That keeps her happy and I have peace of mind since she drives our baby to the daycare apart from commute to her work (~10 Km one way). I am thinking of selling my car NOW, so I can hopefully get $2,000 from it (if I use it for another winter, I expect it to only be $1,000), then lease a 2014 Hyundai Accent base model (manual transmission, no aircon) for $200/month 36-months. Or should I just drive my current car for another year until it breaks down (I still would need to buy winter tires though)?

[2] Wikivoyage: Iowa
Stay safe > Severe weather > Winter storms: While perhaps neither as cold nor as windy as the Dakotas, Iowa winters can still be brutal. Frequent heavy snow storms are possible throughout the winter and even occasionally into April. Most major highways are well maintained, but driving on country roads in the wake of a winter storm can be nerve-racking to say the least. If you choose to travel in winter, keep yourself informed about local weather and road conditions through television, radio, and/or the Iowa DOT website.

[3] Wikivoyage: South Dakota
Stay safe > Severe weather > Winter storms: South Dakota is infamous for its brutal winter storms. Blizzards and freak snow squalls are not uncommon in either of the Dakotas during the winter months. As with any severe weather situation, keep yourself up to date on the latest weather conditions if you are planning to travel to or through the state during the winter season.

[4] Solo-Driving from Florida to New York During the Winter
Answers > Answer (score 6): You almost-certainly will not see ice or snow on this route until past New York City unless you literally drive during a snow storm, which would be rare for that time of year, or if you drive immediately after a large snow storm, which would be rarer still. And heavy use itself can keep roads warmer than the surroundings, preventing much in the way of accumulation.

[5] Should I lease a 2nd car to replace my 12-yr old car?
Answers > Answer (score 4, accepted): Looking purely at the numbers, it will cost you $200/month to lease a Hyundai Accent. That's a cost of $2400/year. If you hold on to your Mazda Protege for another year, it costs you $1000. Now, you say you need new winter tyres. So, your questions are twofold: 1. How much will winter tyres cost? 2. How much will these tyres add to the value of your Protege, when it comes to selling them? Assuming the answers are "less than $1400" and "$0", it makes more financial sense to hold on to your Protege for one more year.

Of course, there are other considerations. A new vehicle is likely to be more reliable, while your Protege may break down over the next year. And most people would recommend you buy rather than lease a vehicle. Or you may want to consider selling the Protege and picking up a second-hand vehicle rather than buying or leasing a new car.

[6] US government: Winter Weather (Ready.gov) (cited)
How to Protect Yourself from Winter Weather > In Case of Emergency: Be prepared for winter weather at home, at work and in your car. Create an emergency supply kit for your car. Include jumper cables, sand, a flashlight, warm clothes, blankets, bottled water and non-perishable snacks. Keep a full tank of gas.

motorist ahead of you, and allow extra time to reach your
destination. Avoid sudden braking or acceleration, and be especially
cautious on hills or when making turns. Make sure your car is
winterized and in good working order.

&&

units.question: Why can't heat flow by itself from a cold object to a warmer one, and how did Clausius and Kelvin each phrase this rule?
units.gold: This is the second law of thermodynamics: in a closed system, entropy (disorder) increases, so differences in temperature, pressure and density tend to even out. Clausius stated it as heat cannot by itself pass from a colder to a hotter body; equivalently, no device can do nothing except move heat from a cooler to a hotter body. Kelvin's equivalent version says it is impossible for the only result of a process to be turning heat taken from a constant-temperature source entirely into work. The law describes likely behaviour of large systems.
rubric: Second law: entropy in a closed/isolated system increases
Clausius: heat cannot of itself pass from colder to hotter body
Kelvin: cannot convert heat from one constant-temperature source wholly into work as the only result
Applies to large systems (statistical)
Penalize: saying the law forbids refrigerators or heat pumps outright, or swapping hot and cold
units.answer: Heat cannot flow spontaneously from a cold to a warmer object because it tends to flow from higher to lower temperature. Clausius stated this as his "second law of thermodynamics," and Kelvin formulated it as his "zeroth law of thermodynamics." [2]
units.sources:
[1] Kelvin's circulation theorem
The differential operator D {\displaystyle \mathrm {D} } is a substantial (material) derivative moving with the fluid particles. Stated more simply, this theorem says that if one observes a closed contour at one instant, and follows the contour over time (by following the motion of all of its fluid elements), the circulation over the two locations of this contour remains constant.

[2] Non-Drug Pain Management (cited)
Pain relievers are medicines that reduce or relieve pain. There are many pain medicines, each with advantages and risks. Some are over-the-counter (OTC) medicines. Others are stronger medicines, which are available by prescription. The most powerful prescription pain relievers are opioids. They are very effective, but people who take them are at risk of addiction and overdose.

Because of the side effects and risks of pain relievers, you may want to try non-drug treatments first. If you need to take medicines, doing some non-drug treatments may allow you to take a lower dose.

What are some non-drug treatments for pain?

Many non-drug treatments can help with pain. It is important to check with your health care provider before trying any of them:

[3] Non-Drug Pain Management (cited)
- Acupuncture involves stimulating acupuncture points. These are specific points on your body. There are different acupuncture methods. The most common one involves inserting thin needles through the skin. Others include using pressure, electrical stimulation, and heat. Acupuncture is based on the belief that qi (vital energy) flows through the body along paths, called meridians. Practitioners believe that triggering the acupuncture points can rebalance the qi. Research suggests that acupuncture can help manage certain pain conditions.
- Biofeedback techniques use electronic devices to measure body functions such as breathing and heart rate. This teaches you to be more aware of your body functions so you can learn to control them. For example, a biofeedback device may show you measurements of your muscle tension. By watching how these measurements change, you can become more aware of when your muscles are tense and learn to relax them.
