For example, a biofeedback device may show you measurements of your muscle tension. By watching how these measurements change, you can become more aware of when your muscles are tense and learn to relax them.

[2] Non-Drug Pain Management (cited)
Pain relievers are medicines that reduce or relieve pain. There are many pain medicines, each with advantages and risks. Some are over-the-counter (OTC) medicines. Others are stronger medicines, which are available by prescription. The most powerful prescription pain relievers are opioids. They are very effective, but people who take them are at risk of addiction and overdose.

Because of the side effects and risks of pain relievers, you may want to try non-drug treatments first. If you need to take medicines, doing some non-drug treatments may allow you to take a lower dose.

What are some non-drug treatments for pain?

Many non-drug treatments can help with pain. It is important to check with your health care provider before trying any of them:

[3] Kelvin's circulation theorem
The differential operator D {\displaystyle \mathrm {D} } is a substantial (material) derivative moving with the fluid particles. Stated more simply, this theorem says that if one observes a closed contour at one instant, and follows the contour over time (by following the motion of all of its fluid elements), the circulation over the two locations of this contour remains constant.

units.question: I keep reading that the Standard Model is incomplete. What exactly can't it explain, and how do physicists fill that gap?
units.gold: The Standard Model is the main theory of particles and fundamental forces. It explains three of the four fundamental forces (electromagnetism, the weak interaction and the strong interaction) very well, but it cannot explain gravity. To describe the whole universe, physicists combine it with general relativity, the separate theory of gravity; together they are the most accepted explanation of how the universe works. Theoretical particle physicists keep working on improved theories, many of which predict particles not yet discovered.
rubric: Explains three of four forces (electromagnetic, weak, strong)
Cannot explain gravity
Combined with general relativity
Ongoing theoretical work; predicted undiscovered particles
Penalize: claiming the Standard Model explains gravity or that it has been replaced
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
The Standard Model doesn't explain why there's more matter than anti-matter, gravity's role in the universe, or dark matter. Physicists use extensions and theories like supersymmetry to address these gaps.
units.sources:
[1] Physics beyond the Standard Model
Another problem lies within the mathematical framework of the Standard Model itself: the Standard Model is inconsistent with that of general relativity, and one or both theories break down under certain conditions, such as spacetime singularities like the Big Bang and black hole event horizons.

[2] Standard Model
Since then, proof of the top quark (1995), the tau neutrino (2000), and the Higgs boson (2012) have added further credence to the Standard Model. In addition, the Standard Model has predicted with great accuracy the various properties of weak neutral currents and the W and Z bosons. Although the Standard Model is believed to be theoretically self-consistent and has demonstrated some success in providing experimental predictions, it leaves some physical phenomena unexplained and so falls short of being a complete theory of fundamental interactions.

[3] Standard Model
For example, it does not fully explain why there is more matter than anti-matter, incorporate the full theory of gravitation as described by general relativity, or account for the universe's accelerating expansion as possibly described by dark energy. The model does not contain any viable dark matter particle that possesses all of the required properties deduced from observational cosmology. The Standard Model without modifications also does not incorporate neutrino oscillations and their non-zero masses, but extensions have been proposed that can account for these features.

[4] Physics beyond the Standard Model
Physics beyond the Standard Model (BSM) is the theoretical developments needed to explain the deficiencies of the Standard Model, such as the inability to explain the fundamental parameters of the Standard Model, the strong CP problem, neutrino oscillations, matter–antimatter asymmetry, and the nature of dark matter and dark energy.

[5] V-chamber vs trapezoid construction
Answers > Answer (score 11, accepted): Other manner of testing could be, completely or in part, based on simple number crunching and in that case it would be difficult to really account for construction unless they do so presuming a "fudge factor" dependent on it (its up to you in this case to decide if this kind of testing is of any value in making a choice between models).

Answers > Answer (score 4): If aviation authorities have mandated inspections of all airplanes with a specific engine model, I suspect they may actually have more merit to claim extraordinary circumstances in this case. This brings it closer to "hidden manufacturing defect", which has been ruled to be extraordinary circumstances. The fact that aviation authorities have mandated the inspection may also be seen as providing the "external" in "unpredictable, unavoidable and external ".

However, you should still ask to see some form of evidence of these mandated inspections before you buy their explanation.

If you give up on trying to argue with Norwegian, you could always try to contact a claim agency specializing in EC261 claims and present your case to them. If they don't think you have a good case they probably will not pursue it, but there's not much harm in trying and if they do agree to pursue it you'll get most of the compensation with a minimum of effort.

units.question: Explain how cosmogony differs from cosmology, and why science still cannot describe the very first instant of the universe.
units.gold: Cosmogony is any theory of how the universe (or things like the Solar System or the Earth-Moon system) originated; cosmology studies the universe in general and can do so without asking about its origin. The leading scientific account is the Big Bang, in which the universe began as an expanding singularity. Science cannot yet model the earliest moments, the Planck time, because there is no testable theory of quantum gravity, although string theory, M theory and loop quantum cosmology offer ideas. Myths offer other cosmogonies.
rubric: Cosmogony = theories of origin; cosmology = study of universe generally
Big Bang from a singularity is the accepted model
Earliest moments (Planck time) unexplained
Reason: no testable theory of quantum gravity
Penalize: treating cosmogony and cosmology as the same field
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
Cosmogony refers to the ancient theories about the origin of the universe, while cosmology is the scientific study of the universe's structure, evolution, and fundamental laws. Science cannot describe the first instant of the universe because the extreme conditions involved (like infinite density and temperature) make it impossible to model with current physics.
units.sources:
[1] Cosmology
In the science of astronomy, physical cosmology is concerned with the study of the chronology of the universe, the observable universe's origin, its large-scale structures and dynamics, and the ultimate fate of the universe, including the physical laws that govern these areas. Physical cosmology is a sub-branch of astronomy that is concerned with the universe as a whole.

[2] Can you make porridge out of P.A.N. harina?
Answers > Answer (score 2): You cannot make grits, because by definition, true hominy grits are treated with alkali which is what makes them different than plain cornmeal or polenta.

Searching for harina pan polenta indicates a variety of recipes are possible (most are in Spanish, so I cannot read them). However, it doesn't appear that a porridge type dish is the usual application for this product.

Still, the nature of the product indicates it should work, although the result may be slightly different in texture and flavor from more traditional Italian style polenta, since the harina PAN is precooked before being dried and ground. It should therefore cook up much faster than one made with regular corn meal, analogous to the difference between instant oatmeal and traditional outmeal.

[3] Can you make porridge out of P.A.N. harina?
Answers > Answer (score 2): There would be no single ratio of water to grain, however, as polenta can range from a thin porridge to a thick enough to cut into slices and fry. You will have to experiment to find the ratio that you like the best. I would suggest starting out at about 2:1 liquid to harina pan by volume.

[4] Where can I go to see the Earth is round?
(It occurs to me that there are definitely a lot of places you can get a similar effect by changing your observing position horizontally rather than vertically. The problem with these is that you necessarily have to move horizontally a much bigger distance than is required in this "vertical observing platform" scenario. This makes it less convincing, even if you're in a car or something and so it doesn't take much time. It's less convincing because necessarily there's a lot of other things changing about your view at the same time which are distracting. You might also start worrying about atmospheric changes as you move, etc.)

units.question: How is one joule defined in mechanics, and how does it relate to the watt?
units.gold: The joule (J) is the SI unit of energy, named after the English physicist James Prescott Joule. In classical mechanics, 1 J is the energy transferred when a force of 1 newton acts on an object over a distance of 1 metre (1 J = 1 N x 1 m, or 1 kg m2/s2). Power is linked to it through the watt: one watt is one joule of energy transferred per second. In electricity, 1 J is the work done when 1 ampere flows through 1 ohm of resistance for one second.
rubric: SI unit of energy named after James Prescott Joule
1 J = 1 N x 1 m
1 W = 1 J per second
Penalize: calling the joule a unit of power or of force
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
One joule is the energy required to move a mass of one kilogram one meter, and one watt is the power equivalent to one joule per second.
units.sources:
[1] Joule
The joule ( JOOL, or JOWL; symbol: J) is the unit of energy in the International System of Units (SI). In terms of SI base units, one joule corresponds to one kilogram-metre squared per second squared (1 J = 1 kg⋅m2⋅s−2). One joule is equal to the amount of work done when a force of one newton displaces a body through a distance of one metre in the direction of that force. It is also the energy dissipated as heat when an electric current of one ampere passes through a resistance of one ohm for one second.

[2] Watt
The watt (symbol: W) is the unit of power or radiant flux in the International System of Units (SI), equal to 1 joule per second or 1 kg⋅m2⋅s−3. It is used to quantify the rate of energy transfer. The watt is named in honor of James Watt (1736–1819), an 18th-century Scottish inventor, mechanical engineer, and chemist who in 1776 improved the Newcomen engine with his own steam engine, which became fundamental for the Industrial Revolution.

[3] How do I adjust cooking time for an under-powered microwave?
Answers > Answer (score 7, accepted): 1100 Watt means 1100 Joules per second (energy over time). 1100 Watt over a period of 240 seconds therefore is 264000 Joules. To deliver 264000 Joules of energy with only 800 Watt takes 330 seconds (5.5 minutes), as you expected.

As KatieK noticed, there are some additional concerns. A good recipe will tell you to let the cooked product stand for a while. This allows heat diffusion, so all those Joules of heat will be distributed well. But if you cook at lower power, then the heat will already be diffused more. I.e. at lower power, you don't need to rest the product as long.

Another difference might be that you're not just heating the product, but you're relying on a secondary effect such as killing germs. For that, you'll need to have the entire product above a critical temperature for a certain time. This in general means that you don't need to adjust the times as much as you'd expect by the simple formula.

[4] How do I adjust cooking time for an under-powered microwave?
Answers > Answer (score 7, accepted): On the other hand, a warm product will lose heat to the environment over time. I.e. not all of those 264000 Joules will stay in the product you're heating. And with more time spent at medium temperatures, there's more heat loss in a low-powered microwave.

[5] Double Mariner Mechanical Advantage
Answers > Answer (score 9): TLDR:
This is a very common setup here and intuitively I always thought it was 4:1. So I needed to check more rigorously and the result is: Petzl made their homework, it is 7:1. Let me try to explain (my handwritten notes are unpublishable...).

The following derivation is (hopefully) rigorous, but as it is only text and some formulas it is potentially not very helpful to get an understanding of the system. Refer to QuantumBrick's answer with pretty pictures for that and skip to the last paragraph of this answer for some real-world information.

[6] How do I calculate how many watts of energy I need when camping?
Answers > Answer (score 9): Power (watts) = Voltage (volts) * Current (amps)

or

Current (amps) = Power (watts) / Voltage (volts)

units.question: I'm curious why the Atacama in Chile gets almost no rain and how people there still manage to collect water.
units.gold: The Atacama in northern Chile is one of the driest places on Earth; some parts get under 25 mm of rain per decade and some have had none for over 400 years. Mountains to the east and the ocean to the west create a rain shadow, and the cold Humboldt Current from Antarctica chills the coastal air so it cannot hold moisture: mostly fog reaches land, not rain. People 'harvest' this fog with plastic sheets that let droplets drip into pans, giving water for crops and drinking. Despite the dryness, temperatures are mild, about 0-30 C.
rubric: Rain shadow from mountains east and ocean west
Cold Humboldt Current keeps moisture as fog
Fog harvesting with plastic sheets and pans
Some areas no rain for 400+ years; mild temperatures
Penalize: saying the Atacama is the hottest desert or that it is in Peru only
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
The Atacama Desert is one of the driest places on Earth, with little to no rain due to its location in a rain shadow. People there manage to collect water by using desalination plants and collecting rainwater in reservoirs.
units.sources:
[1] Atacama Desert
The Atacama Desert (Spanish: Desierto de Atacama [ataˈkama]) is a desert plateau on the Pacific coast of South America, stretching along a 1,600-kilometre-long (1,000-mile) strip of land in northern Chile, west of the Andes. The Atacama is the driest non-polar desert in the world and the largest fog desert on Earth.

[2] Atacama Desert
Extreme aridity results from its position between two mountain chains—the Andes and the Chilean Coast Range—of sufficient height to block moisture from both the Pacific and Atlantic oceans, creating a two-sided rain shadow. 6 in) per year, and some weather stations in the desert have never recorded rain.

[3] What are possible trekking routes in the Atacama region in Chile in mid April?
Answers > Answer (score 3): Hiking in Northern Chile is difficult because it is a high desert with practically no water.

A possible alternative is to rent a good 4x4 truck in Arica, fill it up with water, food, and fuel for several days and explore the area around Putre (on the border with Peru and Bolivia). If you go solo, bring extra spare tires and a satellite phone (for emergencies) - this is very very remote country.

The landscapes are amazing: cactus forests, geisers, volcanoes, high alti-planos, etc.

We did exactly this back in 2015; for photos see https://www.flickr.com/photos/brijsman/albums/72157661317255934

[4] How bad is the rainy season in the Peru highlands?
Has anyone done a similar trip in that season? Do you think it would be one of those miserable "all-of-your-belongings-are-drenched-and-there-is-no-chance-to-get-them-dry-because-it-just-keeps-raining-and-raining" trips, or is there still enough sunshine to make it enjoyable? I have seen that a lot of people still do the Inca trail in the rainy season. Surely it must not be that bad?

Also, what are the chances of finding a hostel or cheap hostel on the spot when arriving to a new city?

[5] How correct is my intuition that tap water is safer in the mountains than in cities?
Is there any basis in fact for this intuition? Are there any reasons, or evidence, that water up in the mountains is likely to be in any way safer and cleaner than that in towns and cities, given broadly similar water purification standards and technologies?

Off the top of my head I'm thinking it could simply be easier to clean in the first place due to being fresher and more quickly replenished, less exposed to pollution of various kinds, etc.

units.question: Why did forecasters find Hurricane Vince of 2005 so surprising, and what did its rain mean for Spain?
units.gold: Vince formed in October 2005 in the northeast Atlantic near the Azores and Madeira, over water colder than 24 C, below the roughly 26.5 C normally needed for tropical storms, so forecasters thought cyclones could not exist there. It still developed an eye and became a weak Category 1 hurricane, then weakened and hit Spain near Huelva as a tropical depression, possibly the first such storm there since 1842. Spain was in a record drought, so the 25-50 mm of rain was welcomed and helped refill reservoirs, though it caused minor floods. No one died.
rubric: Formed over water colder than usual (below 26.5 C threshold)
Became a hurricane far east near Madeira/Azores
Landfall in Spain (Huelva) as a tropical depression
Rain eased a record drought; minor flooding, no deaths
Penalize: saying Vince caused major damage or deaths
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
Forecasters found Hurricane Vince surprising because it weakened rapidly and moved away from the U.S. east coast, contrary to expectations. The storm brought heavy rain to Spain, causing flooding and disrupting travel.
units.sources:
[1] Looking for hurricane advice and sources
Answers > Answer (score 7, accepted): In my opinion (!) you should be fine. Yes there are alarming stories as you mention (eg) but these are offshore and, now it seems, the Florida coastline.

There are were minute by minute updates here.

Strength has dropped to Category 2 (~100mph wind) from Category 4 (~140 mph wind). The Express seems to have lost interest but at present The Weather Channel has news. The eye of the storm is approximately 1,200 miles from Texas and moving away.

Strength has dropped to Category 1 (~75mph wind) and Matthew is moving away from USA.

Weather (all types) warnings and watches here.

It is the nature of hurricanes in that area to dissipate in strength quite quickly once they move over land. There are no signs at present of any significant threat to Texas. The most to fear at present is I think flight disruption, but since not flying in through Miami for example I am confident the airlines would cope with minimum disturbance to passengers flying in to George Bush Intercontinental from abroad.

[2] Looking for hurricane advice and sources
Answers > Answer (score 3): -
BE AWARE OF THE CALM EYE !! I cannot believe this vital information is often left out. In contrast to normal European storms cyclones have the "eye of the storm", a small and very calm center which has often open sky, but it is also surrounded by the most intense winds. People hear the storm howling and suddenly very rapidly the storm is calming down. They think the storm is over and go out when in reality they are in the eye. The back section now surprises them in full force, often killing them. So hurricanes are quieting down over hours, not minutes. If it stops, it is not over, it is simply the eye, DO NOT LEAVE COVER.

units.question: Describe what happened at Lindisfarne in 793 and what the monks eventually did with Saint Cuthbert's remains.
units.gold: Lindisfarne, a tidal island off Northumberland, held a monastery founded by Saint Aidan around 635. In 793 Vikings raided it, destroying the church; the attack shocked Christian Europe and is often taken as the start of the Viking age of raids. The monks eventually left the island and carried Saint Cuthbert's body with them; it now lies in Durham Cathedral. The priory was later re-founded as a Benedictine house in Norman times and lasted until Henry VIII dissolved it in 1536.
rubric: Viking raid in 793
Seen as start of the Viking raids age
Monks fled, taking Cuthbert's body
Body now at Durham Cathedral
Penalize: placing Cuthbert's remains at Lindisfarne today or dating the raid to another century
units.answer: In 793, the Vikings raided Lindisfarne, damaging the abbey and stealing the Gospels' bejeweled cover [1]. The monks eventually reburied Saint Cuthbert's remains, which were discovered in 1861 and later moved to a new site in Durham Cathedral.
units.sources:
[1] Wikivoyage: Lindisfarne (cited)
Understand: A monastery was founded here in 634 AD by Aidan from Iona; its most famous abbot or bishop was St Cuthbert 684-686. In 793 the Vikings raided the abbey, tearing off the Gospels' bejewelled cover, and also raided Jarrow. It's believed these raiders were Norwegians bent on revenge, as monks from Lindisfarne and Jarrow had Christianised their homeland and torn down pagan shrines. Amongst those monks was St Cuthbert, who'd been dead for a century, but everyone marvelled at what good shape he was in.

The Spanish retook Saint Martin in 1633, but the Dutch continued to assert their claims. Saint Martin: The Spanish finally relinquished the island to the French and Dutch, who divided it between themselves in 1648. Saint Martin: The border frequently fluctuated over the next 200 years because of friction between the two countries, with the French eventually holding the greater portion of the island (about 61%).

units.question: My ancestors came from Ulster. Why did the English government settle Scots and English people there in the 1600s, and what conditions did those settlers have to meet?
units.gold: From 1606 the English Crown organised the Plantation of Ulster to stop resistance in the province that had most opposed English rule. After the Nine Years' War and the Flight of the Earls, land held by the O'Neill and O'Donnell chieftains (about half a million acres) was confiscated and given to colonists. Settlers, the 'British tenants', had to be English-speaking Protestants, mostly Presbyterian Scots and Church of England English. Undertakers received estates of about 1,000 acres, had to build fortified houses or bawns and take only English or Scottish tenants.
rubric: Aim: secure loyalty of the most rebellious province
Land taken from O'Neill and O'Donnell after Flight of the Earls
Settlers had to be English-speaking and Protestant
Undertakers: ~1,000 acres, fortified houses, only British tenants
Penalize: describing the settlers as Catholic or the plantation as voluntary Irish migration
units.answer:

The English government settled Scots and English people in Ulster during the 1600s to expand their colonial presence, as Ulster was part of the Kingdom of England. These settlers had to meet conditions such as paying land taxes and agreeing to loyalty oaths.

United Kingdom: background: The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland was created when the Kingdoms of England and Scotland -- which previously had been distinct states under a single monarchy -- were joined under the 1707 Acts of Union. United Kingdom: The island of Ireland was incorporated under the 1800 Acts of Union, while Wales had been part of the Kingdom of England since the 16th century. The United Kingdom has historically played a leading role in developing parliamentary democracy and in advancing literature and science.

[2] Isle of Man
Isle of Man: background: The Isle of Man was part of the Norwegian Kingdom of the Hebrides until the 13th century, when it was ceded to Scotland. Isle of Man: The isle came under English lordship in the 14th century before being purchased by the British Government in 1765. Isle of Man: Current concerns include reviving the almost extinct Manx Gaelic language. The Isle of Man is a British Crown dependency, which makes it a self-governing possession of the British Crown that is not part of the UK. Isle of Man: The UK Government, however, remains constitutionally responsible for its defense and international representation.

units.question: How did the Fatimid Caliphate lose its lands and finally come to an end?
units.gold: The Fatimid state (909-1171), a Shia Ismaili caliphate ruled from Cairo after 969, shrank in stages. In the 1040s its North African governors, the Zirids, declared independence and became Sunni, which triggered the Banu Hilal invasions. After about 1070 Seljuk Turks and then the Crusaders took its Levant and Syrian holdings, leaving only Egypt. As the regime decayed in the 1160s, the Zengid ruler Nur ad-Din sent his general Shirkuh to seize Egypt in 1169; after Shirkuh's death his nephew Saladin took over and founded the Ayyubid dynasty, ending Fatimid rule.
rubric: Zirids broke away in the 1040s
Seljuks and Crusaders took Levant/Syria; only Egypt left
Shirkuh seized Egypt 1169 for Nur ad-Din
Saladin founded the Ayyubid dynasty; end 1171
Penalize: saying the Mongols or Ottomans ended the Fatimids
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
The Fatimid Caliphate lost its lands due to internal strife and external pressures, including the Abbasid Caliphate's collapse and foreign raids. It eventually ended when the caliphate was overthrown and its territories were seized by other powers.
units.sources:
[1] Fatimid Caliphate
The Fatimids were acknowledged as the rightful imams by different Isma'ili communities as well as by denominations in many other Muslim lands and adjacent regions. Starting in Ifriqiya under the Aghlabids, who were themselves nominally under the Abbasid Caliphate, the Fatimids eventually overthrew both, and extended their rule across the Mediterranean coast, ultimately making Egypt the centre of their caliphate. At its height, the caliphate included—in addition to Egypt—varying areas of the Maghreb, Sicily, the Levant, and the Hejaz.

[2] Fatimid conquest of Egypt
By the 960s, however, while the Fatimids had consolidated their rule and grown stronger, the Abbasid Caliphate had collapsed, and the Ikhshidid regime was facing prolonged crisis: foreign raids and a severe famine were compounded by the death in 968 of the strongman Abu al-Misk Kafur.

[3] Fatimid conquest of Egypt
Troops of the Fatimid Caliphate under the general Jawhar captured Egypt, then ruled by the autonomous Ikhshidid dynasty in the name of the Abbasid Caliphate, in 969. The Fatimids launched repeated invasions of Egypt soon after coming to power in Ifriqiya (modern Tunisia and eastern Algeria) in 909, but failed against the still-strong Abbasid Caliphate.

[4] Jordan
Jordan: background (3): In 1967, Jordan lost the West Bank and East Jerusalem to Israel in the Six-Day War but retained administrative claims to the West Bank until 1988, when King HUSSEIN permanently relinquished Jordanian claims to the West Bank in favor of the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO). Jordan: King HUSSEIN signed a peace treaty with Israel in 1994, after Israel and the PLO signed the Oslo Accords in 1993. Jordanian kings continue to claim custodianship of the Muslim holy sites in Jerusalem by virtue of their Hashemite heritage as descendants of the Prophet Mohammad and agreements with Israel and Jerusalem-based religious and Palestinian leaders.

[5] Syria
Syria: background: After World War I, France acquired a mandate over the northern portion of the former Ottoman Empire province of Syria. Syria: The French administered the area until granting it independence in 1946. Syria: The new country lacked political stability and experienced a series of military coups. Syria united with Egypt in 1958 to form the United Arab Republic. In 1961, the two entities separated, and the Syrian Arab Republic was reestablished. In the 1967 Arab-Israeli War, Syria lost control of the Golan Heights region to Israel. During the 1990s, Syria and Israel held occasional, albeit unsuccessful, peace talks over its return.

units.question: Explain how banks manipulated the Libor rate and what reforms Britain introduced afterwards.
units.gold: Libor was an average interest rate built from what major London banks said they paid to borrow from each other. Banks falsely adjusted their submissions to profit on trades and sometimes to look more creditworthy; about 350 trillion dollars of derivatives were tied to it, along with mortgages and student loans. Barclays settlements in June 2012 exposed the fraud. The Wheatley Review then recommended basing submissions on real transactions, keeping records, publishing individual submissions after three months and criminal penalties; the Financial Services Act 2012 put Libor under UK regulation and made false benchmark statements a crime.
rubric: Banks falsified rate submissions for profit/creditworthiness
Exposed by Barclays settlements in 2012
Wheatley Review: real transactions, records, delayed publication, criminal sanctions
Financial Services Act 2012: regulation and criminal offence
Penalize: saying Libor was set by the Bank of England or that no legal reform followed
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
LIBOR was manipulated by banks to benefit themselves, with lower rates favored by borrowers and higher rates favored by lenders. Britain introduced the Alternative Reference Rate (ARR), now called LIBOR, to replace it, aiming to reduce manipulation and improve transparency.
units.sources:
[1] LIBOR Reform creates Winners and Losers
Tags: interest-rate, markets, market-indexes One phrase I heard of the reform to move away from LIBOR is that it would create winners and losers.

[2] LIBOR Reform creates Winners and Losers
Answers > Answer (score 2, accepted): The reason that LIBOR is going away is because it was susceptible to manipulation by its member banks. So whether you're a "winner" or a "loser" depends on what the banks actually did and how it affected you. If the banks artificially kept LIBOR rates low, then borrowers won (because they paid less interest) and lenders/investors lost (because they received less return on their investments). It's hard to say if either actually happened, since there's not a good way to know what rates should have been to know if they were being manipulated.

After reading some other posts here, I realise that Ive done exactly what I shoudn't have - liquidated savings just at the time of the visa application. I do however have emails from the broker saying this is the sale amount, in addition to the earlier statements I mentioned.

Answers > Answer (score 9): In your case, the irregular deposits came from transferring funds from another account which belongs to you. This can be overcome by simply including an explanatory note along with the other statements such that the debits from one account agree with the credits in the other account. This makes the provenance of the funds clear.

In the comments below your question, you ask if you should compound the problems by lying. At the moment, your history now contains a refusal suggesting credibility issues. units.question: Why do Galapagos tortoises on different islands have different shell shapes, and how did that matter for Darwin?
units.gold: Galapagos giant tortoise populations vary with their island's habitat. On islands with humid highlands, tortoises are bigger with domed shells and short necks; on islands with dry lowlands, they are smaller with 'saddleback' shells and long necks. Charles Darwin noticed these differences during the Beagle's second voyage in 1835, and they helped him develop his theory of evolution. The species is the largest living tortoise and is still listed as vulnerable.
rubric: Humid highlands: larger, domed shells, short necks
Dry lowlands: smaller, saddleback shells, long necks
Darwin saw this on the Beagle voyage (1835)
Helped him develop the theory of evolution
Penalize: reversing which habitat gives which shell or attributing the observation to Wallace
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
Galapagos tortoises on different islands have varied shell shapes due to environmental factors, such as island climate and vegetation. These differences were important for Darwin as they supported his theory of evolution by showing how species adapt to their environments.
units.sources:
[1] Galápagos tortoise
For example, a captive individual, Harriet, lived for at least 175 years. Spanish explorers, who discovered the islands in the 16th century, named them after the Spanish galápago, meaning "tortoise". Galápagos tortoises are native to seven of the Galápagos Islands. On islands with humid highlands and abundant low vegetation, the tortoises are larger, with domed shells and short necks; on islands with dry lowlands and less ground-level vegetation, the tortoises are smaller, with "saddleback" shells and long necks.

[2] Galápagos tortoise
Charles Darwin's observations of these differences on the second voyage of the Beagle in 1835 contributed to the development of his theory of evolution. This decline was caused by overexploitation of the subspecies for meat and oil, habitat clearance for agriculture, and introduction of non-native animals to the islands, such as rats, goats, and pigs.

[3] Tortoise
8 centimetres (2. Several lineages of tortoises have independently evolved very large body sizes in excess of 100 kilograms (220 lb), including the Galapagos giant tortoise and the Aldabra giant tortoise. Tortoises are the longest-living land animals in the world, although the longest-living species of tortoise is a matter of debate.

[4] What breed is this very large, black, turtle/tortoise found in the Northeast United States?
I've heard that one difference between a turtle and a tortoise is that turtles fully immerse themselves in water, whereas tortoises spend most of their time on land, and drink at the edge without swimming. I'm not sure if that's true. My husband hasn't gone into those woods, so he doesn't know whether or not there's a pond or other body of water nearby.

What is the breed of this gorgeous creature? Is it a turtle or a tortoise? I'd also like to know some other things, such as approximate age; preferred diet; nesting habits; best place and time of year to see them; conservation status (some turtles in Massachusetts are protected or endangered); and any other interesting characteristics.

Click on pictures for closer view.

[5] Are these tracks in the mud tortoise/turtle tracks?
Tags: animal-identification, massachusetts, turtles, tortoises, animal-tracks

I was having a nice evening walk near one of the nature reservations in Andover MA, close to Tewksbury, when I've found such a footprint. I'm really sorry for image quality, though. So it's a wet, bog-like, piece of ground, two lanes of deep small holes (probably the actual footprints) - the distance between them is like 25-30 centimeters (10-12 inches) - and the ground in the middle looks like something was dragged. In the top left corner of a picture the ground seems to be pushed below, and the hole is filled with water.

I'm not from US, and have almost no idea about Massachusetts fauna, but to me it looks like a tortoise. It was lying on the ground, thinking it's slow thoughts - that's how the hole filled with water appeared - then it decided to do some action, got up and moved, dragging it's plastron upon the ground.

units.question: How do the microbes living in our bodies compare in number with our own cells, and are most of them harmful?
units.gold: The human microbiome is the community of bacteria, archaea, fungi and protozoa living on the skin, in the mouth, eyes and gut. People carry far more microbes than human cells: the body has about 100 trillion cells and roughly ten times as many microorganisms in the intestines alone. Most of these microbes have no known effect and some are useful; the normal flora usually cause no disease and may help health, though reducing gut flora can harm it. Some archaea in the gut produce methane.
rubric: Microbes outnumber human cells
About 100 trillion cells; ~10x as many gut microbes
Most have no known effect; some beneficial; normally not disease-causing
Includes bacteria, archaea, fungi, protozoa
Penalize: claiming most body microbes are pathogens
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
The microbes living in our bodies are vastly outnumbered by our own cells, with trillions of microbes versus billions of human cells. Most of these microbes are not harmful and play a role in maintaining our health.
units.sources:
[1] How does zinc oxide work?
Answers > Answer (score 5, accepted): Zinc oxide has a very slight antimicrobial effect, whilst having little to no impact on human cells.

This is more that the material is toxic to microbes than activating a body defence. It's the Zn^{2+} ions that have the property of being toxic to microbes.

Small particles are more effective. Ideally I'd recommend creams to provide an even distribution of zinc oxide to the surface you wish to recover. The cream itself should help by providing moisture to the site of the wound, or blister.

As a side note, you will be consuming amounts of zinc oxide in your food, so it's definitely not harmful to humans.

Further reading: https://aem.asm.org/content/77/7/2325 https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5940970/

[2] Are many viruses actually good for us?... maybe even essential to our survival?
Tags: virus, immune-system, disease-transmission, bacteria, influenza

We know that a very large proportion of bacteria are essential to our good health. Every other day we see press release about the microbiome, and its multitude of health implications. Is there something equivalent with viruses. Do we have a stealthy microvirome that is essential to our health?

We know a few things about viruses:

1.
Typically, the more successful ones are more contagious but also less lethal. A virus that is more lethal and kills its human host more readily essentially commits suicide by depleting its resources quickly (human host).

2.
Viruses kill a lot of bacteria.

3.
Viruses fight each other off, crowd each other out.

From the above, we can advance an hypothesis of what a smart virus would do:

a) It would be highly contagious, but be rather benign;

b) It would kill "bad" bacteria and not "good" ones;

c) It would crowd out all other viruses to colonize the human host most successfully.

units.question: Tell me how the original walkie-talkie differed from the handie-talkie that Motorola built during World War II.
units.gold: Both were Motorola two-way radios from World War II. The first walkie-talkie, the SCR-300, was so large it had to be worn as a backpack. The handie-talkie (HT), the AM SCR-536, could be held entirely in the hand but had much shorter range. The names are often mixed up today: strictly, 'walkie-talkie' meant the back-mounted set and 'handie-talkie' the hand-held one. Modern walkie-talkies are phone-sized push-to-talk radios.
rubric: SCR-300 walkie-talkie was a backpack set
SCR-536 handie-talkie was hand-held
Hand-held had much shorter range
Terms now often confused
Penalize: saying the walkie-talkie was invented after the war or by a company other than Motorola's team
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
The original walkie-talkie, developed during World War II, had a simpler design with a single antenna and a basic transmit/receive function. The later handie-talkie, built by Motorola, introduced a more compact and portable design with a speaker and microphone, and was used for military and public safety communication.
units.sources:
[1] Walkie-talkie
A walkie-talkie, more formally known as a handheld transceiver or handheld radio, is a hand-held, portable, two-way radio transceiver. Its development during the Second World War has been variously credited to Donald Hings, radio engineer Alfred J. Gross, and to Henryk Magnuski and engineering teams at Motorola. First used for infantry, similar designs were created for field artillery and tank units. After the war, walkie-talkies spread to public safety and eventually commercial and jobsite work.

[2] Walkie-talkie
Typical walkie-talkies resemble a telephone handset, with a speaker built into one end and a microphone in the other (in some devices the speaker is also used as the microphone) and an antenna mounted on the top of the unit. They are held up to the face to talk. A walkie-talkie is a half-duplex communication device. Multiple walkie-talkies use a single radio channel, and only one radio on the channel can transmit at a time, although any number can listen.

[3] Museums about Japan's World War II history
1. I want it to be honest about what Japan did in World War II. Japan would be fine, but I've heard that although some Japanese people attempt to build museums that are honest about World War II, sometimes politics makes things difficult for such museums.

[4] Museums about Japan's World War II history
What museums or the like are available?

[5] I am looking for a two way radio/device with constant contact
Answers > Answer (score 5, accepted): What you are looking for is a walkie-talkie / two-way radio / private mobile radio with voice control.

Normally, to communicate with a walkie-talkie, you need to press a transmit button. Some models, however, have voice-control: they will automatically start transmitting based on voice input. My friend and I used the Midland G7 XTR, that includes this feature. We did not use the voice control, so I don't know how well it works. We were quite worried about battery lifetimes, and wanted to prevent our walkie-talkies from transmitting without need (there are other sounds in nature besides our voice). In principle, though, walkie-talkie with voice control should be exactly what you need.

[6] Possible to transform (at least two) smartphones into walkie-talkie like devices?
Answers > Answer (score 12, accepted): The frequencies used by many 2 way radios have a much greater range than any of the frequencies used by cell phone. A walkie talkie using CB bands (11meter wavelengths), can send and receive signals up to 10 miles away under most conditions, and when using special features such as single sideband modulation, can reach 100s of miles at the right times of the day.

Don't try to use your cell phone for this, this is like the difference between using designer sneakers for ice climbing when you should be using yak tracks.

units.question: I'm visiting Manchester and wondered how its tram network started and how much it has expanded since.
units.gold: Manchester's railway termini were never joined, and a 1970s 'Picc-Vic' tunnel plan to link Piccadilly and Victoria was dropped as too costly. Metrolink was created instead by converting two British Rail lines, to Altrincham and to Bury, into light rail linked by on-street track through the city centre, with a branch to Piccadilly; it opened in 1992. Extensions to Eccles, Didsbury, Ashton, Oldham, Rochdale, MediaCityUK and the airport grew it from 37 km to 97 km with 99 stops, and the network is expected to double by 2040.
rubric: Picc-Vic tunnel abandoned over cost
Converted two British Rail lines (Altrincham, Bury)
Opened 1992
Grew from 37 km to 97 km, 99 stops
Penalize: describing Metrolink as an underground metro
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
The tram network in Manchester began in the 19th century and has expanded significantly since, with modern services now covering the city's major areas. The Metrolink system, including routes to Old Trafford, is part of this expanded network.

Get around > By tram: Manchester Metrolink trams all run through central Manchester via St Peters Square, Deansgate / Castlefield and Cornbrook, except for the yellow line. The lines then fan out: - light blue and orange lines west to Salford Quays, Media City and Eccles; and east to Piccadilly, Etihad Stadium and Ashton-under-Lyne. - yellow line starts at Piccadilly and joins the green line at Victoria then to Bury.

[3] Tram service to Old Trafford from Manchester Picadilly?
Tags: public-transport, manchester How frequent is the tram service from Manchester Piccadilly to Old Trafford and what are the charges?

[4] Wikivoyage: Manchester
Manchester is a vibrant, post-industrial gem at the heart of North West England. The city that used to be nicknamed 'Cottonopolis' (a reference to its most famous export) has hung up its clogs and, thanks to successive regeneration projects, is now a major centre for culture and commerce; seen by many as the capital of the north of England, and sometimes regarded as England's second city. The site of the world's oldest surviving passenger railway station and one of the birthplaces of socialism and the Industrial Revolution, Manchester remains at the vanguard of British culture and technology with a verve and a vibe of its own. This vivacious spirit is augmented by the city's two world-famous football clubs and large student population; whilst the mills have been swapped for Michelin stars and the warehouses for world-class shopping and museums, this is still a city that is very proud of its industrial past and of its influences on music and sport.

[5] Tram service to Old Trafford from Manchester Picadilly?
Answers > Answer (score 6): Note on locations

Note that the Metrolink stop named "Old Trafford" is for the Cricket Ground, not the Football Ground. For MUFC, you should get off the tram at Pomona, Exchange Quay, Old Trafford or, from 2020, Wharfside and walk from there. This question should be useful to you.

Tram Frequency

You can see Tram Frequencies for leaving Picadilly on this page fromm Metrolink (also possible to get them from other stops). Most services run every 12-13 minutes, although some run every 6 minutes during the day. On Match days, extra trams will be put on before kick off and after the final whistle. As you can pick between several different tram lines (see this map, once the work in St Peters Square has finished for the lines), you will probably normally have to wait no more than 3-4 minutes for a tram.

Pricing

[6] Tram service to Old Trafford from Manchester Picadilly?
Answers > Answer (score 6): You can use this tool provided by Metrolink to check the prices at the time you travel. Currently, the journey would cost you £3.00 for an off - peak (after 9:30) return from Picadilly to Exchange Quay. There are also options for singles, on peak tickets, and all day travel cards. There are machines that take (chip and pin) cards and cash on all platforms, and there is also a mobile app called GetMeThere that can be used to purchase tickets. It's also possible to load up an ITSO type card with tickets (Manchester's variant is branded "My GetMeThere", but for a tourist, this is not worth the bother.

units.question: Where does the name Google come from, and how does the company earn money from adverts?
units.gold: The name is a play on 'googol', the number 1 followed by 100 zeros, a word coined in 1937 by Milton Sirotta, nephew of mathematician Edward Kasner; it reflects the aim of making huge amounts of web content easy to find. The headquarters name, Googleplex, plays on the even larger googolplex. Google makes money through advertising: advertisers pay when people click their ads, so Google builds profiles from data such as Google Analytics to show ads to the people most likely to click.
rubric: Name from 'googol' (10^100)
Googleplex from 'googolplex'
Revenue from advertising, paid per click
Targeting uses profiles from data such as Google Analytics
Penalize: inventing a different origin for the name or saying Google earns mainly from subscriptions
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
The name "Google" comes from the word "googol," which refers to 10^100, a number representing a very large quantity. Google earns money primarily through advertising, where companies pay Google to place their ads on its search results.

[2] If a company reaches 100% market share, will the stock price stagnate?

Answers > Answer (score 262): This is clearly not the answer you’re looking for, but you went wrong by trying to pick stocks and time the market. It’s been shown to be a fool’s game.

Furthermore: if you picked several stocks, and think you did something wrong because one of them went down, then you have some rough days ahead of you. There will be long stretches where most or all of your stocks go down. Are you prepared for that, emotionally? It doesn’t sound like it.

[5] Where does Google Flights get its data from?
Answers > Answer (score 12, accepted): Google uses ITA Software's QPX software, which uses algorithms to combine and parse multiple sets of flight information from airlines. This includes any pricing and any other available data, which allows them to keep an up-to-date database that can be searched just like their search engine. This allows them to check against multiple different airlines for the various data that all of those programs like expedia and travelocity have access to. units.question: I just read Winesburg, Ohio. How did Sherwood Anderson go from businessman to writer, and why does he matter to later American authors?
units.gold: Anderson (1876-1941) left school at 14 to help support his family, served in the army, married and ran several businesses in Ohio. In November 1912 he had a mental breakdown, left his wife and children, and decided to become a creative writer, moving to Chicago and working in advertising and publishing. His first book, Windy McPherson's Son, came out in 1916, and Winesburg, Ohio, linked short stories about a small Ohio town, in 1919. He is credited with strongly influencing Hemingway, Faulkner and Steinbeck.
rubric: 1912 breakdown led him to quit business for writing
Moved to Chicago; worked in advertising
First book 1916; Winesburg, Ohio 1919 (short stories)
Influenced Hemingway, Faulkner, Steinbeck
Penalize: calling Winesburg, Ohio a single-plot novel set in Chicago or naming the wrong decade
units.answer: Sherwood Anderson started as a businessman and copywriter before becoming a writer [1]. His work, Winesburg, Ohio, is significant for its subjective portrayals and influence on later American literature.
units.sources:
[1] Sherwood Anderson (cited)
Sherwood Anderson (September 13, 1876 – March 8, 1941) was an American novelist and short story writer, known for subjective and self-revealing works. Self-educated, he rose to become a successful copywriter and business owner in Cleveland and Elyria, Ohio. In 1912, Anderson had a nervous breakdown that led him to abandon his business and family to become a writer. His most enduring work is the short-story sequence Winesburg, Ohio, which launched his career.

[2] Sherwood Anderson (cited)
Throughout the 1920s, Anderson published several short story collections, novels, memoirs, books of essays, and a book of poetry. Though his books sold reasonably well, his only bestseller was Dark Laughter (1925), a novel inspired by Anderson's time in the American army in Cuba, his residing in New Orleans during the 1920s, his employment as a factory worker and in advertising, and his life in the small-town midwest. Dark Laughter remains of contemporary interest with its Joyce-influenced shifting points of view.

[3] Can an author do book promotion on B1/B2 visa in USA?
Tags: usa, b1-b2-visas

Is an author permitted to stop by a few indie bookshops while doing a road trip in the USA to promote the author's self-published book? Would that be considered being paid by a USA entity?

It seems like a grey area. What if the author wasn't paid but their rep was. Would that work?

[4] Business travel to the United States for European company
EDIT 2: I am currently on my trip, and even though some contact information was outdated (e.g. address in the U.S.), at the airport (Pittsburgh) the process was really simple and was let through without any hassle.

I do confirm the issue about "working" vs. "doing business" as we shortly visited the Canadian side of Niagara Falls. On the way back, the officer asked us what we were doing in the U.S. and looked horrified at my colleague saying "working for an American Client". I saved the day, thanks to you guys, explaining that we were just there for business and our salaries were 100% from our company back in Germany.

units.question: Which is older, the Laetoli footprints or the Kabwe skull, and which kind of human relative does each one represent?
units.gold: The Laetoli footprints in Tanzania are far older: about 3.6 million years, left in volcanic ash by three individuals now assigned to Australopithecus afarensis, an upright-walking hominin with an ape-sized brain. The Kabwe (Broken Hill) skull from Zambia, found in 1921, is dated to about 324,000-274,000 years ago. It was first named Homo rhodesiensis, but most experts now place it within Homo heidelbergensis. So Laetoli is more than ten times older than Kabwe.

Laetoli prints attributed to Australopithecus afarensis
Kabwe skull about 324,000-274,000 years old
Kabwe: Homo rhodesiensis, now usually Homo heidelbergensis
Penalize: calling Kabwe older or assigning the footprints to Homo
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
The Laetoli footprints are older, dating back to around 3.6 million years, and represent Australopithecus afarensis. The Kabwe skull is younger, from about 2.5 million years, and represents Homo erectus.

[1] Consumption and Tuberculosis
Answers > Answer (score 3, accepted): Yes, TB can affect bones (in extrapulmonary or more precisely osteoarticular TB), but that form is relatively rare nowadays [even more so in the West], and even rarer for the sternum to be affected. On the other hand, it is one of the ways in which ancient skeletons (or mummies) were diagnosed with TB, but sometimes confirming by some other means (e.g. PCR), as noted in a 2013 review

Bone and joint tuberculosis (TB) is an ancient disease. Evidence of osteoarticular TB has been detected in Egyptian mummies [7, 22, 70], Iron Age remains from Asia [63, 64], and skeletons of Europeans living in the Middle Ages [23] by histological or polymerase chain reaction (PCR) study [70, 71]. [...]

Bone and joint TB currently accounts for 2.2–4.7 % of all TB cases in Europe and the USA and around 10–15 % of EPTB [extrapulmonary tuberculosis] cases [...], whereas in undeveloped countries, particularly Asia, the incidence of EPTB increases to 15–20 % [68].

[...]

Answers > Answer (score 3, accepted): TB is one of the most common causes of rib osteomyelitis. [...]

Tuberculosis of the sternum is rarely reported and accounts for 1.5 % of bone and joint TB cases.

And from a more [paleo]history oriented paper:

Paleopathological diagnosis of tuberculosis (TB) essentially relies on the identification of macroscopic lesions in the skeleton that can be related to different manifestations of TB.

Alas the rest of the paper discusses tuberculous meningitis and its identification from skull impressions.

Another paper on diagnosing ancient skeletons with TB notes that a criterion is:

lesions that are mainly destructive, producing cavitation into the cancellous bone

and on prevalence in older times:

data from the preantibiotic era indicate that about 5–7% of cases showed bone changes (Steinbock, 1976)

As far naming goes, according to Wikipedia, TB

was historically called consumption due to the weight loss.

So that popular name was not due to effects on bones.

units.question: I'm trying to understand why tar-pit asphalt and other fossil oils don't count as biomass even though they came from living things. How do the two compare?
units.gold: Tar pits form when buried decayed organic matter is turned into oil under pressure; the oil seeps up, its lighter parts evaporate and sticky asphalt remains, which can trap animals (La Brea has yielded over a million bones). Biomass, by contrast, is recently living material such as wood, crops or waste, which cycles carbon quickly: plants absorb it and release it again when they rot or burn. Fossil fuels are excluded from biomass because their carbon has been out of the carbon cycle for a very long time, so burning them adds carbon dioxide.

Biomass: recent living matter in the fast carbon cycle
Fossil fuels excluded because carbon long out of the cycle
Burning fossil fuels adds CO2
Penalize: calling asphalt a renewable biomass fuel
units.answer: Tar-pit asphalt and fossil oils are not considered biomass because they are man-made materials derived from non-living sources, whereas biomass refers to organic material from living organisms. The two differ in their origin and composition, with fossil fuels being non-renewable and synthetic, while biomass is renewable and organic. [1]
units.sources:
[1] Fossil fuel (cited)
The origin of fossil fuels is the anaerobic decomposition of buried dead organisms. The conversion from these organic materials to high-carbon fossil fuels is typically the result of a geological process of millions of years. Due to the length of time it takes for them to form, fossil fuels are considered non-renewable resources. In 2023, 77% of primary energy consumption in the world and over 60% of its electricity supply were from fossil fuels.

[2] Diatomaceous earth
Diatomaceous earth ( ), also known as diatomite ( ), celite, or kieselgur, is a naturally occurring, soft, siliceous sedimentary rock that can be crumbled into a fine white to off-white powder. It has a particle size ranging from more than 3 mm to less than 1 μm, but typically 10 to 200 μm. Depending on the granularity, this powder can have an abrasive feel, like that of pumice powder, and has a low density as a result of its high porosity. The typical chemical composition of oven-dried diatomaceous earth is 80–90% silica, with 2–4% alumina (attributed mostly to clay minerals), and 0.5–2% iron oxide.

[3] Biological wood oxidation
Advantages of biological wood oxidation: Another advantage of biological wood oxidation is that the final product is wood compost, which is the final product of wood composting. The wood compost creates a new possibility generating soil conditioner. It was reported that biological wood oxidation could retain about 70% of the CO2 absorbed by wood (through photosynthesis process) in the form of compost.

The next advantage of biological wood oxidation is that it is an environment-friendly technology and can reduce the environmental pressure caused by combustion of fossil fuels. Combustion of fossil fuels cause global warming (due to the emission of CO2) and air pollution (due to the emission of SO2 and NOx). With the rapid increase of worldwide energy demand, the generated heat from biological wood oxidation gains more and more interests, as it can be seen as a sustainable alternative to fossil fuels and one of the primary possibilities for preventing global warming

units.question: Compare Hyundai Motor Company and the Mercedes-Benz S-Class: when each began, and what each is best known for.
units.gold: Hyundai Motor Company is a South Korean carmaker based in Seoul, founded on 29 December 1967 by Chung Ju-yung. With Kia it forms a group that was the world's fourth-largest carmaker in 2009, and it was the fastest-growing automaker for two years running as of 2011. The Mercedes-Benz S-Class is a single flagship line of full-size luxury cars, named S-Class from 1972; it is known for introducing advanced safety technology, starting with anti-lock brakes on the first W116 generation (1972-1980), later airbags and stability control.

Hyundai-Kia 4th largest (2009); fastest growing
S-Class since 1972, Mercedes flagship luxury line
S-Class known for safety tech (ABS on W116, airbags, ESP)
Penalize: treating the S-Class as a company or Hyundai as Japanese
units.answer:

Hyundai Motor Company was founded in 1967, while Mercedes-Benz began in 1926. Hyundai is best known for its affordable, popular cars, while Mercedes-Benz is renowned for its luxury and prestigious S-Class sedan.
units.sources:
[1] Mercedes-Benz
The roots of the brand trace back to the 1901 Mercedes by Daimler-Motoren-Gesellschaft and the 1886 Benz Patent-Motorwagen and 1894 Benz Velo by Carl Benz, which is widely recognised as the first automobile powered by an internal combustion engine. The brand’s slogan is "The Best or Nothing".

[2] Wikivoyage: Surrey
Towns: Hundreds of classic motor cars at its museum (plus aviation, from Concorde to DeHavilland), Mercedes Benz World

[3] Blockchain
Cryptocurrencies > Supply chain: - Fashion industry — There is an opaque relationship between brands, distributors, and customers in the fashion industry, which prevents the sustainable and stable development of the fashion industry. - Motor vehicles — Mercedes-Benz and partner Icertis developed a blockchain prototype used to facilitate consistent documentation of contracts along the supply chain so that the ethical standards and contractual obligations required of its direct suppliers can be passed on to second tier suppliers and beyond. In another project, the company uses blockchain technology to track the emissions of climate-relevant gases and the amount of secondary material along the supply chain for its battery cell manufacturers.

[4] How can I bypass the most expensive drug in the world which goes on sale and get cured?
It affects motor neurons in the spinal cord. Unlike ALS, upper motor region in the brain is not affected. And unlike ALS, the cause of the disease is known. I began to feel the symptoms when I was three years old. I had weak muscle tone, weakness and atrophy developed, so I can not use voluntary muscles effectively, I needed to exert much efforts to do simple movements in the early stages of the disease.

[5] How can I bypass the most expensive drug in the world which goes on sale and get cured?
What reduced me to paralysis stems from deletion of codons from SMN1 gene located in 5th chromosome at 5q13 locus. Luckily another identical backup gene exists in the same chromosome called SMN2 but it unluckily has a single nucleotide transition from `C` to `T` in exon 7 region of SMN2, so it gives rise either to the loss of an SF2/ASF–dependent exonic splicing enhancer or to the creation of an hnRNP A/B–dependent exonic splicing silencer. As a result of that mutation, SMN protein can not include the "end parts" named `exon 7` so it produces short-lived not fully functional protein which is essential for motor neurons.

Clinical trials concentrated on splice modifiers to include exon 7 during pre-mRNA and mRNA process. Trials proved that it's feasible. Another treatment approach is gene therapy.

What do you propose in my situation?

EDIT: I rearranged the question according to request from moderator.

[6] What class of vehicle is commonly called "a Toyota" in Dudhu Chak/Eastern Pakistan?
Tags: transportation, driving, terminology, pakistan

Someone from Dudhu Chak (Pakistan) wrote this:

To get around the town mostly motorbikes are used. Cars and Toyotas are also used, but rarely.

What is "a Toyota" in this context?

I guess that in this area Toyota must be a synonym for a particular class of vehicle.

I have no idea as the Toyota company makes trucks, sedans, vans, cars, bikes, etc.

units.question: Under EIP-1559, how do the base fee, the priority tip cap and the overall fee cap interact when a transaction is mined?
units.gold: Each block has a base fee, the minimum per-gas price for a valid transaction; it moves with how full the previous block was and is burned, so the producer gets none of it. The priority fee is the tip to the block producer, and max priority fee is only a ceiling. Max fee per gas caps the total. Example: max fee 9, max priority 3, base fee 8 gives the producer only 1 and burns 8. All values are per unit of gas.
rubric: Explains the base fee is a protocol minimum that is burned
Explains the priority fee is the tip paid to the miner/validator, capped by max priority fee
Explains max fee per gas caps base plus tip, so the tip can be reduced
Gives or reproduces a correct worked example (e.g. 9/3/8 leads to tip 1, burn 8)
Penalize: saying the base fee goes to the miner
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
Under EIP-1559, the base fee is added to the priority fee to determine the overall fee, with the priority fee capped by the max priority fee per gas. The overall fee cap is the sum of the base fee and the priority fee, ensuring transactions are priced according to the fee market.
units.sources:
[1] Ethereum EIPs/ERCs: EIP-1559: Fee market change for ETH 1.0 chain
Specification: # priority fee is capped because the base fee is filled first priority_fee_per_gas = min(transaction.max_priority_fee_per_gas, transaction.max_fee_per_gas - block.base_fee_per_gas) # signer pays both the priority fee and the base fee effective_gas_price = priority_fee_per_gas + block.base_fee_per_gas

[2] Ethereum EIPs/ERCs: EIP-1559: Fee market change for ETH 1.0 chain
Security Considerations > Miners Mining Empty Blocks: It is possible that miners will mine empty blocks until such time as the base fee is very low and then proceed to mine half full blocks and revert to sorting transactions by the priority fee. While this attack is possible, it is not a particularly stable equilibrium as long as mining is decentralized. Any defector from this strategy will be more profitable than a miner participating in the attack for as long as the attack continues (even after the base fee reached 0). If an attacker had exactly 50% of hashing power, they would make no Ether from priority fee while defectors would make double the Ether from priority fees.

[3] Ethereum EIPs/ERCs: EIP-1559: Fee market change for ETH 1.0 chain
Security Considerations > Transaction Ordering: With most people not competing on priority fees and instead using a baseline fee to get included, transaction ordering now depends on individual client internal implementation details such as how they store the transactions in memory. It is recommended that transactions with the same priority fee be sorted by time the transaction was received to protect the network from spamming attacks where the attacker throws a bunch of transactions into the pending pool in order to ensure that at least one lands in a favorable position. Miners should still prefer higher gas premium transactions over those with a lower gas premium, purely from a selfish mining perspective.

[4] Bitcoin
Technical Details > Mining: The puzzle is determined by the transactions being sent at the time and the previous puzzle solution. This means the solution to one puzzle is always different from the puzzles before. Attempting to change an earlier transaction, maybe to fake bitcoins being sent or change the number of someone's bitcoins, requires solving that puzzle again, which takes a lot of work, and also requires solving each of the following puzzles, which takes even more work. This means a bitcoin cheater needs to outpace all the other bitcoin miners to change the bitcoin history. This makes the bitcoin blockchain very safe to use.

When miners mine a block of bitcoin, they receive a reward. This reward gets cut in half every 210,000 blocks, which occurs roughly once every 4 years. During Bitcoin's inception, the block reward was 50 BTC. It was halved to 25 BTC on November 28th, 2012, and to 12.5 BTC on July 9th, 2016. As of May 11th, 2020, the block reward has been 6.25 BTC.

[5] Advance-fee scam

-

units.question: I'm worried I'll lose my ENS name when it expires. How does renewal work under the permanent registrar?
units.gold: The original expiry date marked when ENS planned to deploy its permanent registrar, after which owners had to manually transfer names to it. The permanent registrar replaces the auction system with an annual fee, the same for all names, set around the price of DNS names (roughly 10 USD per year) to discourage squatting. You can pay for as many years in advance as you like to guard against price changes or forgetting to renew.
rubric: Mentions the move from auctions to a permanent registrar
States renewal is by paying an annual fee (around 10 USD a year)
States you can prepay multiple years in advance
Mentions a manual transfer to the new registrar was required
Penalize: claiming names go back to public auction automatically on expiry
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
Renewal under the permanent registrar ensures your ENS name remains active, but it's important to follow the correct procedures to avoid loss. The process typically involves submitting an application and paying the required fee. If you're unsure, consult the official registrar for specific instructions.
units.sources:
[1] Is it possible to renew my US passport in person at a renewal facility?
I'm afraid of losing my passport in the mail, but if that's the only option then I'll do it. I just wanted to hear from other people who have renewed their passports recently.

[2] Is it possible to renew my US passport in person at a renewal facility?
Answers > Answer (score 3, accepted): When I last renewed my passport, I did it in person. They did require that I show proof of imminent travel. Without it, I suspect that they would not have taken my application.

The previous renewal was by mail. If I recall correctly, I got the new passport in about 2 weeks, despite not having paid for expedited service.

Both experiences were perfectly satisfactory. The mail renewal was about 12 years ago, though, and the demand for passports had increased considerably since then, so even without COVID it's entirely possible that the processing times have increased. I would leave a couple of weeks extra for a mail renewal these days.

[3] What happens if my current residence permit expires before my application for a new one is processed?
Answers > Answer (score 2): My understanding is that you have an attestation de dépôt de demande de renouvellement de carte de séjour, i.e. an acknowledgement that you have made a request to renew your residence permit. Unfortunately, this document doesn't really help.

Cette attestation n'est pas un document provisoire de séjour. Il ne justifie pas de la régularité de votre séjour.

“This attestation is not a temporary residence permit. It cannot be used as evidence that you are in the country legally.”

If they take more than three months (not two) to process your application, you should get either an “attestation de prolongation de l'instruction de la demande” (attestation that the response to the application has been lengthened) or ideally an “attestation de décision favorable à la demande” (attestation that the application has been approved). For a renewal, both allow you to stay in France and work.

units.question: Walk me through recovering ether from an old eth-lightwallet keystore so I can use it in geth.
units.gold: Use Node.js with the eth-lightwallet package: upgrade the old serialized keystore (upgradeOldSerialized), deserialize it, derive the key from your password and export the private key for your address with exportPrivateKey. Then paste that key into a temporary text file and run geth account import on it, and delete the file immediately afterwards. Alternatively you can keep using the Lightwallet APIs to move the funds.
rubric: Mentions installing/using the eth-lightwallet npm package
Mentions upgrading and deserializing the keystore, then exportPrivateKey
Mentions importing the key into geth with 'geth account import'
Advises deleting the plaintext key file afterwards
Penalize: suggesting sharing the private key or keystore with a third-party website
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
To recover Ethereum from an old Eth-lightWallet keystore, you need to export the key file, import it into Geth, and ensure the wallet is active. Follow the steps in the Eth-lightWallet documentation to restore the wallet in Geth.

Account creation: ``` > clef newaccount --keystore <path> WARN [10-28|16:19:09.306] Please backup your key file path=/home/user/go-ethereum/data/keystore/UTC--2022-10-28T15-19-08.000825927Z--5e97870f263700f46aa00d967821199b9bc5a120 Geth documentation

[2] Understanding Ethereum network fees for tax purposes
So I got approximately $100 worth of value in exchange for 1 Ether, but I also paid approximately $1 (the 0.01 Ether) for my transaction to be processed by the blockchain.

Now, the following statements are simultaneously true:

1. I'm allowed to deduct any transaction fees from my proceeds
2. Making a payment with Ether tokens is considered a disposal of Ether tokens

Therefore, the network fee CANNOT be deducted from my proceeds, because it's offset by a disposal of Ether of the same amount, which happened at the exact same time.

The rationale would've been the same if I bought 1 Ether with 100 USDC and paid 0.01 Ether for the network fee, with the only change being that the fee couldn't have been added to the cost basis.

I think this is a bit like buying or selling gold to a broker and paying the brokerage fees directly in gold.

Is my rationale correct?

[3] Understanding Ethereum network fees for tax purposes
Answers > Answer (score 2, accepted): Assuming you're trying to work out CGT, I don't see how your two statements cause you a problem.

As you say, making a payment with Ether tokens is considered a disposal. Make up some value for the payment you made, i.e. the transaction fee. Call it x.

Now, you must have paid a certain amount for your 1.01 Ether. Let's say $80 to keep things fairly simple.

You've made $100 for selling 1.00 Ether, plus x for disposing of 0.01 Ether, and you can deduct x from the $100. Your cost basis was $80 so your gain is $20, no matter what x is.

A simpler way of thinking about is just that you bought 1.01 Ether, and sold 1.01 Ether for $100, the transaction happening to include a payment fee built in to it.

[4] Ethereum
Overview: Ether is a form of cryptocurrency, which means that it is decentralized, and also means that people can use it for payments without revealing who they are. Instead, people can use the Ethereum system by addresses (also called keys) which they can keep secret from others. The Ether coin can be transferred between accounts and used as a payment mechanism. The Ether coin is mined and used as compensation to miners for verifying transactions.

units.question: Which fields make up a raw Ethereum transaction, and what changed with the type-2 format?
units.gold: A legacy transaction is an RLP-encoded list of nonce, gas price, start gas (gas limit), to, value, data and the ECDSA signature values v, r and s; field names are not encoded. Any payload, including contract call data, goes in the data field. Since the London fork, EIP-1559 type-2 transactions encode chain_id, nonce, max_priority_fee_per_gas, max_fee_per_gas, gas_limit, destination, amount, data, access_list and the signature y-parity, r and s.
rubric: Lists the legacy fields: nonce, gasPrice, gas limit, to, value, data, v, r, s
States the fields are RLP-encoded in order
Says contract calls and payloads go in the data field
Describes the EIP-1559 type-2 payload with chain_id, max priority/max fee and access_list
Penalize: listing a 'from' field as part of the signed payload
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
A raw Ethereum transaction includes sender, recipient, value, gas price, and gas limit. The type-2 format introduced in Ethereum 2.0 adds support for proof of stake and sharding, enhancing transaction throughput and security.

[1] Is there a standard for the "transaction type"?
I'm asking because whenever I design my own system, I tend to eventually have to change it around a million times or even scrap it altogether when it eventually turns out (by sheer chance) that there is already a "standard" way of doing it which has had a million thought-hours put into it before I ever was born.

[2] Is there a standard for the "transaction type"?
Answers > Answer (score 4): When it comes to bookkeeping for your personal finances, there are no standards. You are free to use whatever system works for you.

You want to provide yourself with enough data to be able to look at your history and gain insight for making desired changes in your behavior, but you also want to keep it simple enough to ensure that it is not too much work to sustain using it.

For some people, the “type” field you describe would not be necessary. For example, if you watch a movie for entertainment, does it matter if you go to a movie theater (“service in real life”), buy a DVD (“physical object”), or stream it online (“service existing entirely electronically”)? units.question: My CREATE2 address prediction works when the constructor takes uints but breaks when it takes addresses. What am I doing wrong?
units.gold: The init code hash is built with abi.encodePacked on the constructor arguments. The constructor actually receives ABI-encoded arguments, where abi.encode pads each value to 32 bytes. A uint256 is already 32 bytes, so packed and padded encodings coincide, but an address is 20 bytes and loses its padding under encodePacked, producing a different hash. Use abi.encode for the constructor arguments when computing the predicted address.
rubric: Identifies abi.encodePacked as the cause
Explains abi.encode pads each argument to 32 bytes
Explains uint256 is unaffected because it is already 32 bytes while address is shorter
Recommends using abi.encode for the constructor arguments
Penalize: blaming the salt or the factory address
