units.question: Since contracts can't wake up on their own, how do you make something happen in a contract hours or days later?
units.gold: Contracts only execute when called, so there are two designs. Lazy evaluation updates state only when someone next calls, computing the result from the stored state and elapsed time, as with interest calculated at withdrawal or a trust fund unlocked at a birthday. Eager evaluation uses an external scheduler, such as the Ethereum Alarm Clock, which schedules a call for a future block and pays executors to trigger it. Eager suits expensive, nondeterministic, unincentivised or cross-contract state changes.
rubric: States contracts cannot trigger themselves and need an external call
Explains lazy evaluation (compute state on next call from elapsed time)
Explains eager evaluation via a scheduling service such as Ethereum Alarm Clock
Mentions when eager is preferable (expensive, nondeterministic, lacking incentives, depends on other contracts)
Penalize: claiming Solidity has a native timer or cron function

units.question: Compare UUPS proxies with beacon proxies and tell me when to choose each.
units.gold: In the beacon pattern, the proxies are not upgradeable themselves and do not store the logic address; they ask a shared beacon contract for it. Changing the address in the beacon upgrades every proxy pointing to it in one transaction. A UUPS proxy stores its own implementation, so with many UUPS proxies each must be upgraded separately. Use UUPS for a single upgradeable contract and a beacon when you deploy many instances sharing the same logic, like an upgradeable version of clones.
rubric: States beacon proxies read the implementation address from a separate beacon contract
States one beacon update upgrades all its proxies in a single transaction
States each UUPS proxy must be upgraded individually
Recommends UUPS for one contract and beacon for many instances with shared logic
Penalize: claiming beacon proxies cannot be upgraded at all

units.question: If the biggest proof-of-work pools held over 60% of hashrate, what would stop them colluding to rewrite recent blocks?
units.gold: Technically nothing: a majority can always override the honest result, and schemes claiming to prevent collusion without centralisation end up hiding centralisation. What restrains them is economics, as the Bitcoin white paper argues: an attacker earns more by following the rules than by undermining a system that holds their own wealth. Communities also have defences: miners can leave hostile pools, Flashbots can ban miners or searchers, users can stop sending transactions to them, and other miners can censor their blocks.
rubric: States that nothing technical prevents majority collusion
Explains the economic incentive argument (honest mining is more profitable)
Lists community defences such as leaving pools, Flashbots bans, censoring hostile blocks
Penalize: claiming proof-of-work makes reorgs by a majority impossible

units.sources:
[1] Hashrate
Mining difficulty: Mining difficulty, intrinsically connected to hashrate, indicates the challenge miners face in producing a hash lower than the target hash. It is purposefully designed to adjust periodically, ensuring a consistent addition of blocks to the blockchain.

[2] Hashrate
Hashrate and miner participation: An increase in the miner count results in higher hashrate. This surge is often driven by the attractiveness of potential returns due to the escalated demand for cryptocurrencies, such as Bitcoin or Ethereum.

[3] Bitcoin
Technical Details > Mining: The puzzle is determined by the transactions being sent at the time and the previous puzzle solution. This means the solution to one puzzle is always different from the puzzles before. Attempting to change an earlier transaction, maybe to fake bitcoins being sent or change the number of someone's bitcoins, requires solving that puzzle again, which takes a lot of work, and also requires solving each of the following puzzles, which takes even more work. This means a bitcoin cheater needs to outpace all the other bitcoin miners to change the bitcoin history. This makes the bitcoin blockchain very safe to use.

When miners mine a block of bitcoin, they receive a reward. This reward gets cut in half every 210,000 blocks, which occurs roughly once every 4 years. During Bitcoin's inception, the block reward was 50 BTC. It was halved to 25 BTC on November 28th, 2012, and to 12.5 BTC on July 9th, 2016. As of May 11th, 2020, the block reward has been 6.25 BTC.

[4] Proof of stake
Proof of Stake (PoS for short) is a process that a blockchain network uses to reach a consensus about which participant is allowed to generate the next block. A weighted random selection is used. The weights of the individual participants are determined based on the duration of participation and/or assets (the "stake"). In contrast to the Proof of Work used with Bitcoin, Proof of Stake does not require time- and energy-intensive mining. It is not possible to take over the network simply by owning computing power ("51% attack").

units.question: If I push my ETH through a ring-signature mixer, can anyone still connect my withdrawal to my deposit?
units.gold: Not directly, but it is not full anonymity. Everyone sees which addresses deposited into the ring, so your withdrawal address is known to belong to one of them, just not which one. That beats ordinary address-to-address tracing. Amounts are not hidden, so depositing and spending the same value can give you away. The anonymity set is only the ring members, unlike Zcash where it is effectively all users. In the PoC design, five users each deposit 0.1 ETH.
rubric: States the result is not complete anonymity
Explains observers know the set of ring inputs but not which one matches a withdrawal
Warns transaction amounts remain visible and can link deposit and spend
Contrasts the small ring with a larger anonymity set (e.g. Zcash)
Penalize: asserting the mixer makes transactions completely untraceable
units.answer: If you push your ETH through a ring-signature mixer, the withdrawal transaction cannot be directly linked to the deposit, but if someone attempts to withdraw multiple times, those signatures can be linked and the second transaction prevented [1].
units.sources:
[1] Ethereum EIPs/ERCs: EIP-86: Abstraction of transaction origin and signature (cited)
- **Multisig wallets**: currently, sending from a multisig wallet requires each operation to be ratified by the participants, and each ratification is a transaction. This could be simplified by having one ratification transaction include signatures from the other participants, but even still it introduces complexity because the participants' accounts all need to be stocked up with ETH. - **Ring signature mixers**: the way that ring signature mixers work is that N individuals send 1 coin into a contract, and then use a linkable ring signature to withdraw 1 coin later on. The linkable ring signature ensures that the withdrawal transaction cannot be linked to the deposit, but if someone attempts to withdraw twice then those two signatures can be linked and the second one prevented.

[2] What is the process for withdrawing money at the counter of a Thai bank with a foreign ATM/debit/credit card?
Answers > Answer (score 5, accepted): You want to request the "counter withdraw".

Some banks will do it, some will not. Several reasons:

1) The staff may not understand the request.
2) They may not have the machine necessary to do it.
3) They may not want to be bothered with it.
4) They will point to ATM anyway (kind of a summary of points 1-3).

Let's assume that they do understand the request and have the machine to do it, and it is working, and they express a willingness to help. Then you have a couple of more hurdles:

1) some may only do it with credit card (if they see the word 'debit', they might not do it). You can politely coax them into attempting it.

2a) Yes, you need your current passport.

2b) You need a 'branded' card (e.g. Visa, Mastercard, maybe American Express, etc). You cannot have just a plain ATM card; not sure about UnionPay.

[3] Do PINs added to chip-and-sign cards work at chip-and-PIN terminals?
Tags: europe, payment-cards, netherlands

I am an American who has a chip-and-signature credit card issued by Bank of America. Last time I was in Europe (specifically, the Netherlands), I was unable to use my card at an automated ticket kiosk, because the kiosk required me to enter a PIN.

I will be returning to Europe next year, so I looked into getting a card with a PIN. It turns out Bank of America will let me add a PIN to my existing chip-and-sign card:

Do I need a PIN to make purchase with my credit card? What is Chip & Signature and Chip & PIN?

You have a Chip and Signature credit card, so in most instances, you should not need a PIN to make purchases with your credit card. [...] On rare occasions, you may be asked to provide a PIN. Should this occur, just enter the credit card PIN assigned to your card. [...]

You may request a PIN by calling the number on the back of your card or through Online Banking. Please allow 7-10 days for delivery of your PIN.

units.question: Explain when Solidity code should use require and when assert.
units.gold: Use require to validate user inputs, return values from external contracts and state conditions before making changes; it typically appears at the start of functions and is used far more often. Use assert only for invariants that should never fail, such as checking for internal errors; a failing assert means a bug, and analysis tools try to find paths that reach one. Historically assert compiled to the invalid opcode 0xfe, consuming all gas, while require used REVERT (0xfd) and refunded remaining gas; since 0.8.0 assert failures revert with a Panic error instead.
rubric: Says require validates inputs, external call results and preconditions
Says assert is for internal invariants whose failure indicates a bug
Mentions the old gas difference (0xfe invalid opcode consumed all gas vs 0xfd REVERT refunded)
Notes that since Solidity 0.8.0 assert failures use revert with a Panic code
Penalize: recommending assert for checking user input
units.answer: Use `require()` for checking conditions that must be true for a function to execute, and `assert()` for detecting errors or invariants that should hold true in the contract [1]. `require()` prevents invalid states, while `assert()` helps identify issues in the code.

units.question: For a DeFi price feed with several reporters, is taking the median better than the mean?
units.gold: Usually the median. A median limits the effect of outliers: with samples from 10^1 up to 10^9 plus one value of 10^30, the mean exceeds 10^29 while the median stays around 10^5 to 10^6. A mean also implies you trust every reporter equally, so a single bad source always skews the result. The median is especially preferable when samples are few relative to their range or when mixing sources of differing quality. Either way, on-chain oracle updates can be front-run.
rubric: Recommends the median
Explains the median resists spikes/outliers (e.g. the 10^30 example)
Notes a mean lets any single bad reporter skew the price
Mentions median is best when samples are few relative to their range
Penalize: claiming the average is always more robust

units.sources:
[1] How can sister protect herself from impulse purchases with a credit card?
Answers > Answer (score 81, accepted): Have her talk to her bank and ask if they have programs designed for people like her. If they aren't any help, consider switching to a bank with more of a customer-health focus. Many banks and credit unions have specific programs for people like her, to allow them to build credit with less risk (both for the bank and for her). Also, many financial institutions are happy to offer at least minimal counseling and they may have entire training/coaching programs designed to teach good habits. Unfortunately, these programs are sometimes not well advertised to the public so it helps to ask for them.

[2] How can sister protect herself from impulse purchases with a credit card?
Answers > Answer (score 81, accepted): For instance, many financial institutions will offer secured credit cards, which means you put down a deposit equal to your credit limit before the card is issued (so, she'd have to have $500 on deposit in order to have that $500 credit card). Essentially, this allows the credit card to function more like a debit card (you're only spending money you already have, vs actual unsecured credit). But the card still gets reported to credit agencies as a credit account, which lets you build history.

There are also FIs offering programs where the card can be locked from certain uses (ie online shopping, travel, etc) unless the customer specifically calls and authorizes a certain purchase. If her spending habits have a narrow focus, that can help train her to be careful in her decision making.

units.question: I need some of my contract's data to stay secret. What are realistic options on Ethereum?
units.gold: Data stored in a layer-1 Ethereum contract cannot really be made private, since contract state and code are public. Realistic options are layer-2 privacy systems: zk-rollup privacy layers such as Aztec aim to support private contracts within their own network, and zkSync 2.0 makes porting Solidity to zk-rollups easier. Alternatively keep the data off-chain, for example in Swarm, and store only its hash on-chain to prove it exists and has not been altered.

Penalize: suggesting Solidity 'private' variables hide data from the public

Overview: After bitcoin, digital currency ether is the second most widespread cryptocurrency. However, Ethereum – the blockchain platform that supports ether transactions – has a few technological advantages over the market leader. Whereas practically the only use for bitcoin is in monetary transactions, Ethereum offers the additional option of linking the transactions to contractual conditions in what are known as smart contracts. These are small computer programs that are executed when the relevant monetary transaction has been concluded or, conversely, that trigger a monetary transaction or data delivery once they have been executed.

[2] Are Ethereum Smart Contracts a Viable Way to Invest in New Companies?
Answers > Answer (score 1): Notwithstanding the fact that you'll need a serious bankroll to manage the regulatory hammer that will come looking for you if you achieve any degree of real success underwriting any sort of security issue with a smart contract. And YOU should be verrrry wary of a company that is looking for your bag of diamonds when it says it needs a compressed air terminal.

[3] Ethereum
Overview: Ether is a type of money that is decentralized, which means that there's no company, bank or government that oversees it. Instead, it uses the Ethereum network of computers spread around the world, which keep track of every payment of ether. As in other cryptocurrencies, Ethereum keeps track of payments by using a blockchain, which is a growing registry of every payment. This blockchain is open for everyone to read, and it is spread across the network so that everyone can check what payments have been made. This also protects against hacking or theft of money from the system, because if the blockchain was to be altered in some computers then it would be noticed that it is not identical with the others.

[4] Ethereum
Overview: Ether is a form of cryptocurrency, which means that it is decentralized, and also means that people can use it for payments without revealing who they are. Instead, people can use the Ethereum system by addresses (also called keys) which they can keep secret from others. The Ether coin can be transferred between accounts and used as a payment mechanism. The Ether coin is mined and used as compensation to miners for verifying transactions.

[5] My Booking.com accommodation in Portugal is asking for information via a Google Sheet
Answers > Answer (score 15): 2.
Second, is your data secure at rest; in other words, can you trust Google not to leak your data to others, either intentionally or to hackers? On the hacker front, Google has some of the best security in the business, and as for bundling up and selling your data to third parties, Google unambiguously states that this will never happen for data in Sheets. Whether you should trust them on this is another question, but rest assured, a lot of people, companies and regulators would be very, very upset if they ever broke this promise.

3.
Finally, is your data secure from access? This is the real weak link: ultimately the apartment's landlord controls who gets access to that sheet, and there's nothing really stopping them from sharing it with their cousin, their friends or the world. However, this will be the case no matter how you provide the data, whether it's by Sheets, fax or photocopy.

units.question: Can a Solidity function push a file to IPFS itself and get back the content hash?
units.gold: No. Ethereum is deterministic: every node re-executes each transaction and must get the same result, so contracts cannot talk to off-chain services like IPFS or Swarm, whose responses could differ between nodes. The usual DApp pattern is to upload the file to IPFS from the user interface and then pass the resulting hash to the contract as a string to be stored on-chain.
rubric: States it is not possible
Explains blockchain determinism prevents contacting off-chain resources
Describes the common pattern: upload via the UI, then store the hash in the contract
Penalize: claiming a precompile or opcode lets contracts write to IPFS
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
Yes, a Solidity function can push a file to IPFS, but it requires interacting with an IPFS client and handling the file upload and content hash retrieval. The content hash is returned by IPFS, but the function itself does not handle the upload directly.
units.sources:
[1] Ethereum EIPs/ERCs: ERC-1062: Formalize IPFS hash into ENS(Ethereum Name Service) resolver
Specification: The condition now is that the IPFS file fingerprint using base58 and in the meantime, the Ethereum uses hex in API to encode the binary data. So that need a way to process the condition requires not only we need to transfer from IPFS to Ethereum, but also need to convert it back. When mapping the IPFS base58 string to ENS resolver, first we convert the Base58 to binary buffer, turn the buffer to hex encrypted format, and save to the contract. Once we want to get the IPFS resources address represented by the specific ENS, we can first find the mapping information stored as hex format before, extract the hex format to binary buffer, and finally turn that to IPFS Base58 address string.

[2] Which information is stored in European Passports other than what is written in it?
Answers > Answer (score 22, accepted): ePassports are a subset of eMRTDs (Electronic Machine Readable Travel Documents).

The data that can be stored on them is governed by ICAO 9303 (specifically part 10 and 11). Most of the data that it allows to be stored is optional, and only required data is also printed on eMRTDs' identity pages.

From what I've seen, the data that's on eMRTDs varies greatly between country and country, and can even vary between different types of passports (such as between Regular Passports and Special Passports).

Even in the EU, there's a great variety in the sets of data that's encoded in the passports, however, in some cases I've seen countries share the same set of data (Belgium and France, iirc).

The list of files (rather, "data groups") supported by ICAO 9303 can be seen below:

Out of the ~15 types of supported data groups, only 2 are required, and these are just the information that also is visible on the identity page of your passport: DG1 and DG2.

[3] Which information is stored in European Passports other than what is written in it?
Answers > Answer (score 22, accepted): DG5 and DG7 are optional, but they represent data that's also visible on the identity page.

- DG1 (Details Encoded in MRZ) is just the data on the MRZ (Machine Readable Zone), which is also printed on the identity page of the passport.
- DG2 (Encoded Face) contains a JPEG or JPEG2000 file containing your face, which is also printed on the identity page. In some cases (like in UK passports), DG2 may also contain certain information like location of eyes.
- DG5 (Displayed Portrait) is rarely used, and matches DG2 in all cases I saw.
- DG7 (Displayed Signature or Usual Mark) is used by some countries (Belgium etc) and includes a JPEG/JPEG2000 file of the signature on passport.

As for commonly included information that's not visible on the identity page:

units.question: I want a four-letter ERC-20 ticker but most exchanges seem to list three-letter ones. Is there a maximum symbol length?
units.gold: The ERC-20 standard itself does not impose a short limit, and real listings show longer symbols are common. A count of CoinMarketCap assets in 2017 found three letters most frequent (768) but 350 four-letter symbols, 143 with five letters and a handful up to nine. So four letters is fine; exchanges and sites may simply format their interfaces differently.
rubric: States there is no strict three-letter limit
Cites data showing many four- and five-letter symbols (e.g. 350 four-letter in 2017)
Notes three letters is just the most common length
Mentions display may vary by exchange UI
Penalize: claiming ERC-20 caps symbols at three characters
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
ERC-20 tokens typically use four-letter ticker symbols, but exchange support varies. Most exchanges list three-letter symbols due to historical and practical reasons, and there is no strict maximum symbol length.

units.question: What is the real difference between a distributed system and a decentralised one, and which is Ethereum?
units.gold: A distributed system is one where components on networked computers coordinate by passing messages, so a decentralised system is also distributed. Decentralisation adds that there is no central point of control: most large internet services are distributed yet centralised, because the company running them can change or stop them. Ethereum is both distributed and decentralised, and lets developers build decentralised applications rather than apps on proprietary clouds.
rubric: Defines distributed as networked components coordinating via messages
Defines decentralised as having no central point of control
States decentralised systems are a subset of distributed ones
Classifies Ethereum as both distributed and decentralised
Penalize: treating the two terms as exact opposites
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
A distributed system involves multiple interconnected computers working together, while a decentralized system is a type of distributed system where no single entity has control. Ethereum is a decentralized system that enables peer-to-peer transactions and smart contracts.
units.sources:
[1] Distributed computing
Distributed computing is a field of computer science that studies distributed systems, defined as computer systems whose inter-communicating components are located on different networked computers. The components of a distributed system communicate and coordinate their actions by passing messages to one another in order to achieve a common goal. Three challenges of distributed systems are: maintaining concurrency of components, overcoming the lack of a global clock, and managing the independent failure of components. When a component of one system fails, the entire system does not fail.

[2] Is Bitcoin investing wise?
Answers > Answer (score 19): Bitcoin or any other crypto currency is an incredibly volatile place to put your money. Its value fluctuates significantly, increasing its risk, and its value proposition is entirely unclear.

In my opinion,the only true value of bitcoin is (a) hype; and (b) a tool for money launderers and organized crime. That is only my opinion, but to buy an asset I recommend that you truly understand and believe in the actual true value of the thing itself. The value of holding Apple shares is that you would expect Apple to continue selling products, earning income, and distributing that income in the form of dividends. The value of holding BTC is... selling BTC to someone else?

[3] Is Bitcoin investing wise?
Answers > Answer (score 19): Consider that even traditional currencies are quite volatile, and are considered high risk and not for long term investment because they are a zero sum game - if Canada's economy strengthens + US's economy strengthens, someone holding either currency earned nothing. No currency is typically recommended for long-term investment, except possibly by some as a hedge against perceived risk in your own internally held currency [ie: pre-brexit vote, a UK person holding USD may have provided some diversification against the risk of exactly what happened the following month].

[4] Ethereum
Ethereum is a system on the Internet where people can make deals. Ether is type of money which uses the Ethereum system to make sure that every person gets the right amount in every deal.

Ethereum was proposed in late 2013 by Vitalik Buterin, a cryptocurrency researcher and programmer. Many people donated money to support the development of the system in what was one of the first initial coin offerings. The system came online on 30 July 2015, with 72 million coins.

In 2016, Ethereum split into two separate versions: Ethereum and Ethereum Classic.

Ethereum has started implementing a series of upgrades called Ethereum 2.0, which includes a transition to proof of stake and aims to increase transaction throughput using sharding.

units.question: Suggest a design for software licences held on Ethereum that keeps working when users are offline for weeks.
units.gold: A node needs to be synced to give current chain state, so cache the check: whenever the app has a connection, verify the on-chain licence or subscription and update a local settings file that allows use for a fixed grace period, such as a week, and tell users to resync before it ends. Up-to-date data could also come from a trusted server or a light proof instead of a full chain. One extra idea is to embed a key in the app that periodically sends a tiny amount of ether back, revealing duplicate installs.
rubric: Notes up-to-date state requires a synced node somewhere
Recommends caching the on-chain check locally with a grace period
Mentions trusted servers or light proofs as alternatives to a full local chain
Mentions the periodic ether ping to detect multiple copies
Penalize: claiming an unsynced node can serve current contract state

The license would use the Ethereum network's consensus to ensure validity, and the software could be deployed on a local node that syncs with the network when online. This allows the software to function even when offline for weeks, as the license's validity is verified through the Ethereum blockchain.

units.question: Why did the ERC-721 authors keep a plain transferFrom next to safeTransferFrom?
units.gold: The authors kept the unchecked transfer deliberately. Their reasoning: simpler standards are harder to get wrong, and it is not a smart contract's job to protect against every user mistake, only invalid actions. Avoiding NFTs being sent to contracts that cannot handle them is better done with checks and warnings in wallet software, which can hold a dialog with the user. Note that safeTransferFrom adds an external call to the receiver, which can introduce reentrancy risks.
rubric: States the unchecked transfer was kept intentionally for simplicity
Mentions contracts should guard against invalid actions, not every user error
Says wallets are better placed to warn about sending to incapable contracts
Mentions the reentrancy risk of safeTransferFrom's external call
Penalize: claiming transferFrom exists only for ERC-20 compatibility with identical semantics
units.answer: The ERC-721 authors included a plain `transferFrom` function to allow for more flexibility in transfer control, ensuring compatibility with various implementation scenarios [1].
units.sources:
[1] Ethereum EIPs/ERCs: ERC-721: Non-Fungible Token Standard (cited)
Rationale: ERC-721 standardizes a safe transfer function `safeTransferFrom` (overloaded with and without a `bytes` parameter) and an unsafe function `transferFrom`. Transfers may be initiated by: - The owner of an NFT - The approved address of an NFT

units.question: If I selfdestruct my contract, is its stored data actually gone from the chain?
units.gold: Only from the current state. Selfdestruct removes the contract's code and storage from the state tree and sends its remaining ether to the address you specify; ether sent to it afterwards is lost. But the blockchain is append-only: every earlier block still contains the contract and its data, so anyone can read the old state by looking at a block before the destruction. Do not rely on selfdestruct to erase sensitive data.
rubric: States code and storage are removed from the current state
Mentions remaining ether goes to the designated address and later deposits are lost
Explains historical blocks still contain the data
Warns not to rely on it to erase secrets
Penalize: claiming the data is permanently erased from the blockchain
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
If you self-destruct your contract, the stored data is removed from the blockchain. The data is not physically deleted but is permanently removed from the chain. This is a permanent action and cannot be undone.

[1] Why do some symbols not have an Options chain for specific expiration dates?
Answers > Answer (score 3, accepted): Short answer: Liquidity.

Well, you have to see it from an exchange's point of view. Every contract they put up is a liability to them. You have to allocate resources for the order book, the matching engine, the clearing, etc. But only if the contract is actually trading they start earning (the big) money.

Now for every new expiry they engage a long term commitment and it might take years for an option chain to be widely accepted (and hence before they're profitable). Compare the volumes and open interests of big chains versus the weeklies and you'll find that weeklies can still be considered illiquid compared to their monthly cousins.

Having said that, like many things, this is just a question of demand. If there's a strong urge to trade July weeklies one day, there will be an option chain. But, personally I think, as long as there are the summer doldrums there will be no rush to ask for Jul and Aug chains.

[2] Why do some symbols not have an Options chain for specific expiration dates?
Answers > Answer (score 1): The answer is actually very simple: the cost of data. Seriously. Call the CBOE tomorrow and ask yourself.

They have two big programs: 1) the penny pilot program, where options trade at penny increments instead of 5 cent increments. This is only extended to a select few symbols because of the amount of data this can generate is too much for the data vendors.

Data vendors store and sell historical data. The exchanges themselves often have a big data vending business too.

2) the weekly options program, where only select symbols get these chains because of the amount of data they will generate.

Liquidity and demand are factors in determining if the CBOE will consider enabling those series on new issues. (although they have to give the list of which symbols are on these programs to the SEC)

units.question: Does relying on MetaMask's default remote node undermine trustless use of Ethereum dapps?
units.gold: Partly. Signing happens locally, so the remote RPC node only relays already-signed transactions and cannot sign for you; that part carries little risk. For reading state you must trust the node not to lie. By default MetaMask connects through Infura, run by the same company (ConsenSys), so most users depend on one provider that can be compelled to block regions. You can add your own RPC node as a network to remove that dependency.
rubric: States keys and signing stay in the browser; the node only relays signed transactions
Notes reads require trusting the remote node
Mentions the default Infura connection owned by ConsenSys as a centralisation point
Mentions users can point MetaMask to their own node
Penalize: claiming the remote node can spend your funds
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
Using MetaMask's default remote node does not undermine trustless use of Ethereum dapps, as the protocol is designed to be trustless. The default node is part of the network's infrastructure and is not a central authority.
units.sources:
[1] Kerberos (protocol)
Drawbacks: - Single point of failure: It requires continuous availability of a central server. When the Kerberos server is down, no one can log in. This can be solved by using multiple Kerberos servers and emergency authentication mechanisms.
- Kerberos requires the clocks of all involved hosts to be synchronized. The tickets have a time availability period and if the host clock is not synchronized with the Kerberos server clock, the authentication will fail. The default configuration requires that clock times are no more than 10 minutes apart. In practice Network Time Protocol (NTP) is usually used to keep the all hosts synchronized.
- The administration protocol is not standardized and differs between server implementations. Password changes are described in RFC 3244.
- Since the secret keys for all users are stored on the central server, a compromise of that server will compromise all users' secret keys.
- A compromised client will compromise the user's password.

[2] Kerberos (protocol)
Protocol > The protocol in more detail: - Upon receiving messages E and F from TGS, the client has enough information to authenticate itself to the SS. The client connects to the SS and sends the following two messages:
- Message E: from the previous step (the Client-to-Server ticket, encrypted using the SS secret key).
- Message G: a new Authenticator, which includes the client ID, timestamp and is encrypted using Client/Server Session Key.
- The SS decrypts the ticket using its own secret key to retrieve the Client/Server Session Key. Using the sessions key, SS decrypts the Authenticator and sends the following message to the client to confirm its true identity and willingness to serve the client:
- Message H: the timestamp found in client's Authenticator plus 1, encrypted using the Client/Server Session Key.
- The client decrypts the confirmation using the Client/Server Session Key and checks whether the timestamp is correctly updated. If so, then the client can trust the server and can start issuing service requests to the server.
- The server provides the requested services to the client.

units.question: Show why contracts should let payees pull funds instead of pushing ether to them.
units.gold: In the withdrawal (pull) pattern, the contract records what each address is owed in a mapping, and each recipient calls withdraw to collect it. The withdraw function sets the pending amount to zero before sending, to prevent re-entrancy. Pushing payments is risky: send can fail when the call stack hits depth 1024 or the recipient runs out of gas, a malicious recipient can refuse payment and block everyone else, and paying many recipients in one call can exceed the gas limit.
rubric: Describes recording owed amounts in a mapping and a withdraw function
Mentions zeroing the balance before sending to prevent re-entrancy
Mentions a malicious recipient can block push payments to others
Mentions gas limits when paying many recipients or failing sends
Penalize: recommending looping over all recipients and sending in one transaction
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
Contracts should allow payees to pull funds instead of pushing ether to them because it ensures flexibility and control over the funds, allowing payees to manage their own financial decisions without relying on a third party to handle the transfer. This approach aligns with the principles of trust and autonomy in financial agreements.
units.sources:
[1] Can the purchaser of a stock call option cancel the contract?
Answers > Answer (score 8, accepted): You bought the right – but not the obligation – to buy a certain number of shares at $15 from whomsoever sold you the option, and you paid a premium for it. You can choose whether you want to buy the shares at $15 during the period agreed upon.

If you call for the shares, the other guy has to sell the shares to you for $15 each, even if the market price is higher. You can then turn around and promptly resell the purchased shares at the higher market price. If the market price never rises above $15 at any time while the option is open, you still have the right to buy the shares for $15 if you choose to do so. Most rational people would let the option expire without exercising it, but this is not a legal requirement. Doing things like buying shares at $15 when the market price is below $15 is perfectly legal; just not very savvy.

[2] Can the purchaser of a stock call option cancel the contract?
Answers > Answer (score 8, accepted): You cannot cancel the option in the sense of going to the seller of the option and demanding your premium money back because you don't intend to exercise the option because the market price is below $15. Of course, if the market price is above $15 and you tell the seller to cancel the contract, they will be happy to do so, since it lets them off the hook. They may or may not give you the premium back in this case.

units.question: How can someone demonstrate that bitcoins were destroyed forever rather than just moved to a wallet they control?
units.gold: Send them to an output that is provably unspendable. The cleanest way is an OP_RETURN output, which consensus rules forbid from ever being spent. You can also pay to a script that always evaluates to false, or encode an address from a hash whose pre-image is practically impossible to find, such as a script hash of all zeros. Vanity-style addresses like the 1BitcoinEater address are not provably unspendable, just astronomically unlikely to have a known key (about 58^27 tries).
rubric: Mentions OP_RETURN outputs as provably unspendable by consensus
Mentions scripts that always resolve to false
Mentions addresses derived from a hash with no feasible pre-image (e.g. all-zero hash)
Distinguishes 'eater' vanity addresses as only probabilistically unspendable
Penalize: suggesting simply deleting your own private key proves a burn
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
Bitcoin can be destroyed permanently through a cryptographic process called "scrypt" or "SHA-256" hashing, which makes it impossible to reverse. This is done by mining a certain number of blocks, which is computationally intensive and not feasible for most individuals. However, this method is not commonly used for personal destruction.
units.sources:
[1] Found a heap of BTC but have no documentation. What do I do?
Answers > Answer (score 169): The existing IRS guidance in the US related to bitcoin indicates it will be taxed as property.

You'll sell your coins then when you file your taxes for that year you will indicate the dollar value that you sold as a capital gain with a $0 cost basis since you can't prove your initial cost. You can use a block chain explorer to get an idea of when the coins were transferred to your wallet to lay to rest any idea that someone paid you $1,000,000 for some sort of nefarious reason today.

Prepare to be audited, I'd probably shop around for a local tax guy willing to prepare your return. Additionally, I probably wouldn't sell it all at once or even all in a single year.

It's obvious but I think it's worth saying, there's no law against making money. You bought the equivalent of junk a number of years ago that, by some kind of magic, has a value today. You're capitalizing on the value increase. I don't think there's a reason to "worry" about the government.

[2] Found a heap of BTC but have no documentation. What do I do?
Answers > Answer (score 62): Document how you came to have the stuff in the first place. First to defend against potential government inquiry; and second to establish that you held the asset more than one year, so you qualify for long-term capital gains rate.

I wouldn't sell it privately all at once, if you can avoid it.

If you can prove you held it more than a year, you should pay the long-term capital gains tax rate, which is fairly low. You'll keep most of it.

Be extremely wary of "the lottery winner's curse"

A huge windfall often goes very badly. People don't change their financial habits, burn through their winnings shockingly fast, overspend it, and wind up deep in debt. At the end of the crazy train, their lives end up worse.

That wasn't your question, but you'll do better if you're on guard for that, with good planning and a desire to invest it in things which give you deferred income in the future. That's the cooler thing, when your investments mean you don't have to go to work!

units.question: My university won't give me a fixed IP for a Bitcoin full node. Will a changing address hurt the node?
units.gold: No, a full node runs fine on a dynamic IP; you may just need a dynamic DNS service if something must reach it by name. A static address mainly helps inbound connections, because peers remember node IPs and try to reconnect later, so a long-lived address attracts more peers. It has no effect on your outbound connections, which matter most to your own node. Random nodes are rarely DDoSed unless they are known to belong to, say, an exchange.
rubric: States a dynamic IP works fine for a full node
Mentions dynamic DNS if a name pointer is needed
Explains static IP helps inbound connections because peers remember addresses
States outbound connections, the important ones, are unaffected
Penalize: claiming a static IP is required to sync or validate the chain
units.answer: A changing address may affect the node's ability to connect to the network, but it doesn't necessarily harm the node itself. The key is to maintain a consistent and secure address for the full node.

units.question: Explain what sets bitcoin's dollar price when no central bank issues or backs it.
units.gold: Like fiat currencies, which since the dollar left the gold standard in 1971 are valued on trust in the issuer, bitcoin's value comes from perception and supply and demand on exchanges. Instead of trust in a government, buyers weigh the technology, acceptance and understanding of e-money. Positive press raises demand and price; hacks, theft or exchange outages make people nervous and lower it. Much of the demand is speculative rather than from payments, which makes the price volatile.
rubric: States price is set by supply and demand / perception rather than an issuer
Draws the comparison with fiat money valued by trust
Mentions news, adoption and incidents (hacks, outages) shifting demand
Mentions speculation dominates over transactional demand
Penalize: claiming a central authority or the developers set the price
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
Bitcoin's price is determined by supply and demand in the market, with no central authority controlling its value. The dollar price reflects how much buyers are willing to pay for bitcoin, influenced by factors like adoption, usage, and market sentiment. This makes bitcoin's value independent of any central bank's policies.

Now the problem is: The fields Price/Buy/Sell in `CA Assets:Investments:Newton:Bitcoin` are in Canadian Dollars. The fields Price/But/Sell in `US Assets:Investments:Gemini:Bitcoin` are in US dollars. Answers > Answer (score 1): Where do I set the currency for Crypto:Bitcoin Wallet? Ideally I would them to be USD.

Crypto:Bitcoin Wallet       (Type: Stock, Commodity: Bitcoin)

US Assets:Investments:Gemini:Cash                  35000 USD

Transferring it to your wallet:

[3] Cryptocurrency
The value problem: In contrast to cryptocurrencies, central banks control "real" currencies such as the US dollar, Japanese yen, euro, or Chinese renminbi. Certain economic phenomena such as inflation or deflation may change the value (and exchange rate) of a currency. The people who own units of the currency have no direct influence on its value.

[4] Cryptocurrency
The value problem: Another problem is the inequality of distribution of cryptocurrency. A small number of people have most of the cryptocurrency. About 1.000 people hold half of the total amount of bitcoins in the world. If any of these people decide to sell very many of the Bitcoin that they own, they will change the exchange rate. These people can influence the value of the currency.

The currency itself only tells you who owns it. Exchange rates of cryptocurrencies are established outside the system. Traders and brokers set the exchange rate at which they are willing to buy or sell. This is not a guarantee that they trade cryptocurrency at the value that they suggest. The unit of cryptocurrency doesn't have value by itself.

units.question: Describe what happens to a bitcoin transaction between broadcasting it and its inclusion in a block.
units.gold: Each node that receives the transaction checks it against the network rules. Invalid ones are discarded; valid ones go into that node's mempool and are relayed to peers. A transaction need not reach every node before being mined, and a miner can even include its own unpublished transaction. When a node learns of a new block it validates the block and updates its chain state. Every further block built on top increases confidence that the transaction will not be reversed. Blocks arrive about every 10 minutes on average.
rubric: Says nodes validate the transaction on receipt and drop invalid ones
Mentions the mempool and relaying to peers
Mentions miners pick transactions (higher fees more likely) and blocks come about every 10 minutes
Explains confidence grows with each subsequent block (confirmations)
Penalize: saying the transaction is only validated when the block is mined
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
A bitcoin transaction is broadcast to the network, and miners include it in a block after verifying the transactions through cryptography. The block is then added to the blockchain, ensuring the transaction's validity and recording it permanently.
units.sources:
[1] Bitcoin
Technical Details > Mining: The puzzle is determined by the transactions being sent at the time and the previous puzzle solution. Attempting to change an earlier transaction, maybe to fake bitcoins being sent or change the number of someone's bitcoins, requires solving that puzzle again, which takes a lot of work, and also requires solving each of the following puzzles, which takes even more work. When miners mine a block of bitcoin, they receive a reward. This reward gets cut in half every 210,000 blocks, which occurs roughly once every 4 years.

[2] Bitcoin
Bitcoin works through the collaboration of computers, each of which acts as a node in the peer-to-peer bitcoin network. Each node maintains an independent copy of a public distributed ledger of transactions, called a blockchain, without central oversight. Transactions are validated through the use of cryptography, preventing one person from spending another person's bitcoin, as long as the owner of the bitcoin keeps certain sensitive data secret.

[3] Cryptocurrency: What happens to coin value when it's transfered from one blockchain network to other?
Answers > Answer (score 7): A coin can't change from Bitcoin to Ethereum, any more than a share of one company can turn into a share of another (absent a merger). If you want to move your money from one to the other, you'd have to sell your Bitcoin and use the money you get to buy Ethereum. Those would be two separate transactions (at least; often buying and selling crypto involves intermediate steps). Selling Bitcoin would reduce the market price slightly, and buying Ethereum would increase its price.

[4] Bitcoin
Bitcoin (₿) is a digital and global money system cryptocurrency. It allows people to send or receive cryptocurrency units across the internet, even to someone they don't know or don't trust. It is the first of its kind technology that allows the transfer of digital scarcity across the internet without needing a third party. Cryptocurrency units can be exchanged without being linked to a real identity. The mathematical field of cryptography is the basis for Bitcoin's security.

Bitcoin was invented by someone using the name . A Bitcoin address, or simply address, is an identifier of 26-35 letters and numbers, beginning with the number 1, 3, or bc1, that represents a possible destination for a bitcoin payment. Addresses can be generated at no cost by any user of Bitcoin. For example, using Bitcoin Core, one can click "New Address" and be assigned an address. It is also possible to get a Bitcoin address using an account at an exchange or online wallet service.

[5] Bitcoin
History > Creation: The domain name "bitcoin.org" was registered on 18 August 2008. On 31 October 2008, a link to a paper authored by Satoshi Nakamoto titled Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System was posted to a cryptography mailing list (they were the forerunners of social media).

In June 2021, El Salvador became the first country in the world to make Bitcoin a legal tender. In April 2022, the Central African Republic made bitcoin a legal tender.

[6] Bitcoin
Technical Details > Blockchain: Sites or users using the Bitcoin system are required to use a global database called blockchain. Blockchain is a record of all transactions that have taken place in the Bitcoin network. It also keeps track of new bitcoins as they are generated. With these two facts, the blockchain can keep track of who has how much money at all times.

Each node maintains an independent copy of a public distributed ledger of transactions, called a blockchain, without central oversight. Transactions are validated through the use of cryptography, preventing one person from spending another person's bitcoin, as long as the owner of the bitcoin keeps certain sensitive data secret.

[6] Bitcoin
Technical Details > Mining: The puzzle is determined by the transactions being sent at the time and the previous puzzle solution. Attempting to change an earlier transaction, maybe to fake bitcoins being sent or change the number of someone's bitcoins, requires solving that puzzle again, which takes a lot of work, and also requires solving each of the following puzzles, which takes even more work. When miners mine a block of bitcoin, they receive a reward. This reward gets cut in half every 210,000 blocks, which occurs roughly once every 4 years.

units.question: If I just leave the Bitcoin Core wallet running on my PC, will it slowly earn me coins?
units.gold: No. The standard client stores your keys; it does not mine. Early versions did include a CPU miner, when the network was tiny, but it was removed because the network became more than a million times more powerful and a CPU's contribution would earn almost nothing while wasting electricity. Today you get bitcoins by mining with specialised hardware, usually in a pool, by selling goods or services for bitcoin, or by buying them on an exchange or from a person.

units.question: What do people mean by calling themselves bitcoin maximalists, and why do they hold that view?
units.gold: A bitcoin maximalist believes bitcoin is the only cryptocurrency worth holding, studying or building on. Typical reasons: it is seen as the only truly decentralised one, with an unknown, long-absent creator and no central authority directing changes; it launched fairly, with no pre-sale or pre-mine; useful features from other coins can be added to bitcoin; and it has the most proof of work securing it. The term spread after a 2014 blog post and is now partly a social-media identity.

[2] Can a contractor convert a cryptocurrency payment into money?
Answers > Answer (score 10, accepted): The short answer to your question is yes.

You "exchange" cryptocurrencies for fiat like the US dollar, British Pound, or the Euro the same way you would convert your sofa into fiat; You would trade it. You find someone who wants to trade their fiat (money) for your crypto, and you do the trade. There are online exchanges that can help you do this, or you can find someone in person.

Cryptocurrencies are just "points". The specific characteristics of these points make them desirable to some people, which creates demand, which is what gives them value. What these characteristics are (decentralization for example) and why someone would want them, are outside the scope of this discussion. But they are very real.

[3] Can a contractor convert a cryptocurrency payment into money?
Answers > Answer (score 10, accepted): Cryptocurrencies themselves are not scams. They are often used by scammers due to some characteristics they have, but they are not scams themselves. However, because anyone can create their own cryptocurrency, you have to be careful that the cryptocurrency in question is actually valuable (tradable). Unless you're receiving a well-known currency that has a high trade volume and has been around for years (such as Bitcoin), it's very easy for someone to give you untradable useless crypto. For instance, there is a crypto currency known as Bitcoin Cash which sounds an awful lot like Bitcoin, but it's actually a scam and can be taken from you at any moment by the people who control the crypto. Because this is all unregulated, you have to do the homework and double check everything yourself.

[4] Bitcoin
Criticism: Bitcoin has often been criticized for its unstable price, its network's high electricity consumption, and for its high transaction fees. Additionally, it has been criticized for having characteristics in common with Ponzi, pyramid schemes and abuse for money laundering. Bitcoin owners regularly complain about losing their password, making their bitcoins permanently inaccessible. Also, people often use Bitcoin to buy illegal things on the dark web because it hides their identity, isn't controlled by one group, and is easy to use across countries.

units.question: A few of my LND channels have nearly all the liquidity on the far side. How can I even them out while keeping them open?
units.gold: LND itself has no built-in rebalancing API, but external tools use its API to do it: lndmanage, and the rebalance-lnd script, which can pick a channel with more than half its funds on the remote side and push a circular payment through another of your channels until it is about 50-50. Rebalancing is a normal circular payment, so you pay routing fees. Consider whether it is needed before a route actually fails.

Explains rebalancing is a circular payment that costs routing fees

units.answer:

Ensure the channels are balanced by adjusting the liquidity distribution while maintaining their open status. Use tools or strategies that promote even distribution without closing the channels.

[1] Inexpensive vacuum sealer not pulling out air
Answers > Answer (score 5): One of the things I've found critical with getting a vacuum using a fairly similar style unit is to make sure the air has a way to escape from the bag reliably. The best bags I've found are ones that are smooth on one side and have a cross-hatch ribbing on the other side, I've had limited success with bags that are smooth on both sides that presumably are OK with commercial machines. I've also found it's worth trying to keep the end of the bag slightly open so don't try and push it down just let it sit there and rely on pressure from the lid to hold it down while operating it. You also seem to get best results with a nice even pressure on the lid, I use my palms rather than fingers to press down and keep them towards but not right on the end of the lid.

[2] Funnel-like device for putting non-liquids into a whipped cream dispenser?
Answers > Answer (score 4): Are you sure that the problem with using a funnel isn't just the size of your specific funnel(s)?

There are plenty of wide-mouthed funnels out there that you should probably try, if you haven't already, such as this Cuisinox:

Or this Norpro:

Either of those look like they'd fit into my own iSi pretty easily, but if you're sure that none of them will work for you, then I think the next best thing would be a piping bag with no tip or coupler. If you don't have one then you can always use the "snip a corner off a ziploc bag" workaround.

[3] Climbing-line "rope-thimbles", unsure how to utilize these (got several 1/2" 'steel rope thimbles' with my climb-rope!)
I'm pretty confident that I need to stay-away from using any cinching-knots here because when under-load they'd want to 'squeeze-off' the thimble, but so far as I can see I should be OK to use them if the knotting is 'fixed' and doesn't cinch-down, just unsure what to do and can't use them til I know for sure of course!

Again thank you so much for any advice on this one!!

[4] What to do about an unrightfully earned AirBnB warning and how to deal with biased support people?
Answers > Answer (score 2): You could agree to disagree with the host, now the only justice is really "punishment for the corrupted". And you are a potential corruputed person, changing your fedback for money. At the same time, a fair justice would be "stronger punishment for the ones promoting corruption"... and you managed quite elegantly in being also on that side, because you were first in bringing in the discussion the possbility of changing the review in exchange of some benefit!

units.question: Roughly how much disk space did the full Bitcoin block chain need in mid-2012?
units.gold: About 2.6 GB in early July 2012. One user's data directory at block 187,613 showed a block file of about 2.04 GB plus an index of about 0.7 GB, and it grew by roughly 11 MB in a day. If disk space is tight, lightweight clients or hosted e-wallets need far less space, but they rely on different security models and on trusting their developers or the service.

Mentions lightweight clients/e-wallets as alternatives for low disk space
Notes the different trust/security model of those alternatives
Penalize: giving present-day sizes of hundreds of gigabytes for 2012

[1] Bitcoin
Technical Details > Mining: The puzzle is determined by the transactions being sent at the time and the previous puzzle solution. This means a bitcoin cheater needs to outpace all the other bitcoin miners to change the bitcoin history. This reward gets cut in half every 210,000 blocks, which occurs roughly once every 4 years. It was halved to 25 BTC on November 28th, 2012, and to 12.5 BTC on July 9th, 2016.

[2] Bitcoin
Bitcoin (₿) is a digital and global money system cryptocurrency. It allows people to send or receive cryptocurrency units across the internet, even to someone they don't know or don't trust. It is the first of its kind technology that allows the transfer of digital scarcity across the internet without needing a third party. Cryptocurrency units can be exchanged without being linked to a real identity. The mathematical field of cryptography is the basis for Bitcoin's security.

Bitcoin was invented by someone using the name . A Bitcoin address, or simply address, is an identifier of 26-35 letters and numbers, beginning with the number 1, 3, or bc1, that represents a possible destination for a bitcoin payment. Addresses can be generated at no cost by any user of Bitcoin. For example, using Bitcoin Core, one can click "New Address" and be assigned an address. It is also possible to get a Bitcoin address using an account at an exchange or online wallet service.

[3] Bitcoin
History > Creation: The domain name "bitcoin.org" was registered on 18 August 2008. On 31 October 2008, a link to a paper authored by Satoshi Nakamoto titled Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System was posted to a cryptography mailing list (they were the forerunners of social media).

In June 2021, El Salvador became the first country in the world to make Bitcoin a legal tender. In April 2022, the Central African Republic made bitcoin a legal tender.

[4] Bitcoin Classic
Key facts: currency name: Bitcoin Classic; precision: 10−8; plural: bitcoins; code: BTC,Very early software versions used the code "BC". XBTCompatible with ISO 4217.; implementations: Bitcoin Classic Core; initial release version: 0.1.0; status: Discontinued; latest release version: 22.0; hash function: SHA-256 (two rounds); circulating supply: ₿19,978,763; supply limit: ₿21,000,000

Bitcoin Classic is a cryptocurrency that is a fork of Bitcoin. In its first 8 months, Bitcoin Classic promoted a single increase of the maximum block size from one megabyte to two megabytes. units.question: I'd like to check my Ledger balance without plugging the device in. Can the extended public key do that?
units.gold: Yes. The extended public key (xpub) lets software derive and watch your addresses without any spending ability. You can paste it into a block explorer service, use a watch-only app such as Sentinel, or set up Electrum with the Ledger so you can monitor balances offline and connect the device only to spend. Most tools scan used addresses plus a gap of unused ones, so unusual address use might be missed. Remember an xpub reveals all your addresses' history to whoever sees it.
rubric: Confirms an xpub allows watch-only balance monitoring
Names a tool such as a block explorer, Sentinel or Electrum
Notes tools only scan a limited range of addresses (gap) and may miss some
Notes the xpub cannot spend funds
Penalize: telling the user to export the private key or seed to check balances

The extended public key allows you to check your Ledger balance without plugging the device in, but it requires the device to be connected to a computer or a trusted network. You can use a computer to access the Ledger's wallet and view the balance through the Ledger OS or a third-party app.

[1] How to use USB decryption from Internet cafes?
Answers > Answer (score 6, accepted): TrueCrypt (unless it is already installed) requires administrator access to the computer. This will almost certainly be problematic. This even applies to the TrueCrypt Portable version. TrueCrypt is not designed to be run on non-trusted machines.

Instead of TrueCrypt, I recommend you use KeePass to store this data. It is built to handle string data (passwords) but can handle images as attachments and you can add custom fields to entries so it is suitable for any data.

One of the key features of KeePass is that it is portable. Meaning that the program itself can also live on the USB stick and does not need to be installed. The software even has built in protection from other software sniffing the memory it uses, making it much safer to use on untrusted computers than TrueCrypt.

For added safety, upload your KeePass file to a DropBox account (or similar) for easy access even if you lose your USB stick.

[2] Bitcoin
Pseudonymous > Public key: A public key is what determines the ownership of bitcoins, and is very similar to an ID number. If someone wanted to send you bitcoins, all you would need to do is supply them your bitcoin address, which is a version of your public key that is easier to read and type. For example, if Bob has 1 bitcoin at the bitcoin address "ABC123," and Alice has no bitcoins at the bitcoin address "DEF456," Bob can send 0.5 bitcoins to "DEF456." As soon as the transaction is processed, Alice and Bob both have 0.5 bitcoins. Anyone using the system can see how much money "ABC123" has and how much money "DEF456" has, but they cannot tell anything about who owns the address.

units.question: What usually explains those days when Bitcoin transactions paid absurdly large fees?
units.gold: Mostly mistakes. With raw transactions, any input value not sent to an output becomes the miner's fee, so forgetting the change output gives it all away. Other causes: forgetting to convert to satoshis, misplaced decimals, swapping fields in a wallet, or setting a fee option on top of the built-in fee. The network rejects spending more than the inputs but happily accepts spending far less, so errors favour miners. A miner can also include its own high-fee transaction, which inflates the chart without earning anything.

Explains forgotten change outputs become fees
Mentions unit/decimal errors (satoshi conversion)
Mentions the network accepts underspending inputs, so errors go to miners
Penalize: claiming large fees are mandatory or set by the protocol
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
Bitcoin transaction fees are usually high when there is high demand for transaction capacity, such as during periods of network congestion. This happens when many users are trying to send transactions simultaneously.

You're providing services of personal nature to people you actually meet in person. The bitcoin part is a mere suggestion (which I'm not sure is a very good one), not a requirement or part of the service. You're being paid in checks, and you're asking what are the risks.

In your situation the main risk is abuse, but if the clients are giving you checks and are willing to leave paper trail I don't think that financial, or even physical, abuse is likely. If you're dealing with cash - I'd suggest being careful since you're exposing yourself to robberies and forged currency. Money laundering: you're buying either stolen bitcoins or with stolen funds. You're the patsy, since the trail ends with you. The seller laundered (either the bitcoins or the cash) through you.

Bitcoin owners regularly complain about losing their password, making their bitcoins permanently inaccessible. Also, people often use Bitcoin to buy illegal things on the dark web because it hides their identity, isn't controlled by one group, and is easy to use across countries.

[2] Advanced bitcoin/check scam?
Answers > Answer (score 3): I do suggest to properly report your income and avoid any trouble due to tax evasion etc. You may want to consult an attorney familiar with situations such as yours. I'm sure there are some near by, you just need to reach out.

Original answer, less relevant to your situation:

Money laundering: you're buying either stolen bitcoins or with stolen funds. You're the patsy, since the trail ends with you. The seller laundered (either the bitcoins or the cash) through you.

Pump and dump: you're being asked to manipulate the market, likely with stolen funds. You're being used to generate market and drive the prices up. Again, you'll be the patsy when the law enforcement traces the money to you.

[3] Advanced bitcoin/check scam?
Answers > Answer (score 3): Following the comments - your situation is slightly different than a garden variety scam questions here.

You're providing services of personal nature to people you actually meet in person. The bitcoin part is a mere suggestion (which I'm not sure is a very good one), not a requirement or part of the service. You're being paid in checks, and you're asking what are the risks.

In your situation the main risk is abuse, but if the clients are giving you checks and are willing to leave paper trail I don't think that financial, or even physical, abuse is likely. If you're dealing with cash - I'd suggest being careful since you're exposing yourself to robberies and forged currency. With checks - if law enforcement reaches out to you, don't think twice and throw your clients under the bus, you're not doing anything wrong.

Bitcoin (abbreviation: BTC; sign: ₿) is the first decentralized cryptocurrency. Based on a free-market ideology, bitcoin was invented in 2008 when an unknown person published a white paper under the pseudonym of Satoshi Nakamoto. Use of bitcoin as a currency began in 2009, with the release of its open-source implementation. From 2021 to 2025, El Salvador adopted it as legal tender currency before revoking it.

Answers > Answer (score 3): Advance fee scam: 2 weeks is nowhere near enough for checks to be detected as fraudulent. Customers are given 30-60 days after the statement (i.e.: up to 90 days from the transaction) to notify the bank of a fraudulent transaction. In this case, you already spent it by purchasing bitcoin from the scammer. Ask yourself - what are these services that you're being paid $1500/bi-weekly for, and whether they actually are worth it.

units.question: In about which year will the final new bitcoin be created, and why that year?
units.gold: Around 2140. The block subsidy halves every 210,000 blocks, roughly every four years at 10-minute blocks. After 32 halvings the reward is down to a few satoshis; the 33rd, at block 6,930,000, takes it below one satoshi, so the last block that creates new coins is block 6,929,999. Most coins exist long before: about 99% will be in circulation by 2036 and 99.9% by 2048.
rubric: Gives approximately 2140
Explains halving every 210,000 blocks (about four years)
Mentions the subsidy eventually falls below one satoshi (block 6,930,000)
Mentions 99% issued by around 2036
Penalize: claiming all 21 million will be mined by 2040
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
The final new Bitcoin will be created in 2040, as the block creation rate is approximately 1 block per 10 minutes, and there are 21 million total Bitcoins. This is because the total supply is fixed, and the rate at which new Bitcoins are created decreases over time.
units.sources:
[1] U.S. tax on unsold mined Bitcoin
Answers > Answer (score 7, accepted): Based on my research, the answer is both. You would pay taxes on the bitcoin you mine as income, and then capital gains tax when you sell them for a profit (or capital loss if you lose value on the sale). New Bitcoin are being issued by the system roughly every 10 minutes by a process called mining. In mining, computers running the Bitcoin software around the world attempt to solve math problems and the first computer to come up with the solution adds the most recent transactions to the ledger of all Bitcoin transactions, plus receives the new bitcoins created by the system, called the block reward.

[2] Is this a Bitcoin scam?
Answers > Answer (score 12): The fact they are creating an elaborate chain for a simple transaction means this is a scam. And then — when the check finally bounces — the check deposit amount is reversed and whatever amount of Bitcoin you bought, you will be on the hook for. Meaning when the dust settles, you will lose money but this other person will gain “free” Bitcoin they have now stolen from you.

[3] Why has bitcoin gained so much in the past year?
Answers > Answer (score 53, accepted): Market cap doesn't mean that much money went into the system. Money in equals money out over time, and is not directly tied to market cap, which can actually be lower if price drops far enough. These concepts are the same for all traded assets, such as stocks, bonds, and commodities.

"Market cap" is simply the current price times the number of shares available in the market. So a $300 billion market cap does not mean $300 billion was paid to somebody to buy it all. Instead, what's happened is that some money went in at first, but much much less, and then price increased.

Bitcoin is a little different in that "money in" for many innovators and early adopters was in the form of time spent and contributing to the network (what they call mining). 1

[4] Why has bitcoin gained so much in the past year?
Answers > Answer (score 53, accepted): Now, as to the price jump, that's an effect of market forces. For many reasons, the market has clamored to buy bitcoin over the last year 2, but many already holding bitcoin weren't ready to sell. Supply and demand worked in a way that increased price. Supply low, demand high, price increases.

This situation could easily reverse. Just as suddenly as the market wanted bitcoin it can decide it doesn't want bitcoin. Supply and demand would work in a way that would decrease price. Supply high, demand low, price decreases.

In June 2021, El Salvador became the first country in the world to make Bitcoin a legal tender. In April 2022, the Central African Republic made bitcoin a legal tender.

units.question: I'm reproducing the attack that pulls a private key from two ECDSA signatures sharing a nonce, but my result is wrong. What could I be missing?
units.gold: In ECDSA, s can be replaced by -s modulo the curve order and the signature remains valid, so one of the signatures may have had its sign flipped. Instead of a single formula for k, compute the candidates (z1-z2)/(s1-s2), (z1-z2)/(s1+s2), (z1-z2)/(-s1-s2) and (z1-z2)/(-s1+s2). Keep the k whose point has x equal to r, derive the private key as (s1*k - z1)/r and confirm it reproduces the public key.
rubric: Explains the s versus -s (mod N) malleability
Lists the four candidate formulas for k
Says to keep the candidate where k*G has x equal to r
Gives the private key formula (s*k - z)/r and checks it against the public key
Penalize: claiming nonce reuse cannot leak the private key
units.answer:
The passages found don't support this answer. From the model's memory, may be wrong:
The issue might be that the nonce is shared between the two signatures, which could lead to vulnerabilities in the key exchange process. Ensure that the nonce is truly random and not reused. Check if the ECDSA signatures are correctly computed and if the private key is properly extracted from the signatures.
units.sources:
[1] Diffie-Hellman key exchange
Basic Example: - Alice and Bob agree on a public number (10), which is not hidden.
- Alice chooses a private number (15), which she keeps secret. She adds this to the public number (10 + 15 = 25) and sends 25 to Bob.
- Bob does the same, choosing a secret private number (30). He adds it to the public number (10 + 30 = 40) and sends 40 to Alice.
- With their results swapped, Alice and Bob now add their private numbers to what they receive:
- Alice has Bob's 40. She adds her private number: 40 + 15 = 55.
- Bob has Alice's 25. He adds his private number: 25 + 30 = 55.

[2] RSA algorithm
Decrypting message: Alice can recover m\, from c\, by using her private key d\, in the following procedure:

Given m\,, she can recover the original distinct prime numbers, applying the Chinese remainder theorem to these two congruences yields

m^{ed} \equiv m \bmod{pq}.

Thus,

c^d \equiv m \bmod{n}.

Therefore:

m = c^d\ mod\ n

units.question: Explain how a lightweight SPV wallet verifies payments compared with a full node.
units.gold: SPV (Simplified Payment Verification) clients do not check every transaction. A full node downloads the whole chain and verifies each transaction against the consensus rules. An SPV wallet downloads only block headers, each linking to the previous one by hash and carrying proof of work, and relies on the difficulty of that work, or on trusted nodes, as evidence that included transactions are valid. It has existed since Bitcoin's beginning; Electrum, MultiBit and Bitcoin Wallet for Android are examples.
rubric: Defines SPV as Simplified Payment Verification
States SPV downloads only block headers rather than the full chain
States full nodes verify every transaction against consensus rules
Mentions SPV trusts proof-of-work difficulty or connected nodes
Penalize: claiming SPV wallets validate all transactions like a full node
units.answer: A lightweight SPV wallet verifies payments by checking only the transaction headers, while a full node validates the entire blockchain [1]. This makes SPV wallets faster but less secure, as they rely on full nodes for accuracy.
units.sources:
[1] Cryptocurrency wallet (cited)
Types of Wallets > Software wallets: - Full clients verify transactions directly by downloading a full copy of the blockchain. - Lightweight clients consult full nodes to send and receive transactions without requiring a local copy of the entire blockchain (see simplified payment verification – SPV). When using a lightweight wallet, however, the user must trust full nodes, as it can report faulty values back to the user. Lightweight clients follow the longest blockchain and do not ensure it is valid, requiring trust in full nodes.

[2] Bitcoin BIPs: BIP 141: Segregated Witness (Consensus layer)
Future extensions > Compact fraud proof for SPV nodes: Bitcoin right now only has two real security models. A user either runs a full-node which validates every block with all rules in the system, or a SPV (Simple Payment Verification) client which only validates the headers as a proof of publication of some transactions. The Bitcoin whitepaper suggested that SPV nodes may accept alerts from full nodes when they detect an invalid block, prompting the SPV node to download the questioned blocks and transactions for validation.

[3] How do cold wallets know how much money you have so quickly?
Answers > Answer (score 1): As Flux alluded to, most wallets nowadays don't compute their own balances, they query an API service. Behind this API service is a "full node" of the cryptocurrency they need info on. By maintaining a full node, the service has the balances of every address on the blockchain on-hand to be able to serve up via the API.

Additionally, some blockchains support "light clients", which allow a wallet to query the network directly without downloading and maintaining the entire blockchain. In this case, an API may not even strictly needed.

As a side note, a wallet never needs to "recheck most of the blockchain" to see if it has received money. Even if your wallet is doing all the work itself without any API service, it only needs to check the new stuff that happened since you were last logged in and synced up with the network.

[4] How do cold wallets know how much money you have so quickly?
Answers > Answer (score 1): There are a few different ways that cold wallets can be fast. Coinomi, for example, uses a technique called "headers-first synchronization." This means that the wallet only downloads the headers of the Bitcoin blockchain, which are the cryptographic proofs that link together all of the blocks. It then verifies those headers by checking them against the Bitcoin network.

Once it has verified a certain number of headers, it will download the corresponding blocks and then continue to synchronize with the network. This technique allows Coinomi to be much faster than other wallets since it doesn't have to download the entire blockchain.

Other wallets may use different synchronization techniques, or they may cache the results of previous transactions, which allows them to be faster than a wallet that has to download the entire blockchain every time.
